chapters.title: Flows, invariant sets and Lyapunov stability
chapters.summary: An autonomous equation generates a flow: a one-parameter group of maps that moves every state forward in time. Orbits, invariant sets and the ω-limit sets where trajectories end up are the vocabulary of the qualitative theory. Stability is defined by trajectories staying close, and Lyapunov’s method certifies it without solving anything, by exhibiting a function that decreases along solutions; LaSalle’s principle sharpens the conclusion and gradient systems are the cleanest example.

refs: Teschl, Ordinary Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems (AMS GSM 140)
Hirsch, Smale & Devaney, Differential Equations, Dynamical Systems, and an Introduction to Chaos

items.name: Flows and the group property
items.pic: Flow a picture of a cat forward by s and then by t, or by s + t in one go; the two images coincide, and flowing backward by t undoes the deformation.

items.name: Flow-box (straightening) theorem
items.pic: Near a non-equilibrium point, a curvilinear grid built from a transversal and the flow lines straightens the trajectories into parallel lines; at an equilibrium the construction visibly collapses.

items.name: Orbits and invariant sets
items.pic: Click points to draw their full orbits; select a region and the flow is applied to it, flagging it invariant when nothing leaks out and highlighting leaks when it does.

items.name: ω-limit and α-limit sets
items.pic: Integrate a trajectory for a long time and fade out its early part; what remains accumulates on its ω-limit set — a point, a cycle, or a cycle of saddle connections.

items.name: ω-limit sets of bounded orbits
items.pic: For trajectories confined to a box, the long-time tail is shown to settle on a nonempty, closed, connected, invariant set; an unbounded orbit escaping to infinity shows the ω-limit set can be empty.

items.name: Lyapunov and asymptotic stability
items.pic: Choose ε, then shrink a δ-disc of starting points until every trajectory from it stays within ε; a centre passes the test without attracting, a stable spiral passes and attracts.

items.name: Attracting but unstable equilibria
items.pic: In a planar flow built around a homoclinic loop, every trajectory eventually reaches the equilibrium, yet starting points arbitrarily close to it first make a large excursion — readouts show the attraction and the failure of stability together.

items.name: Lyapunov functions
items.pic: Draw the level sets of a candidate function V over a phase portrait; points are coloured by the sign of V̇ = ∇V·f, and V qualifies when V̇ ≤ 0 everywhere near the equilibrium.

items.name: Lyapunov’s stability theorem
items.pic: Trajectories launched inside a sublevel set of a strict Lyapunov function cut each level curve inward and spiral down to the equilibrium; plot V along each trajectory to see it decrease.

items.name: LaSalle’s invariance principle
items.pic: For a damped pendulum the energy is only weakly decreasing; the set where V̇ = 0 is highlighted, and trajectories pass through it but converge to its largest invariant subset, the rest point.

items.name: Chetaev’s instability theorem
items.pic: A wedge where a function W is positive and increasing along trajectories is shaded near a saddle; trajectories starting in it escape no matter how close to the equilibrium they begin.

items.name: Basins of attraction
items.pic: Colour each starting point of a bistable system by the attractor its trajectory reaches; the basin boundary is a separatrix through the saddle, and a parameter slider moves it.

items.name: Gradient systems
items.pic: Edit a landscape V by dragging hills and pits; the flow ẋ = −∇V crosses the contours at right angles and every trajectory slides down to a minimum or stops at a saddle.

items.name: Gradient systems have no periodic orbits
items.pic: Along any trajectory of a gradient flow V keeps decreasing, plotted in a strip below the phase portrait; a closed orbit would need V to return to its starting value, which never happens.

items.name: First integrals and conservative systems
items.pic: For a system with a conserved quantity E, trajectories are confined to level curves of E, drawn in the background; numerical solutions stay on their level curve as long as the step size is small.

items.name: Newton’s equation in one dimension and energy portraits
items.pic: Sketch a potential U(x); the phase portrait of ẍ = −U′(x) is built from the energy levels, with closed orbits in the wells and separatrices through the humps.

items.name: Liouville’s theorem: divergence controls phase volume
items.pic: Advect a patch of initial conditions; its area is tracked and compared with ∫div f along the way, staying constant for a divergence-free field and shrinking for a damped one.

items.name: The general problem of the stability of motion
items.pic: Lyapunov’s direct method: the reader picks a planar system (a damped pendulum, a nonlinear spiral) and sketches a candidate function V by shaping its level curves; trajectories are overlaid and the sign of V̇ = ∇V·f is painted, so a V with V̇ < 0 proves stability without solving anything and a failed V shows where trajectories leak out.

chapters.title: Laplace’s equation and harmonic functions
chapters.summary: Harmonic functions are the equilibria of diffusion. They equal their averages over spheres, so they obey a strong maximum principle, are infinitely smooth, satisfy Harnack’s inequality and, when bounded on all of space, are constant. The Dirichlet problem is solved explicitly on rectangles by separation, on discs by Poisson’s formula, and in general through Green’s identities and Green’s functions, constructed for half-spaces and balls by the method of images.

refs: Strauss, Partial Differential Equations: An Introduction

items.name: Harmonic functions; the Laplacian in polar coordinates
items.pic: Type a function of (r, θ); its Laplacian is computed in polar form and in Cartesian form on a grid, and both vanish exactly for rⁿcos nθ and log r.

items.name: Fundamental solution of the Laplacian
items.pic: The radial solutions log|x| (2D) and 1/|x| (3D) are plotted; the flux of their gradient through spheres of any radius is the same constant, read out, revealing the point source.

items.name: Mean-value property
items.pic: Drag a ball inside a domain where u is harmonic; the averages over the sphere and over the solid ball are computed and both match u at the centre.

items.name: Strong maximum principle
items.pic: On a connected domain, an interior maximum forces the harmonic function to be constant; try to sculpt a harmonic bump with an interior peak and the solver flattens it.

items.name: Uniqueness and stability of the Dirichlet problem
items.pic: Perturb the boundary data by at most ε; the interior solution moves by at most ε everywhere, with the maximum deviation read out and compared with ε.

items.name: Separation of variables in rectangles and cubes
items.pic: Prescribe temperatures on one side of a rectangle; the solution is a series of sin(nπx)sinh(nπy) terms whose partial sums converge, with high modes decaying quickly away from the heated edge.

items.name: Poisson’s formula for the disc
items.pic: Draw boundary values on a circle; the Poisson kernel for a draggable interior point is plotted as weights on the boundary, sharpening into a spike as the point nears the edge.

items.name: Wedges, annuli and exteriors
items.pic: Solve Laplace’s equation in a wedge of adjustable angle; the leading term r^{π/α}sin(πθ/α) is shown, and at re-entrant corners its gradient blows up at the tip.

items.name: Harmonic functions are smooth (and analytic)
items.pic: Mollify a harmonic function with radial bumps of decreasing radius; the result is identical to the original, demonstrating that averaging changes nothing and so u inherits the bump’s smoothness.

items.name: Liouville’s theorem for harmonic functions
items.pic: Compare u at two points by averaging over huge balls centred at each; for a bounded harmonic function the non-overlapping parts become negligible, and the difference readout tends to zero.

items.name: Harnack’s inequality
items.pic: For positive harmonic functions on a disc, the ratio max/min on a smaller concentric disc stays below a constant depending only on the radii, shown against random examples.

items.name: Green’s identities and the representation formula
items.pic: For a harmonic u in a disc, its value at an interior point is computed from boundary values and normal derivatives by the representation formula and matched against the true value.

items.name: Green’s function of a domain
items.pic: Click a source point inside a square; the Green’s function is computed numerically, vanishing on the boundary and symmetric when the source and observation points are swapped.

items.name: Method of images: half-space and ball
items.pic: Drag a source near a plane or sphere; the image charge (reflected, or inverted with scaled strength) is drawn, and the combined potential vanishes on the boundary exactly.

items.name: Dirichlet’s principle
items.pic: Among surfaces with fixed boundary values, the energy ∫|∇w|² is read out as you sculpt; it is minimal exactly for the harmonic interpolant, and gradient descent on it converges there.

items.name: Compatibility condition for the Neumann problem
items.pic: Prescribe heat flux through the boundary of a plate; the steady state exists only when the net flux is zero (readout), otherwise the simulated temperature drifts forever.

chapters.title: Line integrals and conservative fields
chapters.summary: Integrating a vector field along a curve measures work or circulation. When the field is a gradient, the fundamental theorem for line integrals makes the answer depend only on the endpoints, so loop integrals vanish. Conservative fields are exactly the path-independent ones; on simply connected domains they are detected by zero curl, and the vortex field around a puncture is the famous warning about holes.

refs: Schey, Div, Grad, Curl, and All That

items.name: Path integral of a scalar function
items.pic: A fence built along a curve with height f: its area is the scalar path integral, independent of how fast the curve is traversed, as a reparametrization slider shows.

items.name: Line integral of a vector field (work)
items.pic: Drag the waypoints of a path through a force field; small tangent segments are coloured by F·dr and their running sum is the work, which flips sign when the path is reversed.

items.name: Fundamental theorem for line integrals
items.pic: Wiggle a path between two fixed endpoints in a gradient field: the work stays exactly f(B) − f(A), while the same experiment in a rotational field changes it.

items.name: Conservative (path-independent) fields
items.pic: Draw two different paths between the same points; the readout compares their work integrals and the loop formed by them, flagging the field conservative when the loop integral is zero for every drawn loop.

items.name: Path independence ⇔ zero loop integrals ⇔ gradient
items.pic: Build a potential by integrating from a base point along random paths; for a conservative field every path gives the same value and the reconstructed potential is smooth, otherwise it is multi-valued.

items.name: Curl-free on a simply connected domain ⇒ conservative
items.pic: On a disc, any curl-free field you design integrates to zero around every drawn loop; punch a hole in the domain and loops around it start to collect circulation.

items.name: The vortex field: curl-free but not conservative
items.pic: For (−y, x)/(x²+y²), drag a loop around: the circulation is 2π times the number of times it winds around the origin and 0 for loops that avoid it, though the curl vanishes everywhere it is defined.

items.name: Circulation and flux across a planar curve
items.pic: For a closed curve in a planar flow, tangential arrows (circulation) and normal arrows (flux) are drawn separately along it with running totals.

items.name: Conservation of energy for gradient forces
items.pic: Roll a particle through a potential landscape; kinetic plus potential energy stays flat in the plot, until a non-conservative swirl force is mixed in and the total drifts.

items.name: Path-dependent work: heat is not a state function
items.pic: Take a gas around different paths on a pressure–volume diagram between the same two states; the work ∫p dV (a line integral) differs from path to path, and a closed cycle encloses net work equal to its area.

chapters.title: Algebraic Coding Theory
chapters.summary: To send bits across a noisy channel, messages are padded with redundant check bits so that errors can be detected or corrected, and the Hamming distance between codewords measures how many errors a code survives. Codes that are subgroups of $\mathbb Z_2^n$ — null spaces of parity-check matrices — are especially tractable: their minimum distance is a minimum weight, their power to detect and correct single errors can be read off the columns of the matrix, and they are decoded with syndromes and coset leaders.

items.name: Even-parity check bit
items.pic: Type a 7-bit ASCII character: an eighth bit makes the number of 1s even, flipping any one bit by clicking rings the parity alarm, and flipping two slips through.

items.name: Triple-repetition code
items.pic: Each bit is sent three times through a channel with a flip-probability slider; majority voting fixes single flips, and the decoded error rate is plotted against the raw one.

items.name: Maximum-likelihood decoding
items.pic: A received word is compared with every codeword and decoded to the nearest one in Hamming distance, with ties shown in amber.

items.name: Binary symmetric channel
items.pic: Bits stream through a channel drawn as two crossing arrows taken with probability p; a slider sets p and a counter tallies the flipped bits.

items.name: Probability of exactly k errors
items.pic: Send thousands of n-bit words through the channel and histogram the number of flipped bits; the bars settle onto the binomial probabilities as the run grows.

items.name: Block codes and codewords
items.pic: An (n, m)-block code as a lookup table from m-bit messages to n-bit codewords, messages and codewords drawn as rows of lights.

items.name: Hamming distance, weight and minimum distance
items.pic: Click two binary words to highlight and count the positions where they differ; a matrix of all pairwise distances in a code marks the minimum.

items.name: Hamming distance is a metric
items.pic: Three binary words sit at the corners of a triangle labelled with their distances; editing bits never breaks d(x, z) ≤ d(x, y) + d(y, z).

items.name: Minimum distance 2n + 1 corrects n errors
items.pic: Codewords are centres of Hamming balls of radius n on the cube of words; with minimum distance 2n + 1 the balls are disjoint, so any word with at most n flips decodes to the right centre.

items.name: Group code
items.pic: XOR two codewords of a candidate code by clicking them; the code is a group code when every such sum is again in the code.

items.name: w(x + y) = d(x, y)
items.pic: XOR two words bit by bit: the 1s of the sum line up exactly with the positions where the words differ.

items.name: The minimum distance of a group code is its minimum weight
items.pic: For a group code the full distance table and the list of codeword weights are shown side by side; the minima agree, found with n instead of n² comparisons.

items.name: Null space of a binary matrix
items.pic: Edit a binary matrix H by clicking cells; the words x with Hx = 0, computed mod 2, are listed live.

items.name: The null space of H is a group code
items.pic: Add two words from the null space of an editable H: the sum is checked to satisfy H(x + y) = 0 as well.

items.name: Linear code
items.pic: Choose k basis words: all 2ᵏ of their XOR combinations appear as the codewords of the linear code they span.

items.name: Canonical parity-check and standard generator matrices
items.pic: Edit the block A in H = (A | I) and the matching generator G (I stacked on A) updates; messages fed through G become codewords whose final bits are checks.

items.name: Codewords of a canonical parity-check code
items.pic: Type the information bits of a word freely; the check bits are then forced, filling in as each row equation of H is solved.

items.name: A standard generator matrix gives an (n, k) group code
items.pic: All k-bit messages are fed through G; the 2ᵏ outputs are distinct and closed under XOR, verified in a table.

items.name: HG = 0
items.pic: Multiply the editable H and G mod 2: the product grid stays all zeros for every choice of the block A.

items.name: The code generated by G is the null space of H
items.pic: Codewords produced by G and solutions of Hx = 0 are computed independently and merge into a single list, whatever block A is chosen.

items.name: Heᵢ is the ith column of H
items.pic: Flip bit i of the zero word and the product Heᵢ lights up as column i of H.

items.name: Single-error detection iff H has no zero column
items.pic: Zero out a column of H: a single flip in that position now passes undetected, and the blind bit is flagged.

items.name: Single-error correction iff columns are nonzero and distinct
items.pic: Make two columns of H equal: two different single-bit errors then give the same syndrome, and the decoder cannot tell which bit to fix.

items.name: Syndrome
items.pic: Received words are run through H and their syndromes appear as short binary tags beside them.

items.name: The syndrome depends only on the error
items.pic: Add different codewords to the same error pattern: every received word carries the same syndrome tag.

items.name: Decoding a single error by matching a column
items.pic: Flip one bit of a transmitted codeword; its syndrome is matched to a column of H, that bit is flipped back, and the message is recovered.

items.name: Coset decoding and coset leaders
items.pic: All 2ⁿ words are arranged in a standard array, one coset of the code per row with its lightest word as leader; a received word is decoded by subtracting its row’s leader.

items.name: Same coset iff same syndrome
items.pic: Colour every word once by its syndrome and once by its coset of the code: the two colourings coincide, so a short syndrome table replaces the whole array.

chapters.title: The group algebra, Fourier analysis and integrality
chapters.summary: Functions on a finite group form an algebra under convolution, and the irreducible representations diagonalize it: the group algebra is a direct sum of matrix algebras. This is Fourier analysis on a finite group, with inversion and Plancherel formulas that reduce to the discrete Fourier transform for cyclic groups and that bound how fast random walks mix. The centre of the group algebra yields arithmetic: character values are algebraic integers, degrees divide the group order, and Burnside’s pᵃqᵇ theorem follows.

refs: Serre, Linear Representations of Finite Groups

items.name: The group algebra ℂ[G]
items.pic: Elements of ℂ[G] are formal combinations of group elements drawn as weights on a Cayley graph; multiplying two of them spreads weight along the graph, and a representation is the same as a module.

items.name: Convolution on a finite group
items.pic: Convolve two functions on S₃ or ℤ/n; the result is computed term by term and shown to equal the product in the group algebra, non-commutative for S₃.

items.name: Discrete Fourier transform on ℤ/n
items.pic: Bars of a signal on ℤ/n and its Fourier coefficients: shift the signal and only phases change, convolve two signals and the coefficients multiply.

items.name: Circulant matrices are diagonalized by the DFT
items.pic: Edit the first row of a circulant matrix; its eigenvalues, computed numerically, coincide with the DFT of that row, and the eigenvectors are the Fourier modes.

items.name: The dual group of a finite abelian group
items.pic: Characters of ℤ/m × ℤ/n multiply pointwise into a group isomorphic to the original; the isomorphism (non-canonical) and the canonical double-dual map are drawn.

items.name: Wedderburn decomposition ℂ[G] ≅ ⊕ End(Vᵢ)
items.pic: For S₃ the six-dimensional group algebra is mapped to ℂ ⊕ ℂ ⊕ M₂(ℂ); multiplying elements on either side gives matching answers, shown as block matrices.

items.name: Fourier transform on a finite group
items.pic: A function on S₃ is transformed into one matrix per irreducible representation (two numbers and a 2×2 matrix), and convolution becomes matrix multiplication.

items.name: Fourier inversion and Plancherel for finite groups
items.pic: Transform a random function on a group and invert: the original returns exactly, and the energy Σ|f(g)|² matches the dimension-weighted sum of squared matrix norms.

items.name: Random walks on finite groups converge to uniform
items.pic: Shuffle a small deck by random transpositions and track the distance to uniform; the Fourier bound computed from the non-trivial irreducibles is plotted above the true distance.

items.name: The centre of ℂ[G] and central characters
items.pic: Class sums commute with everything and span the centre; each acts on an irreducible as the scalar |C|χ(g)/χ(1), computed and compared for every class.

items.name: Character values are algebraic integers
items.pic: Character values are sums of roots of unity, plotted in the complex plane; their minimal polynomials are computed and have integer coefficients.

items.name: Degrees of irreducibles divide the group order
items.pic: For each group in a menu, the irreducible degrees are listed against |G|; the quotients are integers, and the algebraic-integer argument is traced for one case.

items.name: Burnside’s pᵃqᵇ theorem
items.pic: For a group of order pᵃqᵇ, a conjugacy class of prime-power size is found and a character value forced to vanish, producing a normal subgroup; the induction is shown on a group of order 72.

items.name: Normal subgroups from the character table
items.pic: Click rows of a character table: the elements where the selected characters equal their degrees form a normal subgroup, which lights up in a picture of the group.

chapters.title: Countability and separation axioms
chapters.summary: Countability axioms say a space can be probed with countably many open sets; separation axioms say open sets can pull points and closed sets apart. Metric spaces enjoy all of these, which makes them necessary conditions for metrizability. The Sorgenfrey line and plane, and the uncountable ordinal space, show how the axioms come apart from one another.

items.name: First- and second-countable spaces
items.pic: Rational discs form a countable basis for the plane: pick any open set and a point inside it, and a rational disc squeezed between them is found automatically.

items.name: In first-countable spaces sequences suffice
items.pic: A countable shrinking neighbourhood base at a closure point yields a sequence converging to it, built one neighbourhood at a time; in the co-countable line the construction has nothing to work with.

items.name: Separable and Lindelöf spaces
items.pic: The rationals sprinkled in the plane meet every open set you draw (separable); an arbitrary open cover of the plane is thinned to a countable subcover (Lindelöf).

items.name: Second-countable spaces are separable and Lindelöf
items.pic: From a countable basis, one point is picked in each basic set (giving a dense set) and one cover element per basic set (giving a countable subcover), both shown growing.

items.name: For metric spaces: second countable ⇔ separable ⇔ Lindelöf
items.pic: From a countable dense set, balls of rational radius are generated and checked to form a basis; an uncountable discrete metric space shows all three properties failing together.

items.name: The Sorgenfrey line is separable but not second countable
items.pic: Each point x needs its own basic set beginning at x, so a basis must contain uncountably many sets; meanwhile the rationals still meet every half-open interval.

items.name: Separation axioms: T₁, Hausdorff, regular, normal
items.pic: For each axiom a challenge: separate a point from a point, a point from a closed set, or two closed sets by open sets; spaces failing a challenge display the obstructing configuration.

items.name: Separation axioms in subspaces and products
items.pic: Products and subspaces of Hausdorff or regular spaces stay so, verified on examples, while the Sorgenfrey line (normal) produces the non-normal Sorgenfrey plane.

items.name: Metrizable spaces are normal
items.pic: Two disjoint closed sets drawn in the plane; the function d(x,A)/(d(x,A) + d(x,B)) colours the plane and its level sets 1/3 and 2/3 bound separating open sets.

items.name: Compact Hausdorff spaces are normal
items.pic: Separate a point from a compact set by finitely many neighbourhood pairs, then two compact sets by repeating the trick; the open sets produced are drawn and verified disjoint.

items.name: Regular second-countable spaces are normal
items.pic: Countably many basic sets cover each closed set; the staircase construction trims them alternately so the two unions become disjoint, with each trimming step animated.

items.name: The Sorgenfrey plane is regular but not normal
items.pic: The antidiagonal x + y = 1 is closed and discrete in the Sorgenfrey plane: its rational and irrational points form disjoint closed sets, and a counting argument shows no open sets separate them.

items.name: The ordinal space [0, ω₁) is sequentially compact, not compact
items.pic: Every sequence of countable ordinals has a countable supremum below ω₁, shown by stacking ordinal bars; the cover by initial segments [0, α) has no finite subcover.

items.name: The long line
items.pic: Glue ω₁ copies of [0,1) end to end: a zoomable ruler shows every point has an interval-like neighbourhood, yet no sequence climbs to the top, so the space is not second countable and not metrizable.

items.name: ℝ^ω is metrizable, ℝ^J for uncountable J is not
items.pic: A metric weighting coordinate n by 1/n reproduces the product topology on ℝ^ω; on ℝ^J for uncountable J the sequence lemma fails, and a closure point unreachable by sequences is exhibited.

chapters.title: The first fundamental form
chapters.summary: The first fundamental form is the inner product on tangent planes, written in a patch as E, F, G. It measures lengths, angles and areas without leaving the surface, so maps that preserve it — isometries — preserve all intrinsic geometry. Conformal maps preserve angles only and equiareal maps only areas, which is the whole story of map projections.

refs: do Carmo, Differential Geometry of Curves and Surfaces

items.name: First fundamental form
items.pic: Draw tiny circles in the parameter plane; their images on the surface are tiny ellipses (Tissot’s indicatrix) whose shapes are governed by E, F and G, read out at the cursor.

items.name: Lengths and angles of curves on a surface
items.pic: Draw a curve in the parameter domain; its length on the surface is computed from E, F, G and checked against a polyline measured in space.

items.name: Area of a region on a surface
items.pic: Paint a region on a surface; its area is computed by integrating √(EG − F²) over the parameter region and compared with a fine triangulation of the painted patch.

items.name: Isometries and local isometries
items.pic: Roll a flat sheet into a cylinder or cone: a triangle drawn on the sheet keeps its side lengths, verified by readouts before and after rolling.

items.name: The catenoid and helicoid are locally isometric
items.pic: Morph the catenoid into the helicoid through the associate family; curves drawn on the surface keep their lengths at every stage, as the readout confirms.

items.name: Conformal maps
items.pic: Two curves crossing on a surface and their images under a map; the angle between them is read out in both places and agrees exactly for conformal maps.

items.name: Stereographic projection is conformal
items.pic: Draw intersecting circles on the sphere; their stereographic images are circles or lines meeting at the same angles, while areas near the north pole blow up.

items.name: Mercator projection
items.pic: Tissot circles on a Mercator map grow toward the poles while staying round; a route of constant compass bearing is a straight segment on the map and a spiral on the globe.

items.name: Archimedes: cylindrical projection preserves area
items.pic: Project the sphere horizontally onto the circumscribed cylinder; areas of painted regions are computed on both and match, though their shapes distort.

items.name: Isothermal coordinates exist
items.pic: On a surface patch, coordinates in which the first fundamental form is a multiple of dx² + dy² are computed numerically; the grid becomes small squares everywhere, tilted and scaled but not sheared.

chapters.title: Lie groups
chapters.summary: A Lie group is a group that is also a smooth manifold with smooth operations, and its left-invariant vector fields form a Lie algebra that captures it infinitesimally. The exponential map turns Lie algebra elements into one-parameter subgroups; for matrix groups it is the matrix exponential. Closed subgroups are Lie subgroups, subalgebras correspond to connected subgroups, and smooth group actions produce homogeneous spaces and quotient manifolds.

items.name: Lie groups
items.pic: On the circle group and on SL₂(ℝ), multiplication and inversion are applied to a draggable element, and their smoothness is checked by finite differences in coordinates.

items.name: Matrix Lie groups: SO(3), SU(2), SL₂(ℝ), Heisenberg
items.pic: Each group acts on a sample object (a rigid body, a spinor, a planar shape, a lattice), and its dimension is read off from the number of independent sliders needed to move within it.

items.name: Left-invariant vector fields and the Lie algebra
items.pic: Push a vector at the identity around the group by left translations to get a left-invariant field; brackets of two such fields are again left-invariant, matching the matrix commutator.

items.name: One-parameter subgroups and the exponential map
items.pic: The integral curve of a left-invariant field through the identity is a one-parameter subgroup; on the torus they are lines of every slope, and on SO(3) rotations about a fixed axis.

items.name: Baker–Campbell–Hausdorff to second order
items.pic: Compare e^{tA}e^{tB} with e^{t(A+B)} and with e^{t(A+B) + t²[A,B]/2}: error curves on log axes show the bracket term is exactly the leading discrepancy.

items.name: Closed subgroup theorem
items.pic: A line of rational slope on the torus closes into a circle, a closed embedded subgroup; irrational slope gives a dense subgroup that is not closed and not embedded.

items.name: The Lie correspondence
items.pic: Pick a subalgebra of 𝔰𝔩₂ (a line or a plane closed under brackets); the connected subgroup it generates is swept out by exponentials, and a non-subalgebra plane fails to close up.

items.name: The adjoint representation
items.pic: Conjugation by a rotation g acts on the Lie algebra of SO(3) — angular velocity vectors — by rotating them, so Ad(g) is drawn as g acting on ℝ³.

items.name: SU(2) double covers SO(3)
items.pic: Unit quaternions rotate a 3D object; q and −q give the same rotation, and a path from q to −q traces a loop in SO(3) that cannot be shrunk, while its double can.

items.name: Smooth group actions and homogeneous spaces
items.pic: SO(3) acting on the sphere: the stabilizer of the north pole is the circle of rotations about the axis, and the sphere is identified with SO(3)/SO(2) by following orbits.

items.name: Quotient manifold theorem
items.pic: Free proper actions (ℤ² on the plane, antipodal ℤ/2 on the sphere) yield manifolds; a non-proper action, such as an irrational flow on the torus, yields a non-Hausdorff quotient, shown by orbit closures.

chapters.title: Ergodic Theorems
chapters.summary: Stationary sequences are recast as measure-preserving maps, with i.i.d. sequences, Markov chains and rotations of the circle as the running examples. Birkhoff's ergodic theorem, proved through the maximal ergodic lemma, turns time averages into conditional expectations on the invariant σ-field and yields Weyl equidistribution and Benford's law. Recurrence results (the range of a random walk, Kac's return-time formula) follow, then Kingman's subadditive ergodic theorem with applications to random matrices, longest increasing and common subsequences, and first passage percolation.

items.name: Stationary sequence
items.pic: A window slides along a seeded stationary sequence (AR(1), a stationary Markov chain); the histograms of the windowed blocks do not change with the shift.

items.name: Rotation of the circle
items.pic: Iterate x ↦ x + θ mod 1 from a point on the circle; for rational θ the orbit is a finite polygon, for irrational θ it fills the circle.

items.name: Measure-preserving map, invariant set, ergodicity
items.pic: Push a cloud of uniform points through a map (rotation, doubling, a non-preserving map): the histogram is preserved or not, and invariant sets are highlighted.

items.name: Birkhoff’s ergodic theorem
items.pic: Time averages of X along orbits of a map are plotted for many starting points: they converge to the space average for an ergodic map and to different values for a non-ergodic one.

items.name: Maximal ergodic lemma
items.pic: Shade the set where some partial sum S_k is positive; the integral of X over it is computed and is always ≥ 0.

items.name: Weyl’s equidistribution theorem
items.pic: The fractional parts of nθ fill a histogram on [0,1) that flattens for irrational θ, while rational θ leaves gaps; the discrepancy is plotted against n.

items.name: Equidistribution for every starting point
items.pic: Start the rotation orbit anywhere you click: the visit frequency to an interval [a, b) converges to b − a for every start, not just almost every.

items.name: Benford’s law for powers of 2
items.pic: Leading digits of 2ⁿ are tallied as n grows and approach the Benford frequencies log₁₀(1 + 1/d).

items.name: Range of a random walk (Kesten–Spitzer–Whitman)
items.pic: The number of distinct sites visited by a seeded walk in d = 1, 2, 3 is divided by n; it tends to the escape probability, 0 for recurrent walks.

items.name: Stationary integer walks with zero mean are recurrent
items.pic: Partial sums of a stationary dependent integer sequence with mean zero (a Markov-modulated walk) keep returning to 0 in a long seeded run.

items.name: Kac’s recurrence theorem
items.pic: For a set A of measure a under an ergodic map, return times to A are histogrammed and their mean is 1/a.

items.name: Kingman’s subadditive ergodic theorem
items.pic: For a subadditive family (the range of a walk, first-passage times), X₀,ₙ/n along seeded realizations converges to a constant, with the subadditivity gaps drawn.

items.name: Longest common subsequences (Chvátal–Sankoff)
items.pic: Two seeded random binary strings of length n: dynamic programming finds a longest common subsequence, and its length over n settles near 0.81.

items.name: Products of random matrices (Furstenberg–Kesten)
items.pic: Multiply seeded random 2×2 matrices: (1/n) log ‖Aₙ⋯A₁‖ is plotted and converges to the top Lyapunov exponent, the same on every run.

items.name: Longest increasing subsequence (Hammersley)
items.pic: Uniform points in a square are joined by the longest increasing chain; its length over √n is plotted and approaches 2.

items.name: Poissonization: τ(n)/√n → 1
items.pic: The side length of the square needed to contain n Poisson points, divided by √n, is plotted along a seeded run and converges to 1.

items.name: First passage percolation: the time constant
items.pic: Edges of a grid get seeded random passage times; the fastest route from the origin to (n, 0) is drawn and its time over n converges.

chapters.title: Coupling and mixing times
chapters.summary: How long must a chain run before its distribution is close to stationary? Total variation distance measures closeness, and it equals the smallest probability with which two random variables with the given laws can disagree. Running two copies of a chain until they meet bounds the distance, giving mixing times of order n² for the cycle and n log n for the hypercube. Bottlenecks and distinguishing statistics give matching lower bounds, and coupling from the past turns the same idea into exact sampling.

refs: Levin, Peres & Wilmer, Markov Chains and Mixing Times
Grimmett & Stirzaker, Probability and Random Processes

items.name: Total variation distance
items.pic: Draw two distributions as overlapping bar charts; the non-overlapping area, halved, is the total variation distance, equal to the largest difference in probability of any event.

items.name: Total variation via couplings
items.pic: Pair samples of μ and ν by any coupling you design; the fraction of disagreements is always at least the TV distance, and the maximal coupling built from the overlap attains it.

items.name: Mixing time
items.pic: Plot the worst-case distance d(t) to stationarity for a chosen chain; the first time it drops below 1/4 is marked as t_mix and reported for growing sizes.

items.name: Submultiplicativity of the distance to stationarity
items.pic: Plot d̄(t) on a log scale beside d̄(s)d̄(t − s) for all splits; the inequality holds everywhere, so once below 1/4 the distance halves every further t_mix steps.

items.name: Markovian couplings
items.pic: Two walkers on a graph are driven by shared random numbers; once they land on the same vertex they move together forever, and the meeting time is recorded.

items.name: Coupling bound on mixing
items.pic: For many coupled runs, the tail P(τ_couple > t) is plotted above the exact distance d(t); the coupling curve always lies above, and better couplings hug it more closely.

items.name: Doeblin’s coupling proof of convergence
items.pic: Run one chain from a fixed state and an independent copy from π until they meet; after meeting the first chain is indistinguishable from stationarity, and the meeting time is finite for aperiodic chains.

items.name: Random walk on the cycle mixes in order n²
items.pic: Couple two lazy walkers on an n-cycle so their distance performs a random walk; measured mixing times scale like n², shown on a log–log plot with slope 2.

items.name: Lazy walk on the hypercube mixes in about ½ n log n
items.pic: Couple two hypercube walks by updating the same coordinate to the same random bit; they meet once every coordinate has been touched, a coupon-collector time near n log n.

items.name: Bottleneck ratio lower bound
items.pic: Join two dense clusters by a thin bridge; the bottleneck ratio of the cut is computed, and the mixing time grows as 1/Φ when the bridge is thinned.

items.name: Diameter and distinguishing-statistic lower bounds
items.pic: Track a statistic such as the number of ones on the hypercube; its mean and variance at time t separate the chain from equilibrium until about ½ n log n steps.

items.name: Coupling from the past (Propp–Wilson)
items.pic: Start copies of the chain from every state at times −1, −2, −4, … with shared randomness; once all copies coalesce by time 0, the common value is an exact sample from π, checked by a histogram.

chapters.title: Flows
chapters.summary: Flows are circulations with a source and a sink: Kirchhoff's law at every vertex forces zero net flow across every cut, and in networks the maximum value of a flow equals the minimum capacity of a cut, with integral optima for integral capacities. Replacing numbers by elements of an abelian group gives H-flows, whose number is a polynomial in the order of H; so the existence of a k-flow depends only on k, and small k are characterised by even degrees, bipartiteness and edge colourings. For plane graphs, flows of G and colourings of the dual G* correspond exactly, which makes Tutte's flow conjectures generalisations of colouring theorems; Seymour's 6-flow theorem is the best general result.

items.name: Circulations and Kirchhoff’s law
items.pic: Assign values to oriented edges by dragging arrows; each vertex shows its net inflow, turning green when Kirchhoff’s law holds there.

items.name: A circulation sends zero net flow across every cut
items.pic: Select a vertex set X in a graph carrying a circulation; the net flow across the cut from X to its complement is summed live and is always zero.

items.name: Circulations vanish on bridges
items.pic: Add a bridge to a graph with a circulation: whatever values you try, Kirchhoff’s law forces the flow on the bridge to be zero.

items.name: Circulations on G/e extend to G
items.pic: Contract an edge, draw a circulation on the smaller multigraph, then uncontract: the value on e is solved for so that Kirchhoff’s law holds at both ends.

items.name: Networks, flows and cuts
items.pic: Draw a network with source s, sink t and capacities; drag flow values along edges within capacity, with flow conservation checked at inner vertices.

items.name: Net flow across any cut equals the flow value
items.pic: Move vertices between the s-side and t-side of a cut; the net flow across it stays equal to the value leaving s.

items.name: Max-flow min-cut theorem (Ford–Fulkerson)
items.pic: Run augmenting paths in the residual network step by step; when no s–t path remains, the vertices reachable from s define a cut whose capacity equals the flow value.

items.name: Integral capacities admit an integral maximum flow
items.pic: With integer capacities, every augmentation adds an integer, so the maximum flow found has integer values on all edges, as the edge labels show.

items.name: H-flows for an abelian group H
items.pic: Choose a group such as ℤ₄ or ℤ₂ × ℤ₂ and label oriented edges with non-zero elements; vertices show their net sums, green when they vanish in H.

items.name: Tutte’s flow polynomial
items.pic: Count nowhere-zero H-flows for groups of orders 2 to 8 by brute force; the counts fall on a polynomial in |H| − 1 computed by deletion–contraction.

items.name: The number of H-flows depends only on the order of H
items.pic: Compare ℤ₄ and ℤ₂ × ℤ₂ on the same graph: the numbers of nowhere-zero flows are equal, though the flows themselves differ.

items.name: k-flows and the flow number φ(G)
items.pic: Label edges with integers 1 − k, …, k − 1 avoiding 0; the app finds the least k admitting a k-flow, φ(G), for the graph you draw.

items.name: Tutte: a k-flow exists iff a ℤₖ-flow exists
items.pic: Start from a ℤₖ-flow and lift its values to integers, then repair the vertices with non-zero excess along paths until a genuine k-flow appears.

items.name: A graph has a 2-flow iff all its degrees are even
items.pic: Try to label all edges ±1 with zero net flow at each vertex; this succeeds by orienting an Euler tour exactly when all degrees are even.

items.name: A cubic graph has a 3-flow iff it is bipartite
items.pic: For cubic graphs, a ℤ₃-flow orients every edge from one class to the other; the app finds one for bipartite cubic graphs and an odd cycle obstruction otherwise.

items.name: φ(Kⁿ) = 3 for even n ≥ 4
items.pic: Pick an even n: the app constructs a 3-flow on Kⁿ inductively from K^(n−2), while Kⁿ has odd degrees and so no 2-flow.

items.name: Every 4-edge-connected graph has a 4-flow
items.pic: Find two edge-disjoint spanning trees, send ℤ₂ flows around fundamental cycles of each, and add them in ℤ₂ × ℤ₂ to get a nowhere-zero flow.

items.name: 4-flows, even subgraphs and 3-edge-colourings
items.pic: Colour the edges of a cubic graph with three colours and read off a ℤ₂ × ℤ₂-flow by assigning each colour a non-zero group element, and back.

items.name: Cubic 3-edge-colourable graphs are bridgeless
items.pic: Add a bridge to a cubic graph and try to 3-edge-colour it; the app always fails and explains via the zero flow on bridges.

items.name: Consistent orientation of dual edges
items.pic: Orient an edge of a plane graph: its dual edge is oriented to cross it from left to right, and these orientations are drawn for all edges at once.

items.name: Colour differences give circulations on the dual
items.pic: Colour the faces of a plane graph with integers; colour differences across edges define values on dual edges, and the net flow at every dual vertex is zero.

items.name: Tutte’s flow–colouring duality χ(G) = φ(G*)
items.pic: Colour a plane graph with k colours and watch the dual graph light up with a nowhere-zero k-flow derived from colour differences, and conversely.

items.name: Tutte’s 5-flow conjecture
items.pic: Search for nowhere-zero 5-flows on bridgeless graphs you draw, including snarks; one is always found, while the Petersen graph refuses a 4-flow.

items.name: Tutte’s 4-flow conjecture
items.pic: For bridgeless graphs without a Petersen minor, the app searches for a 4-flow and finds one; snarks such as the Petersen graph itself are shown to need 5.

items.name: Tutte’s 3-flow conjecture
items.pic: For 4-edge-connected graphs you draw, the app finds a nowhere-zero 3-flow, the dual analogue of Grötzsch’s theorem for planar graphs.

items.name: Seymour’s 6-flow theorem
items.pic: For any bridgeless multigraph, the app builds a ℤ₂ × ℤ₃-flow: a ℤ₂-flow covering a cycle structure and a ℤ₃-flow on the rest, combined into a nowhere-zero 6-flow.

chapters.title: Catalan numbers and lattice paths
chapters.summary: The Catalan numbers count more than two hundred different families of objects, and a handful of bijections explain why so many structures share them. Lattice paths that stay above a line are counted by André’s reflection, ballot problems by the cycle lemma, and both give the formula C(2n, n)/(n + 1). We also meet Motzkin numbers, the Chung–Feller surprise and parking functions.

items.name: Catalan numbers and their recurrence
items.pic: Split structures at their first return or root; the recurrence Cₙ₊₁ = Σ CᵢCₙ₋ᵢ is computed as a sum of products of smaller cases and reproduces 1, 1, 2, 5, 14, 42, ….

items.name: André’s reflection principle
items.pic: Draw a lattice path that touches a forbidden line; its segment up to the first touch is reflected, showing the one-to-one correspondence between bad paths and all paths from a reflected start.

items.name: Dyck paths and the formula C(2n, n)/(n + 1)
items.pic: Enumerate all up–down paths of length 2n; those dipping below the axis are reflected away, and the surviving count matches the Catalan number.

items.name: The Catalan generating function
items.pic: Iterate C = 1 + xC² on truncated series and watch the coefficients stabilise into the Catalan numbers, matching the expansion of (1 − √(1 − 4x))/(2x).

items.name: Cycle lemma
items.pic: Rotate a sequence of +1s and −1s with total sum +1 through all its cyclic shifts; exactly one shift keeps every partial sum positive, and it is highlighted.

items.name: Bertrand’s ballot theorem
items.pic: Count votes for A and B in random order; the fraction of orderings in which A stays strictly ahead throughout converges to (a − b)/(a + b).

items.name: Triangulations of a convex polygon
items.pic: Click diagonals to triangulate an (n + 2)-gon; flipping diagonals walks through all triangulations, which are counted and matched with Cₙ.

items.name: Binary trees and plane trees
items.pic: Convert a binary tree to a Dyck path by a depth-first walk and back; every tree with n internal nodes appears once in the gallery of Cₙ shapes.

items.name: Non-crossing partitions
items.pic: Group points on a circle into blocks drawn as polygons; crossing blocks are refused, and the non-crossing partitions are counted and matched with Cₙ.

items.name: Stack-sortable permutations
items.pic: Feed a permutation through a single stack with push and pop buttons; it can be sorted exactly when it avoids the pattern 231, and the sortable ones are counted by Cₙ.

items.name: Chung–Feller theorem
items.pic: Histogram all paths of length 2n by the number of steps spent below the axis; every bar from 0 to n has the same height Cₙ.

items.name: Motzkin numbers
items.pic: Add flat steps to Dyck paths, or allow points on a circle to stay unmatched by chords; both families are enumerated and give 1, 1, 2, 4, 9, 21, ….

items.name: Catalan asymptotics
items.pic: Plot Cₙ·n^(3/2)√π/4ⁿ on a log scale out to n = 10⁴ and watch it converge to 1, with the square-root singularity of the generating function drawn alongside.

items.name: Parking functions: (n + 1)ⁿ⁻¹
items.pic: Cars with preferred spots drive along a one-way street, taking the first free spot; Pollak’s circular street with n + 1 spots shows that exactly one rotation of each preference list parks everyone.

chapters.title: Sums of squares and Diophantine equations
chapters.summary: Which numbers are sums of two, three or four squares, and in how many ways? Fermat’s two-squares theorem, Lagrange’s four-squares theorem and Legendre’s three-squares theorem answer the first question; Jacobi’s formulas answer the second. Pythagorean triples are parametrized, infinite descent rules out x⁴ + y⁴ = z², and the Gaussian and Eisenstein integers recast these problems as factorization in larger rings. Fermat’s Last Theorem and Catalan’s conjecture show how hard the general questions are.

refs: Hardy & Wright, An Introduction to the Theory of Numbers
Ireland & Rosen, A Classical Introduction to Modern Number Theory
Apostol, Introduction to Analytic Number Theory

items.name: Pythagorean triples
items.pic: Drag a rational point around the unit circle; the chord from (−1, 0) through it has rational slope m/n and produces the triple (n² − m², 2mn, n² + m²), plotted as primitive triples fill the plane.

items.name: Fermat’s two-squares theorem
items.pic: For each prime up to N, search for p = a² + b²; representations exist exactly for p = 2 and p ≡ 1 (mod 4), and each is unique up to order and sign.

items.name: Zagier’s windmill involution
items.pic: Solutions of x² + 4yz = p are drawn as windmills (a square with four rectangles); Zagier’s involution rearranges them in pairs, and its unique fixed windmill exposes p as a sum of two squares.

items.name: Which integers are sums of two squares
items.pic: Colour the integers up to 500 by whether they are sums of two squares; every miss has a prime ≡ 3 (mod 4) to an odd power, shown in its factorization.

items.name: Jacobi’s two-square formula
items.pic: Count lattice points on the circle x² + y² = n and compare with 4(d₁(n) − d₃(n)), the excess of divisors ≡ 1 over divisors ≡ 3 (mod 4).

items.name: Lagrange’s four-square theorem
items.pic: Every n up to 10⁴ is written as a sum of four squares by search; Euler’s four-square identity multiplies representations, as shown for the factors of a chosen n.

items.name: Jacobi’s four-square formula
items.pic: The number of representations r₄(n) is counted by brute force and plotted against 8 times the sum of divisors of n not divisible by 4; the two curves coincide.

items.name: Legendre’s three-square theorem
items.pic: Mark the integers that are not sums of three squares; they are exactly 4ᵃ(8b + 7), and squares mod 8 show why no three of them can add to 7.

items.name: Waring’s problem (Hilbert–Waring theorem)
items.pic: For k = 2, 3, 4, compute the least number of k-th powers needed for each n up to 10⁴; 23 and 239 need nine cubes, illustrating g(3) = 9, and few numbers need many.

items.name: Fermat’s descent: x⁴ + y⁴ = z² has no solutions
items.pic: Start from a hypothetical solution and follow the descent step on screen: each would-be solution manufactures a strictly smaller one, an infinite staircase that the positive integers cannot support.

items.name: Fermat’s Last Theorem (Wiles, Taylor–Wiles)
items.pic: Search for near misses aⁿ + bⁿ ≈ cⁿ; the closest found are listed with their relative errors, and none is exact for n ≥ 3.

items.name: Sophie Germain’s theorem
items.pic: For a Sophie Germain prime p (with 2p + 1 prime), the p-th powers mod 2p + 1 are only 0 and ±1; the app shows why x^p + y^p = z^p then forces 2p + 1 to divide xyz.

items.name: Legendre’s theorem on ax² + by² = cz²
items.pic: Enter coefficients; the local conditions (signs and quadratic-residue tests for each prime) are checked, and a search finds a nontrivial solution exactly when they all pass.

items.name: Catalan’s conjecture (Mihăilescu’s theorem)
items.pic: List perfect powers up to 10¹² and plot the gaps between consecutive ones; the only gap of 1 is between 8 and 9.

items.name: Gaussian integers as a Euclidean domain
items.pic: Divide one Gaussian integer by another: the exact quotient lands in a unit square of the lattice, rounding to the nearest corner leaves a remainder of smaller norm, and Euclid’s algorithm runs to the gcd.

items.name: Gaussian primes
items.pic: Plot the Gaussian primes in the complex plane; ordinary primes ≡ 3 (mod 4) stay prime on the axes, while those ≡ 1 (mod 4) split into conjugate pairs a ± bi.

items.name: Euler: x³ + y³ = z³ has no solutions
items.pic: Work in the Eisenstein integers drawn as a triangular lattice; the descent argument through the prime 1 − ω is stepped through on a hypothetical solution.

items.name: Modular elliptic curves and Fermat’s Last Theorem
items.pic: Modularity made visible: for the curve y² + y = x³ − x² of conductor 11 the reader counts its points mod p and compares aₚ = p + 1 − #E(𝔽ₚ) with the coefficients of the modular form q∏(1 − qⁿ)²(1 − q¹¹ⁿ)²; the two sequences agree prime after prime — the match Wiles proved for every semistable curve, which rules out Frey’s curve and so any counterexample to Fermat.

chapters.title: Arithmetic and Gödel’s incompleteness theorems
chapters.summary: Arithmetic can talk about its own syntax: formulas and proofs become numbers, and every computable relation is expressible by a formula. The diagonal lemma then produces sentences that speak about themselves. From this one device come Tarski’s theorem that truth is undefinable, Gödel’s theorems that no consistent effective theory of arithmetic is complete or proves its own consistency, and Church’s theorem that validity is undecidable.

refs: Enderton, A Mathematical Introduction to Logic

items.name: Peano arithmetic and Robinson’s Q
items.pic: Check axioms of Q and PA against candidate structures — ℕ, ℕ plus an extra point, polynomials with positive leading coefficient — and see which axioms each satisfies, isolating the role of induction.

items.name: Gödel numbering
items.pic: Type a formula: each symbol gets a code and the formula becomes 2^a₁·3^a₂·5^a₃⋯; factor any number back and recover the formula, or learn that it codes nothing.

items.name: Representable relations and functions
items.pic: A relation on ℕ is represented by a formula when the theory proves each instance or its negation; a table of instances fills with “proved” and “refuted” marks as a proof search runs.

items.name: Recursive relations are representable in Q
items.pic: Pick a primitive recursive definition and watch it compiled into a formula of arithmetic, using Gödel’s β-function to code finite sequences; the formula is then checked on small inputs.

items.name: Diagonal (fixed-point) lemma
items.pic: Choose a property P(x) of Gödel numbers; the substitution machinery builds a sentence G and shows, step by step, that the theory proves G ↔ P(⌜G⌝).

items.name: Tarski’s undefinability of truth
items.pic: Propose any formula T(x) as a truth predicate; the diagonal lemma produces a sentence L with L ↔ ¬T(⌜L⌝), and the evaluator shows that T must misclassify L.

items.name: Gödel’s first incompleteness theorem
items.pic: A proof-search engine enumerates theorems of the theory while the Gödel sentence “I am not provable” sits on the screen; neither it nor its negation ever appears, and a readout explains why each appearance would be a contradiction.

items.name: Rosser’s theorem
items.pic: The Rosser sentence races proofs against refutations: “if I am provable, a refutation of me appears earlier”; the race is simulated and shows why plain consistency now suffices.

items.name: Church’s theorem: validity is undecidable
items.pic: A halting question is translated into a first-order sentence that is valid exactly when the machine halts; a decider for validity would therefore solve the halting problem, shown as a reduction diagram.

items.name: Gödel’s second incompleteness theorem
items.pic: The first theorem’s argument is itself formalised: the theory proves Con → G, so a proof of Con would yield a proof of G; the chain of implications is drawn with each link certified.

items.name: Löb’s theorem
items.pic: Build the sentence “if this sentence is provable then φ” and follow the derivation showing that proving “Prov(φ) → φ” already proves φ; the second incompleteness theorem appears as the case φ = falsehood.

items.name: Presburger arithmetic is decidable
items.pic: Eliminate quantifiers from a formula of (ℕ, +, <) by adding congruences; the set the formula defines is drawn as an eventually periodic pattern on the number line, and adding multiplication breaks the method.

items.name: Über formal unentscheidbare Sätze der Principia Mathematica
items.pic: Gödel’s own coding: symbols get the odd codes 1, 3, 5, …, 13, variables powers of primes above 13, and a formula s₁s₂s₃… the number 2^{s₁}·3^{s₂}·5^{s₃}…; the reader types a short formula to see its Gödel number, decodes numbers back into formulas, then follows the diagonal step to the sentence that says ‘my number is not the number of a provable formula’ while a proof search runs and never settles it.

chapters.title: Piecewise polynomials and numerical differentiation
chapters.summary: Instead of raising the degree, we can cut the interval into pieces and use low-degree polynomials on each. Cubic splines are the smoothest such interpolants, minimizing bending energy, and B-splines give them a local basis. Differentiating interpolants yields finite-difference formulas whose accuracy can be boosted by Richardson extrapolation, while differentiating a global Chebyshev interpolant gives spectrally accurate derivatives.

refs: Süli & Mayers, An Introduction to Numerical Analysis
Trefethen, Approximation Theory and Approximation Practice

items.name: Piecewise linear interpolation and its O(h²) error
items.pic: Join data points with straight segments; refining the mesh, the max error drops by four when h halves, measured on a log–log plot for a smooth function and a kink.

items.name: Cubic splines
items.pic: Drag data points; the natural, clamped and not-a-knot cubic splines through them are drawn, each with continuous first and second derivatives shown in panels below.

items.name: Computing splines by a tridiagonal solve
items.pic: The equations for the second derivatives at the knots form a tridiagonal system, displayed as a matrix; solving it by the Thomas algorithm costs linear time, counted as points are added.

items.name: Minimum curvature property of natural splines
items.pic: Among all smooth curves through the data, the bending energy ∫f″² is computed for random competitors and for the natural spline, which always has the smallest value.

items.name: O(h⁴) convergence of cubic splines
items.pic: Halve the knot spacing repeatedly for a smooth function; the spline error falls by about 16 each time, and the error curve stays small everywhere instead of growing at the ends.

items.name: B-splines
items.pic: Show the bell-shaped B-spline basis functions for a knot vector you edit; they are nonnegative, sum to one, and each spans only four intervals, so moving one coefficient changes the curve only locally.

items.name: Locality: splines versus global interpolation
items.pic: Perturb a single data value; the change in the spline decays rapidly away from it, while the change in the high-degree global interpolant spreads across the whole interval.

items.name: Finite-difference formulas from interpolation
items.pic: Choose a stencil of points; the difference formula for the first or second derivative is derived by differentiating the interpolant, with its weights and order of accuracy displayed.

items.name: Richardson extrapolation
items.pic: Combine difference quotients with steps h and h/2 to cancel the leading error term; the extrapolated estimate gains orders of accuracy, shown in a Richardson table with errors per entry.

items.name: Spectral differentiation with Chebyshev points
items.pic: Differentiate a smooth function using the Chebyshev differentiation matrix; the error falls geometrically with n until rounding, compared with second-order finite differences.

chapters.title: Eigenvalue problems: what can be computed
chapters.summary: Eigenvalues are roots of a polynomial, so by Abel’s theorem they must be computed iteratively; good algorithms first reduce a matrix to Hessenberg or tridiagonal form by orthogonal similarity. How accurately they can be computed depends on normality: eigenvalues of symmetric matrices move no more than the perturbation, while those of non-normal matrices can be wildly sensitive, which pseudospectra make visible. Gershgorin discs, Bauer–Fike, min–max and interlacing give the practical localization tools.

items.name: Eigenvalue decomposition and multiplicities
items.pic: Drag the entries of a 2×2 matrix; eigenvectors are drawn as invariant lines, and a defective matrix (Jordan block) shows geometric multiplicity dropping below algebraic multiplicity.

items.name: Schur factorization
items.pic: For any matrix, the unitary triangularization is computed; the diagonal of T shows the eigenvalues and the size of its strictly upper part measures departure from normality.

items.name: Gershgorin circle theorem
items.pic: Edit the entries of a matrix; the Gershgorin discs centred at diagonal entries are drawn in the complex plane and the computed eigenvalues always land inside their union.

items.name: Bauer–Fike theorem
items.pic: Perturb a diagonalizable matrix by random E with ‖E‖ = δ; the perturbed eigenvalues stay within discs of radius κ(V)·δ, drawn around the original eigenvalues.

items.name: Sensitivity of eigenvalues of non-normal matrices
items.pic: Perturb a large Jordan block by ε in its bottom-left corner; the eigenvalue at 0 splits into a circle of radius ε^{1/n}, enormous compared with ε.

items.name: Pseudospectra
items.pic: The contours of the smallest singular value of zI − A are drawn for several ε; for a normal matrix they are round discs about the eigenvalues, for a non-normal one they bulge far out.

items.name: Transient growth in non-normal dynamics
items.pic: Plot ‖e^{tA}‖ for a stable matrix with a slider for non-normality; the curve rises by orders of magnitude before decaying, predicted by how far the pseudospectra reach into the right half-plane.

items.name: Eigenvalue algorithms must be iterative
items.pic: Every monic polynomial is the characteristic polynomial of its companion matrix, shown by computing both; a solver for eigenvalues in finitely many steps would solve quintics in radicals, which Abel ruled out.

items.name: Symmetric eigenvalues are perfectly conditioned (Weyl)
items.pic: Perturb a symmetric matrix by symmetric E; each eigenvalue moves by at most ‖E‖₂, plotted as error bars that the computed eigenvalues never leave.

items.name: Courant–Fischer min–max theorem
items.pic: For a 3×3 symmetric matrix, the Rayleigh quotient is drawn on the unit sphere; the middle eigenvalue is found as the max over great circles of the min on each, visualized by rotating the circle.

items.name: Cauchy interlacing theorem
items.pic: Delete the last row and column of a symmetric matrix repeatedly; the eigenvalues of each leading submatrix are plotted on a ladder and interlace with those of the next.

items.name: Reduction to Hessenberg or tridiagonal form
items.pic: Apply Householder similarity transformations from both sides; entries below the first subdiagonal vanish while the eigenvalues readout stays unchanged, and a symmetric input becomes tridiagonal.

chapters.title: Lagrange duality and the KKT conditions
chapters.summary: Attaching prices to constraints gives the Lagrangian, and minimizing it over the variables gives a dual function that bounds the optimal value from below — weak duality, always. For convex problems with a strictly feasible point the bound is tight (Slater), and the optimal primal–dual pairs are characterized by the KKT conditions, including complementary slackness. Multipliers measure the sensitivity of the optimum to constraint changes, and theorems of alternatives such as Farkas’ lemma are duality in its purest form.

items.name: Lagrangian and dual function
items.pic: For a 1D problem with one inequality constraint, the Lagrangian f + λg is drawn for a λ slider; its minimum over x traces out the concave dual function g(λ) in a second panel.

items.name: Weak duality
items.pic: Every dual feasible λ gives a lower bound on the optimal value; the bounds are plotted as horizontal lines below the primal optimum, and the best one is the dual optimum.

items.name: Strong duality under Slater’s condition
items.pic: Shrink the feasible set of a convex problem toward a single point; the duality gap readout stays zero while a strictly feasible point exists and can open when Slater’s condition fails.

items.name: Geometric picture: the set of attainable values
items.pic: Plot the set of pairs (g(x), f(x)) over all x; each λ is a supporting line of slope −λ, the dual value is its intercept, and convexity of the set is what closes the gap.

items.name: Duality gaps in non-convex problems
items.pic: Make the attainable set non-convex by editing the objective; supporting lines can no longer reach the lowest feasible point and a positive duality gap appears in the readout.

items.name: Saddle-point interpretation
items.pic: The Lagrangian surface over (x, λ) is drawn in 3D; the primal–dual optimum is a saddle — a minimum in x and a maximum in λ — and max-min equals min-max there.

items.name: Complementary slackness
items.pic: For each constraint of a small problem, the slack and the multiplier are shown as paired bars; at the optimum at least one bar in every pair is zero.

items.name: Karush–Kuhn–Tucker conditions
items.pic: At a candidate point, the negative objective gradient and the gradients of active constraints are drawn; the point is KKT when the first lies in the cone of the others with nonnegative weights, read out.

items.name: KKT conditions are sufficient for convex problems
items.pic: Solve the KKT system of a convex QP by hand with sliders; whenever all conditions are met, the brute-force minimum over a grid confirms the point is optimal.

items.name: KKT can fail without a constraint qualification
items.pic: Minimize x subject to y ≤ x³ and y ≥ 0; the optimum at the cusp has gradients of the active constraints that cannot balance the objective gradient, so no multipliers exist there.

items.name: Multipliers as sensitivities (shadow prices)
items.pic: Loosen a constraint by u; the optimal value is recomputed and plotted against u, and its slope at u = 0 equals minus the optimal multiplier.

items.name: Linear programming duality
items.pic: A 2D LP and its dual are solved side by side; both optimal values coincide, and the dual variables are shown as the weights that combine the active constraints into the objective.

items.name: Farkas’ lemma
items.pic: Drag b relative to the cone generated by the columns of A; either b lies in the cone (Ax = b, x ≥ 0 solvable) or a separating vector y certifying infeasibility is drawn — never both.

items.name: Theorems of alternatives
items.pic: For a system of strict linear inequalities, either a solution region is shaded or a nonnegative combination of the inequalities producing a contradiction is displayed.

items.name: Fenchel duality
items.pic: For min f(x) + g(x), the graphs of f and −g are drawn with parallel supporting lines; the largest vertical gap between such lines is the dual value, equal to the primal minimum for convex f and g.

items.name: Nonlinear programming
items.pic: At a constrained optimum −∇f must lie in the cone of the active constraint gradients: the reader drags constraints in the plane and watches the multipliers appear; then the paper’s own counterexample, maximise x subject to y ≤ (1 − x)³ and y ≥ 0, shows the optimum (1, 0) where the constraint gradients line up and no multipliers exist.

chapters.title: The bootstrap and resampling
chapters.summary: When the sampling distribution of a statistic is out of reach, the bootstrap estimates it by resampling the data themselves, letting the empirical distribution stand in for the unknown one and Monte Carlo do the arithmetic. We build bootstrap standard errors and intervals, compare them with the jackknife, and see why the method works for smooth statistics. Then we break it on purpose: sample maxima, infinite variance and serial dependence each defeat the naive bootstrap, and each has a repair.

items.name: Monte Carlo integration
items.pic: Estimate an integral by averaging the integrand at seeded random points; on a log–log plot the error falls like 1/√N in every dimension, beside a grid rule whose error worsens as dimension grows.

items.name: Bootstrap principle
items.pic: Side by side: thousands of samples drawn from the true population and thousands of resamples drawn from one observed sample; the two histograms of the statistic have nearly the same spread, the bootstrap one centred at the observed value.

items.name: Bootstrap standard error
items.pic: Press Resample to draw one bootstrap sample with its duplicates highlighted, or draw B at once; the bootstrap standard error of the median stabilizes as B grows and is compared with the true value from fresh populations.

items.name: Bootstrap percentile interval
items.pic: The 2.5% and 97.5% quantiles of the bootstrap histogram form the interval; repeating the whole procedure 500 times accumulates its coverage for the mean, the median and a correlation.

items.name: Studentized bootstrap-t interval
items.pic: Resample the t-statistic instead of the estimate; for skewed exponential data at n = 15 the coverage readout of the bootstrap-t sits closer to 95% than those of the percentile and normal intervals.

items.name: Parametric bootstrap
items.pic: Fit a model, simulate new datasets from the fit and refit each; parametric and nonparametric bootstrap standard errors agree when the model is right and part ways for overdispersed counts fitted as Poisson.

items.name: Jackknife
items.pic: Leave out each point in turn and plot the n leave-one-out estimates; the jackknife standard error matches the bootstrap for the mean but is badly off for the median, whose leave-one-out values take only two distinct values.

items.name: Bootstrap consistency for smooth statistics
items.pic: The Kolmogorov distance between the bootstrap and the true sampling distribution of √n(X̄ − μ) is tracked over seeded replications as n grows, and falls toward zero.

items.name: Bootstrap failure for the sample maximum
items.pic: For Uniform(0, θ) the bootstrap distribution of the maximum puts an atom of mass about 1 − 1/e ≈ 0.63 on the observed maximum while the true sampling law is continuous; the parametric bootstrap repairs it.

items.name: Bootstrap failure under infinite variance
items.pic: With Pareto data of tail index 1.5, bootstrap intervals for the mean keep under-covering as n grows, while the identical code on finite-variance data reaches 95%.

items.name: Block bootstrap for dependent data
items.pic: Resample an AR(1) series point by point and in blocks of adjustable length: the iid bootstrap underestimates the standard error of the mean by a factor that grows with the autocorrelation, and long enough blocks recover it.

items.name: Accept–reject sampling
items.pic: Darts are thrown uniformly under M times an envelope density; those landing under the target are kept, the kept histogram matches the target exactly, and the acceptance-rate readout equals 1/M as the envelope is loosened or tightened.

items.name: Bootstrap methods: another look at the jackknife
items.pic: Resample a small data set with replacement and recompute a statistic — the sample median, where the jackknife fails, is the paper’s leading case: the reader draws B bootstrap samples, watches the histogram of medians build up and the bootstrap standard error settle, and compares it with the jackknife value and the truth from fresh samples.

chapters.title: The Bias–Complexity Tradeoff
chapters.summary: Is there a universal learner that needs no prior knowledge? The No-Free-Lunch theorem says no: on a domain at least twice the size of the sample, every algorithm has a distribution on which it fails although another learner would succeed, so the class of all functions is not PAC learnable. Restricting to a hypothesis class exchanges this failure for an approximation error, and the error of ERM splits into an approximation part and an estimation part that move in opposite directions as the class grows.

collectionSource.author: Shai Shalev-Shwartz & Shai Ben-David
collectionSource.title: Understanding Machine Learning: From Theory to Algorithms

items.name: The No-Free-Lunch theorem
items.pic: The reader fixes any learning rule on a domain of 2m points; the app averages over all labellings of the unseen half, exhibits a target on which the rule errs on a quarter of the domain on average, and shows ERM over {f} succeeding on that same target.

items.name: The class of all functions is not PAC learnable
items.pic: On an infinite domain, whatever sample size the reader allows, the No-Free-Lunch adversary keeps the learner’s error above 1/8 with probability above 1/7, the two thresholds drawn on the error histogram.

items.name: Error decomposition: approximation and estimation error
items.pic: A stacked bar splits the true error of ERM into the best error in the class and the excess over it; enlarging the class (more pieces in a piecewise-constant rule) shrinks the first bar and grows the second.

items.name: The bias–complexity tradeoff
items.pic: A U-shaped curve of test error against class complexity for a fixed sample size is recomputed live as the reader changes m; the best complexity moves right as data grow.

chapters.title: Generalization and regularization
chapters.summary: Classical capacity arguments predict that networks with more parameters than data should overfit, yet trained networks generalize — while also being able to fit random labels. Explicit regularizers (weight decay, dropout, augmentation, ensembles, early stopping) help, but much of the story is implicit: gradient descent prefers minimum-norm and maximum-margin solutions, test error descends a second time past the interpolation threshold, and norm-based rather than parameter-count measures track generalization. The chapter ends with phenomena that theory is still catching up with: grokking, lottery tickets, adversarial examples and scaling laws.

items.name: Bias–variance trade-off for neural networks
items.pic: Many small networks of a given width are trained on resampled training sets; the spread of their predictions (variance) and the error of their average (bias) are plotted against width.

items.name: Weight decay (L2 regularization)
items.pic: A wide network is trained on noisy 1D data with a weight-decay slider: the fit goes from wiggly interpolation to smooth to flat, with the test error read out.

items.name: Early stopping
items.pic: Training and validation loss traces part ways; the stop marker sits at the validation minimum, and for linear least squares the early-stopped iterates are shown to track ridge solutions with λ ≈ 1/(ηt).

items.name: Dropout
items.pic: Hidden units blink off at random during training; the average over many dropout masks is compared with the weight-scaled network used at test time, and validation loss is compared with and without dropout.

items.name: Data augmentation
items.pic: A classifier is trained on a few 2D points with and without random rotations of the training set; with augmentation the decision boundary becomes rotation-symmetric and accuracy on a rotated test set rises.

items.name: Ensembles
items.pic: Networks trained from different seeds are averaged; the ensemble’s test error falls below every member’s, and the gain concentrates where the members disagree.

items.name: Networks can fit random labels
items.pic: The same network is trained on true labels and on shuffled labels: both reach zero training error, the shuffled run more slowly, while test accuracy is high in one and at chance in the other.

items.name: VC dimension of ReLU networks
items.pic: For a tiny ReLU network, weight space is searched for each of the 2ⁿ labelings of n points; the count of realizable labelings is plotted against n and stops being 2ⁿ near the scale set by the parameter count times depth.

items.name: Norm-based margin bounds for deep networks
items.pic: Networks of growing width are trained on the same data: the parameter count rises a hundredfold while a spectrally normalized margin measure stays flat and tracks test error; on random labels the same measure climbs steeply.

items.name: Double descent
items.pic: Random-feature regression with a growing number of features on seeded data: test error rises to a peak at the interpolation threshold (features = samples) and falls again beyond it, and a ridge slider flattens the peak.

items.name: Gradient descent finds the minimum-norm interpolant
items.pic: Gradient descent from zero on an underdetermined least-squares problem moves within the row space and stops at the minimum-norm solution, drawn as the point of the solution line closest to the origin.

items.name: Benign overfitting in linear regression
items.pic: Noisy data are interpolated by the minimum-norm solution in a high-dimensional feature space whose covariance spectrum is set by sliders: with a few strong directions plus many weak ones the noise is absorbed and test error stays near the noise level, while an isotropic spectrum makes interpolation harmful.

items.name: Implicit bias toward the max-margin classifier
items.pic: Logistic regression is trained by gradient descent on separable data: the weight norm grows like log t while the direction creeps toward the hard-margin SVM direction, the angle between them plotted on a log-time axis.

items.name: Grokking
items.pic: A small network on modular addition memorizes its training set quickly; long after the training loss is near zero, test accuracy jumps from chance to perfect, and the weight-decay slider moves the jump earlier or later.

items.name: Lottery ticket hypothesis
items.pic: A trained network is pruned to 10% of its weights and the sparse mask is retrained from its original initialization and from a fresh one; the original-initialization ticket matches the full network while the re-initialized one lags.

items.name: Adversarial examples
items.pic: A correctly classified input is nudged along the sign of the input gradient; a perturbation of small max-norm flips the prediction, and a dimension slider shows the required ε shrinking roughly like 1/d for a linear model.

items.name: Neural scaling laws
items.pic: Test loss of small networks trained with growing data and parameter budgets falls along a straight line on log–log axes until it hits a floor set by whichever resource is held fixed.

chapters.title: Adjusting for confounding in observational studies
chapters.summary: When treatment is not randomized, the propensity score — the probability of treatment given covariates — summarizes everything the covariates say about treatment, and matching, stratifying or weighting on it mimics a randomized trial.
