Weighting breaks down near violations of positivity, outcome models can be misspecified, and doubly robust estimators combine the two so that either can fail; cross-fitting lets flexible machine-learning fits play either role. Marginal structural models and g-estimation extend the toolkit, and negative controls, Cornfield’s inequality and the E-value ask how strong an unmeasured confounder would have to be.

refs: Hernán & Robins, Causal Inference: What If

items.name: Propensity score
items.pic: The probability of treatment is fitted from covariates and each person is coloured by it; overlaid histograms of the score for treated and controls show the region of overlap.

items.name: Balancing property of the propensity score
items.pic: Within narrow bins of the propensity score the covariate distributions of treated and controls match, although they differ overall; a balance table shows standardized differences before and after.

items.name: Propensity score matching and stratification
items.pic: Each treated unit is paired with the control of nearest score (drawn as connecting lines), or the score is cut into quintiles; the matched estimate approaches the true effect, and units outside the overlap go unmatched.

items.name: IP-weighted estimators and stabilized weights
items.pic: Unstabilized and stabilized weights are applied to the same data: both centre on the truth, and the stabilized version narrows the spread of estimates across 500 resamples.

items.name: Extreme weights near positivity violations
items.pic: Strengthen a covariate’s effect on treatment until some propensities approach 0: a handful of points acquire enormous weights, the estimator’s spread explodes, and truncating the weights trades that variance for bias.

items.name: Outcome regression and the parametric g-formula
items.pic: An outcome model predicts everyone’s outcome under treatment and under control and the predictions are averaged; a straight-line model fitted to a curved truth leaves a visible gap from the true effect.

items.name: Doubly robust (augmented IPW) estimation
items.pic: Two toggles misspecify the propensity model, the outcome model or both: the augmented estimator stays unbiased if either model is right and fails only when both are wrong.

items.name: Marginal structural models
items.pic: A weighted regression of outcome on a continuous dose in the IP-weighted pseudo-population recovers the true counterfactual dose–response curve, while the unweighted fit does not.

items.name: Double/debiased machine learning
items.pic: An effect is estimated with flexible nuisance fits, with and without cross-fitting and orthogonalization: the naïve plug-in estimates are shifted and under-cover, while the cross-fitted estimates centre on the truth with near-nominal coverage.

items.name: G-estimation of structural nested models
items.pic: Candidate effect values ψ are swept: for each, the outcome is “un-treated” by subtracting ψ·A and its association with treatment given covariates is measured; the estimate is the ψ at which that association vanishes.

items.name: Negative controls
items.pic: An outcome the treatment cannot affect is analysed exactly like the real one; adding a hidden confounder with a slider produces a non-zero “effect” on the negative control, flagging residual confounding.

items.name: Cornfield’s inequality
items.pic: For an observed risk ratio of 9 between smoking and lung cancer, the reader tries to explain it away with a hidden binary factor; the factor’s prevalence ratio between smokers and non-smokers must be at least 9, and weaker factors fail.

items.name: Sensitivity analysis and the E-value
items.pic: Drag the strength of an unmeasured confounder’s links to treatment and outcome; the bias-adjusted estimate moves, and the contour where it crosses the null is labelled with the E-value.

items.name: The central role of the propensity score
items.pic: Units with two covariates coloured by treatment: the reader fits a propensity score, stratifies on it, and watches covariate balance tables equalise within strata and the treated-minus-control difference approach the true effect, while matching on the score alone balances both covariates at once.

chapters.title: Randomized, online and streaming algorithms
chapters.summary: Coin flips buy simplicity and speed: Las Vegas algorithms are always right but have random running time, Monte Carlo algorithms run on schedule but may err, and repetition drives the error down exponentially. Shuffling, sampling, collision estimates, Karger’s contraction and Bloom filters illustrate the toolkit, and the tail bounds of Markov and Chernoff turn expectations into guarantees that hold with high probability. Online algorithms must act before seeing the future and are judged by their competitive ratio against an all-knowing optimum; streaming algorithms see data once and keep only a small sketch of it.

refs: Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest & Stein, Introduction to Algorithms (4th ed.)

items.name: Las Vegas and Monte Carlo algorithms
items.pic: Run randomized quicksort and a random-sampling majority test many times; one histogram shows random running time with always-correct output, the other fixed time with a measured error rate.

items.name: Amplification by independent repetition
items.pic: Slide the single-run success probability p and the number of repetitions k; the failure probability (1 − p)ᵏ is plotted under e^(−pk), showing that about (1/p) ln(1/δ) runs push it below δ.

items.name: Fisher–Yates shuffle
items.pic: Shuffle a four-element array thousands of times with Fisher–Yates and with the naive swap-with-anyone loop; the histogram over all 24 permutations is flat for the first and visibly lopsided for the second.

items.name: Reservoir sampling
items.pic: Items stream past a reservoir of size k, the t-th replacing a random slot with probability k/t; over many runs each stream position’s inclusion frequency settles at k/n.

items.name: Birthday paradox: collisions after about √n draws
items.pic: Throw keys into n slots one at a time; the probability of a first collision is plotted against the number thrown, crossing 1/2 near 1.18√n, with a live simulation overlaid.

items.name: Coupon collector: n Hₙ expected draws
items.pic: Draw random coupons until all n types have appeared; the wait for each new type is a bar of expected height n/(n − i), and their sum tracks n Hₙ over many runs.

items.name: Random assignments satisfy 7/8 of 3-SAT clauses
items.pic: Generate a random 3-CNF formula and flip random assignments: the satisfied fraction fluctuates around 7/8, and conditional expectations fix the variables one at a time without ever dropping below it.

items.name: Karger’s contraction algorithm
items.pic: Click Contract to merge the endpoints of a random edge; supernodes absorb vertices and keep parallel edges until two remain, and their crossing edges are compared with a true minimum cut.

items.name: Karger finds a min cut with probability ≥ 2/(n(n − 1))
items.pic: Run thousands of contractions on an editable graph and plot the empirical success rate above the 1/C(n, 2) bound, along with the count of distinct minimum cuts, which never exceeds C(n, 2).

items.name: Bloom filters
items.pic: Insert words into a bit array where k hash functions each light a bit; query a word never inserted and see a false positive when all of its bits happen to be lit already.

items.name: Bloom filter false-positive rate and the best k
items.pic: Sliders for m, n and k plot the predicted rate (1 − e^(−kn/m))ᵏ with its minimum at k = (m/n) ln 2, overlaid with rates measured on random insertions.

items.name: Count–min sketch
items.pic: A stream increments one counter in each row of a d × w array; querying an item takes the minimum of its d counters, and its overestimate is plotted against the εN bound for w = e/ε.

items.name: Online algorithms and the competitive ratio
items.pic: Requests arrive one by one to an online algorithm while the offline optimum sees them all; the running cost ratio is plotted, and an adversary button builds the sequence that maximizes it.

items.name: Ski rental: the break-even rule is 2-competitive
items.pic: Choose the purchase price B and a renting threshold; the adversary picks the season length, and the worst-case ratio curve bottoms out at 2 − 1/B exactly when the threshold matches B.

items.name: Paging: LRU is k-competitive, the best deterministic ratio
items.pic: An adversary always requests the page the online rule just evicted; LRU’s misses are compared with the furthest-in-future count phase by phase, and their ratio approaches the cache size k.

items.name: Randomized marking for paging is O(log k)-competitive
items.pic: Pages are marked when requested and a uniformly random unmarked page is evicted; over adversarial phases the average miss count stays within about 2H_k times the optimum, far below k.

items.name: Markov’s inequality: from Las Vegas to Monte Carlo
items.pic: A histogram of running times of a Las Vegas algorithm is cut at t times its mean; the mass beyond the cut stays below 1/t, so stopping at twice the mean and restarting fails with probability at most one half.

items.name: Chernoff bounds
items.pic: Sum n fair or biased coins many times; the empirical tail beyond (1 + δ)μ is plotted on a log scale beneath the Chernoff curve, which falls exponentially in μ while the Markov and Chebyshev bounds lag far above.

items.name: Balls into bins: maximum load Θ(log n / log log n)
items.pic: Throw n balls into n bins and watch the fullest bin; over many trials its load tracks ln n / ln ln n, and a “two choices” toggle that places each ball in the emptier of two random bins flattens the maximum dramatically.

items.name: Karger–Stein recursive contraction
items.pic: Contract down to n/√2 vertices, branch into two independent copies and recurse; the recursion tree shows survival probabilities per level, and the overall success rate stays near 1/log n instead of 1/n².

items.name: Estimating distinct elements (Flajolet–Martin)
items.pic: Each stream item is hashed and the largest number of trailing zeros seen so far is kept; the estimate 2^z jumps around the true count, and taking the median of several independent copies pulls it into a narrow band.

items.name: Move-to-front is 4-competitive for list access
items.pic: Requests to a linked list are served by move-to-front and by an offline optimum; the potential (twice the number of pairs the two lists order differently) is drawn as a bar that pays for every expensive access, keeping the ratio under 4 (and under 2 in Sleator and Tarjan’s cost model).

items.name: Weighted majority (multiplicative weights)
items.pic: A panel of experts predicts a sequence of outcomes; each wrong expert’s weight is halved, the weighted vote is plotted, and its mistake count stays below about 2.41 times the best expert’s plus a log₂ n term.

chapters.title: Context-free grammars
chapters.summary: Grammars generate strings by rewriting variables, and their parse trees expose nested structure that no finite automaton can track: balanced brackets, arithmetic expressions, the syntax of programming languages. We meet ambiguity, its practical cures, and languages where it cannot be cured at all. Normal forms tame grammars, and Chomsky normal form yields the cubic-time CYK algorithm, which decides membership for every context-free language; practical parsers trade that generality for linear time.

refs: Sipser, Introduction to the Theory of Computation

items.name: Context-free grammar
items.pic: Edit grammar rules in a text box and click variables to rewrite them, building a derivation; all generated strings up to a chosen length are listed alongside.

items.name: Derivations and parse trees
items.pic: A derivation and its parse tree grow side by side; switching between leftmost and rightmost derivations reorders the steps but leaves the tree unchanged.

items.name: Balanced brackets: the Dyck language
items.pic: Type brackets to draw their height profile as a mountain range; the string is balanced exactly when the walk never dips below zero and ends at zero, and its parse tree mirrors the mountains.

items.name: Ambiguity
items.pic: For the naive grammar E → E+E | E×E | a, type a+a×a and flip between its two parse trees, each evaluated with numbers to show they compute different results.

items.name: Precedence and associativity by grammar layering
items.pic: A layered grammar of expressions, terms and factors yields exactly one tree for any input; toggling left or right associativity makes 8−3−2 evaluate to 3 or 7.

items.name: Inherently ambiguous languages
items.pic: For {aⁱbʲcᵏ : i = j or j = k} the reader tries candidate grammars; each one is shown giving two different trees for some aⁿbⁿcⁿ, and the count of such strings grows with length.

items.name: Regular languages are context-free
items.pic: A DFA is turned rule by rule into a right-linear grammar; stepping through a derivation highlights the matching transition of the automaton at every step.

items.name: Closure under union, concatenation and star
items.pic: Two grammars are combined with a fresh start variable; test strings from each piece and their concatenations are derived in the combined grammar.

items.name: Chomsky normal form
items.pic: The conversion runs in stages — new start variable, remove ε-rules, remove unit rules, binarize — with the grammar text updated at each step and its language checked unchanged on test strings.

items.name: CYK parsing
items.pic: The triangular CYK table fills diagonal by diagonal for the typed string (v.table); clicking the top cell reconstructs a parse tree when the start variable is present.

items.name: Greibach normal form
items.pic: After conversion every rule begins with a terminal, so a derivation of a string of length n takes exactly n steps; left recursion is removed visibly along the way.

items.name: Backus–Naur form and programming-language syntax
items.pic: A small BNF grammar parses a typed program into an abstract syntax tree, and a syntax error is pinpointed at the first token no rule can continue.

items.name: The dangling-else ambiguity
items.pic: For “if a then if b then s else t” both parses are drawn; switching on the rule that else binds to the nearest if leaves one tree and re-indents the code to match.

items.name: Predictive LL(1) parsing
items.pic: FIRST and FOLLOW sets and the parse table are computed for an editable grammar; conflicts appear as red cells, and a left-recursive rule sends the naive recursive-descent parser into endless recursion.

items.name: Shift-reduce (LR) parsing
items.pic: A stack and the remaining input are animated as the parser shifts and reduces on a typed expression, building the tree bottom-up; an ambiguous grammar produces a visible shift/reduce conflict.

items.name: On the Translation of Languages from Left to Right
items.pic: Feed an arithmetic expression to an LR(1) parser built from an editable grammar: the stack of states, the lookahead and each shift or reduce are animated on the characteristic automaton, and a grammar edit shows exactly where a conflict appears.

chapters.title: Randomized computation
chapters.summary: Allowing an algorithm to flip coins and err with small probability gives the classes BPP, RP and ZPP. Repetition drives the error down exponentially, polynomial identities can be tested by evaluating at random points, and randomness gives fast algorithms for primality, matchings and verification. Yet randomness seems weaker than it looks: BPP has polynomial-size circuits and sits low in the polynomial hierarchy, and primality turned out to be deterministic after all.

refs: Arora & Barak, Computational Complexity: A Modern Approach

items.name: Probabilistic Turing machines and BPP
items.pic: Run a randomized algorithm many times on one input; the fraction of accepting runs is plotted and must stay above 2/3 on yes-inputs and below 1/3 on no-inputs.

items.name: RP, coRP and ZPP
items.pic: Three panels show one-sided error (never wrong on no-inputs), the opposite side, and zero error with a random running time whose histogram is drawn.

items.name: ZPP = RP ∩ coRP
items.pic: Alternate an RP and a coRP algorithm until one gives a certain answer; the number of rounds needed is geometrically distributed, as the simulated histogram shows.

items.name: Error reduction by repetition
items.pic: Take the majority of k independent runs; the error probability is plotted on a log scale against k and falls in a straight line, matching the Chernoff bound.

items.name: Schwartz–Zippel lemma
items.pic: A nonzero polynomial of degree d over a grid Sⁿ is evaluated everywhere; its zeros are coloured, and their fraction never exceeds d/|S|, whatever polynomial the reader types.

items.name: Polynomial identity testing
items.pic: Two arithmetic circuits are compared at random points; when they differ, a witness point is found within a few trials, while expanding them symbolically would explode.

items.name: Perfect matchings via random Tutte matrices
items.pic: Fill the Tutte matrix of a graph with random numbers and compute its determinant; it is nonzero with high probability exactly when a perfect matching exists, tested on graphs the reader draws.

items.name: Freivalds’ check of matrix products
items.pic: Claimed product C = AB is tested by multiplying both sides by a random 0/1 vector; plant an error in C and it is caught at least half the time, at quadratic rather than cubic cost.

items.name: PRIMES is in P (Agrawal–Kayal–Saxena)
items.pic: The identity (X + a)ⁿ ≡ Xⁿ + a modulo (X^r − 1, n) is checked for small a; composites fail some check while primes pass all, and the running time is plotted against bit length.

items.name: Random-walk algorithm for 2SAT
items.pic: Start from a random assignment and flip a random variable of a violated clause; the Hamming distance to a fixed solution performs a random walk that hits zero in about n² steps.

items.name: Adleman: BPP ⊆ P/poly
items.pic: After amplification, a grid of inputs against random strings has bad cells so sparse that some column is good for every input; the reader shades bad cells and finds that column.

items.name: Sipser–Gács–Lautemann: BPP ⊆ Σ₂ ∩ Π₂
items.pic: A large set of accepting random strings can be covered by a few XOR-shifts of itself, a small one cannot; the reader tries shifts and sees the cube covered or not.

items.name: PRIMES is in P
items.pic: Enter n and run the AKS test: find a small r with large multiplicative order of n, then check (X + a)ⁿ ≡ Xⁿ + a modulo (X^r − 1, n) for each a, and watch a Carmichael number that fools Fermat’s test fail one of these congruences.

chapters.title: Channel capacity
chapters.summary: A discrete memoryless channel is a matrix of transition probabilities, and its capacity is the largest mutual information between input and output over input distributions. Shannon’s noisy-channel coding theorem says every rate below capacity can be achieved with vanishing error — by random codebooks decoded through joint typicality — and no rate above it can. Capacity is computable by alternating maximization, is not raised by feedback, combines with compression through the separation theorem, and has a zero-error cousin with a very different, combinatorial character.

refs: Cover & Thomas, Elements of Information Theory
MacKay, Information Theory, Inference, and Learning Algorithms

items.name: Discrete memoryless channel
items.pic: Send a typed message through a channel given by an editable transition matrix; received symbols appear with corrupted ones marked in red.

items.name: Channel capacity
items.pic: Drag the input distribution of a channel; I(X;Y) is plotted over the simplex and its maximum, the capacity, is marked.

items.name: Capacity of the binary symmetric channel
items.pic: The capacity 1 − H(p) is plotted against the crossover probability; at p = ½ it vanishes, and for p > ½ the receiver simply flips every bit.

items.name: Capacity of the binary erasure channel
items.pic: Erased bits arrive as question marks and capacity 1 − ε is plotted; with feedback the sender just repeats erased bits and achieves the same rate.

items.name: The noisy typewriter
items.pic: Each letter arrives as itself or its neighbour; using every other letter gives error-free transmission at log₂ 13 bits per use, drawn on the confusion graph.

items.name: Symmetric channels: uniform input achieves capacity
items.pic: For a channel whose rows are permutations of each other, the mutual-information surface over input distributions peaks at the uniform point, located by the reader’s search.

items.name: Mutual information is concave in the input distribution
items.pic: I(X;Y) is drawn as a surface over input distributions for an editable channel; chords always lie below it, so any local maximum is the capacity.

items.name: Blahut–Arimoto algorithm
items.pic: Alternating updates move the input distribution of an editable channel; the iterates climb to capacity while computable upper and lower bounds close in.

items.name: Codes, rates and error probability
items.pic: A code is shown as a codebook table; its rate log M / n and its maximal and average error under simulated noise are read out.

items.name: Jointly typical sequences
items.pic: Pairs sent through the channel are jointly typical with high probability, independent pairs almost never; both empirical fractions are plotted as n grows.

items.name: Noisy-channel coding theorem
items.pic: Random codebooks of rate R are decoded by joint typicality over a binary symmetric channel; block error falls toward zero with n when R < C and rises to one when R > C.

items.name: Converse to the channel coding theorem
items.pic: For any code above capacity, Fano’s inequality forces a floor on the error probability; the floor 1 − C/R − 1/(nR) is plotted and simulated codes sit above it.

items.name: Feedback does not increase capacity
items.pic: A feedback link lets the sender see every received symbol; schemes using it simplify coding on the erasure channel but the achieved rate never passes C.

items.name: Source–channel separation theorem
items.pic: Send a biased-coin source over a noisy channel: compress, then channel-code; end-to-end error stays small while H < C and jumps once the reader pushes H past C.

items.name: Zero-error capacity and the pentagon
items.pic: On the five-letter cyclic confusion graph, single letters give 2 safe messages but pairs give 5; listing the independent set of the product shows √5 messages per use.

items.name: Capacity of constrained noiseless channels
items.pic: Forbid the pattern 11 on a binary line: the number of allowed strings grows like φⁿ, so capacity is log₂ of the golden ratio, read from the largest eigenvalue of the constraint graph.

items.name: Error exponents
items.pic: Block error of random codes is plotted on a log scale against n for several rates; each line is straight, and its slope, the error exponent, shrinks to zero as R approaches C.

chapters.title: Message integrity and hash functions
chapters.summary: Secrecy is not integrity: an attacker who cannot read a message may still alter it. Message authentication codes detect tampering, built from pseudorandom functions, universal hashing or hash functions. Collision-resistant hash functions compress arbitrary data to a short fingerprint; the birthday bound sets their output length, the Merkle–Damgård and sponge constructions build them, and Merkle trees and the random-oracle model put them to work. Combining encryption with a MAC in the right order yields authenticated encryption.

refs: Katz & Lindell, Introduction to Modern Cryptography
Boneh & Shoup, A Graduate Course in Applied Cryptography

items.name: Message authentication codes
items.pic: An attacker sees tagged messages and tries to tag a new one; the forgery game is stepped through, and a truncated tag shows how forgery probability depends on tag length.

items.name: A pseudorandom function is a secure MAC
items.pic: Tag = F_k(m) for fixed-length messages; a forger’s success is compared with guessing a random tag, 2^(−n), over many attempts.

items.name: CBC-MAC
items.pic: Chain a block cipher over the message to produce a tag; for variable-length messages the reader splices two tagged messages into a valid forgery, and length-prepending blocks it.

items.name: One-time MACs from universal hashing (Carter–Wegman)
items.pic: Tag = (a·m + b) mod p with a fresh key; even an unbounded forger who sees one tag guesses another correctly with probability only 1/p, checked by exhaustive search.

items.name: GMAC and Poly1305
items.pic: The message is treated as polynomial coefficients evaluated at a secret point and masked by a cipher output; the collision probability bound is plotted against message length.

items.name: Collision resistance
items.pic: A toy hash with a short output is attacked: collisions, second preimages and preimages are searched for, and the three costs are compared on a log scale.

items.name: Birthday attack on hash functions
items.pic: Hash random inputs with an n-bit truncated hash until two outputs agree; the number of tries clusters near 2^(n/2), plotted for n from 16 to 40.

items.name: Small-space collision finding (cycle detection)
items.pic: Iterate a hash from a seed until the sequence cycles; Floyd’s tortoise and hare find the collision at the tail of the ρ-shaped path with constant memory.

items.name: Merkle–Damgård transform
items.pic: A compression function is chained over padded blocks; given a collision of the full hash, the reader walks back along the chains to find a collision of the compression function.

items.name: Length-extension attacks
items.pic: With tag = H(k ‖ m), the attacker continues the chain from the published tag and appends data, producing a valid tag for an extended message without the key.

items.name: HMAC
items.pic: Inner and outer keyed hashes wrap the message; the length-extension trick that broke the naive MAC is replayed and now fails.

items.name: Davies–Meyer and the sponge construction
items.pic: A sponge absorbs message blocks into the rate part of its state and squeezes output, while the hidden capacity part — whose size the reader adjusts — sets the security level.

items.name: The random-oracle model
items.pic: Every party queries a shared box that answers fresh random strings for new inputs and repeats old answers; a lazily filled table grows as the proof’s reduction programs it.

items.name: Merkle trees
items.pic: Hash file blocks into a binary tree; a proof that one block belongs to the root needs only log n sibling hashes, highlighted, and tampering with any block changes the root.

items.name: Password hashing and salting
items.pic: A leaked table of unsalted hashes is cracked against a dictionary in one pass; adding per-user salts and a slow hash multiplies the attacker’s cost, shown by a cost meter.

items.name: Chosen-ciphertext attacks and malleability
items.pic: Flip bits of a counter-mode ciphertext and the plaintext changes in exactly the same positions — “pay $100” becomes “pay $900” — showing that CPA security is not enough.

items.name: Encrypt-then-MAC gives authenticated encryption
items.pic: Compare encrypt-and-MAC, MAC-then-encrypt and encrypt-then-MAC against a tampering adversary; only the last rejects every modified ciphertext before decrypting it.

chapters.title: Consensus and its impossibility
chapters.summary: Consensus — agreeing on one of the proposed values despite failures — underlies replication and commit. With synchronous rounds and crash failures it takes exactly f + 1 rounds, but two generals over a lossy link can never agree, and the FLP theorem shows that in an asynchronous system a single crash makes deterministic consensus impossible. The escape routes are randomization, failure detectors and partial synchrony. Herlihy’s hierarchy ranks shared objects by how many processes they can bring to consensus.

items.name: The consensus problem
items.pic: Processes start with input bits and must output one; a checker flags violations of agreement, validity or termination in runs the reader schedules and faults.

items.name: The two generals problem is unsolvable
items.pic: Remove the last delivered message of a successful run, then the one before, and so on; each step leaves one general’s view unchanged, until a run with no messages must still attack.

items.name: FloodSet: crash-tolerant consensus in f + 1 rounds
items.pic: Processes flood the set of values seen each round while the reader crashes processes mid-broadcast; after f + 1 rounds every survivor holds the same set.

items.name: f + 1 rounds are necessary
items.pic: A chain of runs, each differing from the next by one crash at one round, links an all-0 decision to an all-1 decision; with only f rounds some adjacent pair would disagree.

items.name: Two-phase commit
items.pic: A coordinator collects votes and broadcasts commit or abort; crash the coordinator after the votes and the participants block, waiting indefinitely, in the message diagram.

items.name: Three-phase commit
items.pic: An extra pre-commit phase lets survivors decide after a coordinator crash in synchronous runs; adding a network partition shows the protocol going wrong.

items.name: FLP impossibility
items.pic: Configurations are coloured 0-valent, 1-valent or bivalent; the adversary scheduler keeps the run bivalent forever by delaying one critical message, stepped through on a small system.

items.name: Consensus number hierarchy (Herlihy)
items.pic: Registers solve consensus for one process, test-and-set and queues for two, compare-and-swap for any number; each level’s protocol runs and the next level’s valency argument breaks it.

items.name: Universality of consensus
items.pic: A wait-free queue is built from consensus objects by agreeing on each next operation in a shared log; concurrent histories are checked to be linearizable.

items.name: Ben-Or randomized consensus
items.pic: Processes exchange proposals and flip coins when no majority appears; the number of phases until decision is histogrammed, finite with probability one despite crashes.

items.name: Failure detectors and Ω
items.pic: Each process’s suspect list changes over time; an eventually accurate detector stops suspecting correct processes after an unknown moment, shown on a timeline.

items.name: Consensus under partial synchrony
items.pic: Rotating coordinators propose until timing stabilizes; safety holds throughout, and the decision comes a few rounds after the reader’s chosen stabilization time.

items.name: Wait-free k-set agreement is impossible
items.pic: Executions of three processes form a subdivided triangle coloured by decisions; Sperner’s lemma forces a fully coloured simplex, an execution where three values are decided.

items.name: Approximate agreement
items.pic: Real values are repeatedly averaged after discarding extremes; the spread of correct values halves every round despite faulty inputs, plotted on a log scale.

items.name: Impossibility of Consensus with One Faulty Process
items.pic: Explore the configuration tree of a small asynchronous consensus protocol with configurations coloured 0-valent, 1-valent or bivalent; the reader plays the adversary, delaying one message at each step to keep the run bivalent forever.

chapters.title: Data, recursion and effects
chapters.summary: Real languages add structured data — tuples, records, sums and lists — and general recursion, which gives up termination but keeps safety. Effects need more care: references require store typings to keep preservation true, exceptions and continuations alter control flow, and the continuation-passing transform makes control explicit. Monads package effects inside types, so the type of a computation tells which effects it may perform.

items.name: Let, products and records
items.pic: Build and project records in typed programs; the typing derivation shows the record type assembled field by field and a missing field rejected.

items.name: Sums, variants and pattern matching
items.pic: A variant type for shapes is matched by cases; the checker warns about a missing case and the evaluator shows which branch each value takes.

items.name: General recursion with fix
items.pic: Typed recursive functions run with an unfolding counter; adding fix lets the reader write a well-typed program that loops, and the normalization badge disappears.

items.name: Lists
items.pic: Typed map and fold run on a list the reader edits; the cons-cell diagram is drawn alongside the typing of each operation.

items.name: References and the store
items.pic: Allocate, read and update reference cells; the store is drawn as a heap of labelled cells with arrows from variables, and aliasing is visible when two names share a cell.

items.name: Safety with references via store typings
items.pic: Without a store typing, a cyclic store makes the type of a location undefinable; with one, preservation is checked live as the program allocates and updates.

items.name: Landin’s knot: recursion through the store
items.pic: A function stored in a reference calls whatever the reference holds, then the reference is updated to point to that function; a factorial runs with no fix, breaking normalization.

items.name: Exceptions
items.pic: Raise an exception deep inside nested calls; the evaluation context is unwound frame by frame until a handler catches it, animated on a call stack.

items.name: First-class continuations (call/cc)
items.pic: Capture the rest of the computation as a value and invoke it later; the call stack is snapshotted and restored, making early exit and generators visible.

items.name: Continuation-passing style transform
items.pic: A direct-style program is transformed so every call passes its continuation explicitly; the transformed program runs with a constant-size stack.

items.name: Monads for effects
items.pic: The same program is written with state, exceptions and logging threaded explicitly and then with a monad; the types record which effects are possible, and the two runs agree.

items.name: Recursive Functions of Symbolic Expressions
items.pic: Type S-expressions and watch McCarthy’s eval and apply walk them: atom, car, cdr, cons and cond are evaluated by a short interpreter written in the language itself, and a free-storage counter shows abandoned cells being reclaimed.

chapters.title: Voronoi diagrams and Delaunay triangulations
chapters.summary: The Voronoi diagram divides the plane into the regions closest to each site; its dual, the Delaunay triangulation, connects sites whose circumcircles are empty. Both have linear size and are computed in O(n log n) time by Fortune’s sweep or by randomized incremental insertion with edge flips. Delaunay triangulations maximize the smallest angle, contain the minimum spanning tree and are a lower convex hull in disguise — which is why they underlie terrain interpolation, mesh generation and nearest-neighbour search.

refs: de Berg, Cheong, van Kreveld & Overmars, Computational Geometry
Pharr, Jakob & Humphreys, Physically Based Rendering

items.name: Voronoi diagram
items.pic: Click to add sites; the Voronoi cells are coloured live, and dragging a site shows its cell and its neighbours’ cells deforming.

items.name: Voronoi diagrams have linear complexity
items.pic: For random site sets of growing size, Voronoi vertices and edges are counted and plotted against n, staying under 2n − 5 and 3n − 6.

items.name: Fortune’s sweep-line algorithm
items.pic: A sweep line descends with a beach line of parabolic arcs behind it; site and circle events are queued, and the Voronoi edges are traced by the breakpoints.

items.name: Triangulations of point sets
items.pic: Different triangulations of the same points are generated; all have the same number of triangles, determined by the number of hull and interior points.

items.name: Delaunay triangulation and the empty-circle property
items.pic: Click any triangle to draw its circumcircle; in the Delaunay triangulation every circle is empty, while in an arbitrary triangulation offending points are highlighted.

items.name: Delaunay–Voronoi duality
items.pic: The Voronoi diagram and the Delaunay triangulation are overlaid; each Delaunay edge crosses the Voronoi edge it is dual to, and each Voronoi vertex sits at a circumcentre.

items.name: Delaunay triangulations maximize the minimum angle
items.pic: The sorted angle vectors of the Delaunay triangulation and of random triangulations are compared; Delaunay wins lexicographically every time.

items.name: Edge flipping (Lawson)
items.pic: Start from any triangulation and flip illegal edges whose quadrilateral violates the circle test; flips proceed until none remain and the result is Delaunay.

items.name: Randomized incremental Delaunay triangulation
items.pic: Points are inserted in random order, the containing triangle split and illegal edges flipped; the expected number of structural changes per insertion is plotted and stays constant.

items.name: Lifting map: Delaunay is a lower convex hull
items.pic: Points are lifted onto the paraboloid z = x² + y² in 3D; projecting the lower hull back down gives exactly the Delaunay triangulation, rotated into view.

items.name: The Euclidean minimum spanning tree lies in the Delaunay triangulation
items.pic: The minimum spanning tree of the reader’s points is drawn over the Delaunay triangulation; every tree edge is a Delaunay edge, so only O(n) candidates need to be examined.

items.name: Farthest-point Voronoi diagrams
items.pic: Each region collects the locations farthest from one site; only hull vertices have regions, and the smallest enclosing circle is centred on a vertex or edge of this diagram.

items.name: Lloyd’s algorithm and centroidal Voronoi tessellations
items.pic: Move every site to the centroid of its cell and recompute; the cells relax into a near-hexagonal pattern and the energy readout falls at every step.

items.name: Terrain interpolation on triangulations
items.pic: Height samples are interpolated linearly over two triangulations of the same points; the skinny-triangle version produces spurious ridges, the Delaunay version looks natural.

chapters.title: Electric fields in matter
chapters.summary: An applied field stretches atoms and turns polar molecules, filling matter with tiny dipoles whose average is the polarization P. Its effect is exactly that of bound surface and volume charges, and bookkeeping them separately from free charge leads to the displacement field D. In linear dielectrics this reduces to a permittivity that weakens fields, bends field lines at boundaries, raises capacitance and pulls dielectrics into capacitors.

refs: Feynman, Leighton & Sands, The Feynman Lectures on Physics, Vol. II

items.name: Induced dipoles and atomic polarizability
items.pic: A model atom — a point nucleus in a uniform electron cloud — sits in an applied field: the nucleus shifts until forces balance, and the induced dipole grows linearly until the field nears ionization.

items.name: Orientational polarization of polar molecules
items.pic: A gas of rotating dipoles is jostled by random kicks in an applied field: their mean alignment grows with the field, falls with the agitation, and saturates at strong fields.

items.name: Polarization density
items.pic: Zoom out from a lattice of tiny dipoles to a smooth arrow field P: a sliding averaging window shows how the microscopic jumble becomes a continuum quantity.

items.name: Bound charges: σ_b = P·n̂ and ρ_b = −∇·P
items.pic: Draw a polarization field in a slab: bound charge appears where P meets the boundary or converges, and the field of that charge matches the field of the summed dipoles.

items.name: Uniformly polarized sphere
items.pic: A sphere with uniform P has a uniform interior field −P/3ε₀ and a pure dipole field outside; the bound charge P cos θ is coloured on its surface.

items.name: Displacement field and Gauss’s law in matter
items.pic: A Gaussian surface cuts through a dielectric around a free charge: the flux of D counts only the free charge, the flux of E counts free plus bound, both as live counters.

items.name: Linear dielectrics: permittivity
items.pic: Sweep the applied field on a sample and plot P against E: a straight line of slope ε₀χ at modest fields that bends and saturates at large ones, where the linear model ends.

items.name: Boundary conditions at a dielectric interface
items.pic: A field crosses the boundary between two dielectrics: D⊥ and E∥ are continuous, and a slider for ε₂/ε₁ bends the field lines so that tan θ₂/tan θ₁ = ε₂/ε₁.

items.name: Dielectric-filled capacitor
items.pic: Slide a dielectric slab into a capacitor held at fixed charge or at fixed voltage: capacitance, field and stored energy update, and the two constraints change the energy in opposite directions.

items.name: Dielectrics are pulled into capacitors
items.pic: A slab half inside a capacitor feels the fringing field tug it inward; the force computed from the energy gradient matches the simulated tug at both constant Q and constant V.

items.name: Dielectric sphere in a uniform field
items.pic: Dial the sphere’s ε_r: the interior field stays uniform, reduced by 3/(ε_r + 2), and approaches the conducting-sphere picture as ε_r grows.

items.name: Clausius–Mossotti relation
items.pic: Raise the number density of polarizable atoms: the local-field correction makes ε_r climb faster than the dilute-gas straight line, diverging where the model signals a polarization catastrophe.

items.name: Image charges at a dielectric boundary
items.pic: A charge above a dielectric half-space: an image −q(ε_r − 1)/(ε_r + 1) above and a transmitted charge below satisfy both boundary conditions; ε_r → ∞ recovers the conductor image.

items.name: Energy in dielectric systems
items.pic: Charge a dielectric capacitor and compare ½∫D·E with ½ε₀∫E²: the difference — energy spent stretching the atoms — is shown as its own bar.

items.name: Dielectrophoresis
items.pic: Neutral scraps near a charged comb: each induced dipole is drawn toward stronger field whatever the comb’s sign, and in a uniform field the net force drops to zero.

chapters.title: Geometrical optics
chapters.summary: When wavelengths are short compared with everything else, waves travel along rays that obey the eikonal equation, and Fermat’s principle — the ray takes a path of stationary optical length — is the shadow of stationary phase. The paraxial approximation turns lenses and mirrors into simple formulas and 2×2 matrices that design microscopes, telescopes and the eye; real systems suffer aberrations. Ray optics is Hamiltonian mechanics in disguise, so phase-space volume (étendue) is conserved, which limits how bright an image can be and resolves Olbers’ paradox of the dark night sky.

items.name: Eikonal equation: rays from short waves
items.pic: Shrink the wavelength of a wave crossing a smoothly varying medium: the full wave solution concentrates along curves that match rays traced from the eikonal equation, and diffraction blurs them as λ grows.

items.name: Fermat’s principle from stationary phase
items.pic: Contributions from many trial paths between two points are summed as phasors: only paths near the stationary optical length add up, and that bundle is the ray Fermat predicts.

items.name: Mirages and graded-index optics
items.pic: Set a temperature profile above hot ground: rays bend upward toward lower index and an inverted image of the sky appears on the road; a graded-index rod refocuses rays periodically.

items.name: Optical–mechanical analogy
items.pic: Trace a ray through a graded-index medium and a particle through the matching potential side by side: with n² playing the role of energy minus potential, the two trajectories coincide.

items.name: Perfect imaging by conic surfaces
items.pic: Equal optical paths make a paraboloid focus parallel rays to one point and an ellipsoid image one focus onto the other; switch the mirror to a sphere and the focus smears.

items.name: Thin-lens and lensmaker’s equations
items.pic: Drag an object in front of a lens whose curvatures and index you set: paraxial rays cross where 1/s + 1/s′ = 1/f predicts, and steep rays drift off as the approximation fails.

items.name: Spherical mirrors
items.pic: Move an object along the axis of a concave or convex mirror: the image moves according to the mirror equation, flipping from real and inverted to virtual and upright at the focal point.

items.name: Magnification; real and virtual images
items.pic: Principal rays from the tip of an arrow locate its image; where they actually cross the image is real and can be caught on a screen, where only their extensions meet it is virtual.

items.name: Ray-transfer matrices
items.pic: Stack lenses and gaps from a palette: the system’s 2×2 matrix multiplies live, its determinant stays 1, and rays traced through it agree with the matrix acting on (height, angle).

items.name: Stops, pupils and numerical aperture
items.pic: Move and resize an aperture in a lens system: the cone of accepted rays, the entrance pupil and the numerical aperture update, and image brightness tracks the pupil area.

items.name: The human eye
items.pic: Adjust the eye’s lens power to focus objects at different distances: the near point appears when accommodation runs out, and a corrective lens slider restores focus for a short- or long-sighted eye.

items.name: Microscopes and telescopes
items.pic: Two-lens systems built from focal-length sliders: the telescope’s angular magnification is f₁/f₂ and the microscope’s grows with tube length, with ray bundles traced to the eye.

items.name: Spherical aberration
items.pic: Trace exact rays through a spherical lens at increasing heights: marginal rays focus closer than paraxial ones, and the caustic and blur spot grow with aperture.

items.name: Seidel aberrations
items.pic: Tilt the field angle and the aperture: spot diagrams show coma, astigmatism, field curvature and distortion appearing at their characteristic rates in angle and aperture.

items.name: Chromatic aberration and the achromat
items.pic: A single lens focuses blue closer than red; pair it with a weaker lens of more dispersive glass and choose the powers so two colours share a focus, with the residual colour error plotted.

items.name: Abbe sine condition
items.pic: For a lens corrected for spherical aberration, move a point slightly off axis: the image stays sharp only if n sin θ scales the same way for all rays, which a readout tests ray by ray.

items.name: Conservation of étendue
items.pic: A beam’s rays are plotted as points in (height, angle) space: lenses shear and rotate the patch but never shrink its area, so no passive optics can make an image brighter than its source.

chapters.title: Kinetic theory and transport
chapters.summary: Molecules travel a mean free path between collisions, which sets the rates of effusion, heat conduction, diffusion and viscosity. Random kicks make suspended particles diffuse, Einstein linked their diffusion to mobility, and the Langevin equation shows that the same fluctuations cause friction — the fluctuation–dissipation theorem, with Johnson noise and Onsager’s reciprocal relations as consequences. Boltzmann’s equation, derived from the BBGKY hierarchy, drives gases toward equilibrium through the H-theorem.

refs: Schroeder, An Introduction to Thermal Physics

items.name: Mean free path and collision time
items.pic: Track one molecule in a hard-sphere gas: its free paths are exponentially distributed with mean 1/(√2 nσ), shortening as density and molecular size increase.

items.name: Effusion and Graham’s law
items.pic: Let gas leak through a tiny hole: the escaping flux is nv̄/4, faster molecules escape preferentially, and light isotopes leak faster by √(m₂/m₁).

items.name: Fourier’s law of heat conduction
items.pic: A gas between hot and cold plates: the measured heat flux is proportional to the temperature gradient, with conductivity independent of density as kinetic theory predicts.

items.name: Heat equation
items.pic: Paint an initial temperature profile on a rod: it diffuses and smooths, sharp features fading fastest, and the total energy stays constant with insulated ends.

items.name: Newton’s law of cooling
items.pic: A hot object loses heat through a thin boundary layer: its temperature decays exponentially toward the surroundings, until radiation at high temperature bends the curve.

items.name: Fick’s law of diffusion
items.pic: Dye molecules random-walk from a concentrated region: the net flux across any plane is proportional to the concentration gradient and the profile spreads like √t.

items.name: Viscosity of a gas is independent of pressure
items.pic: Shear a gas between moving plates and lower its density: the drag stays the same because fewer molecules each carry momentum over proportionally longer free paths.

items.name: Brownian motion
items.pic: A large particle in a bath of small molecules: its jittery path is simulated from individual collisions, and its mean kinetic energy settles at (3/2)kT like any molecule.

items.name: Random walks and diffusion
items.pic: Thousands of random walkers spread from the origin: their mean squared displacement grows linearly in time and their histogram approaches a Gaussian of variance 2Dt.

items.name: Einstein relation
items.pic: Apply a weak force to Brownian particles: their drift velocity gives the mobility μ, their spreading gives D, and the ratio D/μ equals kT for every particle size.

items.name: Langevin equation
items.pic: Integrate m dv/dt = −γv + random force: the velocity autocorrelation decays as e^{−γt/m}, and the noise strength needed to keep ⟨½mv²⟩ = ½kT is fixed by γ.

items.name: Fokker–Planck equation
items.pic: Evolve the probability density of Langevin particles in a potential: the density computed from the Fokker–Planck equation matches the histogram of simulated trajectories and relaxes to e^{−V/kT}.

items.name: Fluctuation–dissipation theorem
items.pic: Measure a system’s equilibrium fluctuations and separately its response to a small kick: the response function is the time derivative of the correlation function, plotted together.

items.name: Johnson–Nyquist noise
items.pic: A resistor at temperature T connected to a transmission line: equipartition over the line’s modes gives a voltage noise power 4kTRΔf, verified by the simulated spectrum.

items.name: Onsager reciprocal relations
items.pic: A material carrying heat and charge together: the measured cross-coefficients — current driven by a temperature gradient and heat driven by voltage — come out equal as microscopic reversibility demands.

items.name: Sedimentation equilibrium and Avogadro’s number
items.pic: Colloidal grains settle in a column: their density falls exponentially with height at a rate set by their buoyant weight over kT, from which Perrin extracted Avogadro’s number.

items.name: BBGKY hierarchy
items.pic: From the full N-particle Liouville flow, the one-particle distribution’s evolution depends on the two-particle one, and so on; truncating with an uncorrelated closure is shown to give a closed but approximate equation.

items.name: Boltzmann equation
items.pic: Evolve a velocity distribution under free streaming plus binary collisions: an initially lopsided distribution relaxes to a Maxwellian, matching a direct hard-sphere simulation.

items.name: Boltzmann’s H-theorem
items.pic: Track H = ∫f ln f during the relaxation: it decreases monotonically to its Maxwellian value, while the exact N-body entropy of the simulation stays constant.

items.name: Studien über das Wärmegleichgewicht unter Gasmolekülen
items.pic: Start a hard-sphere gas with every molecule at the same speed and watch the speed histogram relax to Maxwell’s curve while Boltzmann’s H = ∫f ln f falls monotonically; reverse all velocities mid-run to see the objection Loschmidt raised four years later.

items.name: Bewegung von in Flüssigkeiten suspendierten Teilchen
items.pic: Track simulated colloidal beads and plot their mean squared displacement against time: it grows linearly as 2Dt with D = kT/6πηa, so timing the jiggling of a micron-sized bead yields Avogadro’s number — the test Perrin carried out in 1908.

chapters.title: Three dimensions and the hydrogen atom
chapters.summary: In three dimensions separation of variables gives boxes and oscillators with degenerate levels, and central potentials reduce to a radial equation with a centrifugal barrier. The Coulomb potential produces the hydrogen spectrum −13.6 eV/n² with an extra degeneracy explained by a hidden SO(4) symmetry, and orbitals whose shapes underlie chemistry. Reduced-mass corrections, hydrogen-like ions, Rydberg atoms, rotational spectra and the binding threshold of a 3D well complete the picture.

refs: Griffiths & Schroeter, Introduction to Quantum Mechanics (3rd ed.)

items.name: Three-dimensional box and degeneracy
items.pic: Stretch a box’s three sides: levels labelled (n_x, n_y, n_z) split and merge, with degeneracies peaking when the box is a cube.

items.name: Isotropic oscillator in three dimensions
items.pic: Levels of a 3D oscillator are (N + 3/2)ħω with degeneracy (N+1)(N+2)/2, counted both in Cartesian quanta and in (n_r, l) and shown to agree.

items.name: Separation for central potentials
items.pic: For any spherically symmetric potential you draw, eigenstates factor as R(r)Y_l^m(θ, φ): the 3D density is built from a radial plot and a spherical-harmonic surface.

items.name: Radial equation and centrifugal barrier
items.pic: Add the l(l+1)ħ²/2mr² barrier to a potential with an l slider: the effective potential well rises and shifts outward, pushing radial wave functions away from the origin.

items.name: Infinite spherical well
items.pic: Levels of a hard sphere are fixed by zeros of spherical Bessel functions; an l slider shows how angular momentum raises the energies and reorders the spectrum.

items.name: Hydrogen energy levels
items.pic: Solve the radial equation for the Coulomb potential at each l: the energies line up at −13.6 eV/n² independent of l, and screening the potential lifts the coincidence.

items.name: Hydrogen orbitals
items.pic: Render |ψ_nlm|² as a 3D point cloud and radial probability plot: radial and angular nodes add to n − 1, and the most probable radius of 1s is the Bohr radius.

items.name: Hidden SO(4) symmetry of hydrogen
items.pic: Apply the quantum Runge–Lenz operator to a hydrogen eigenstate: it maps between different l at the same n, explaining the degeneracy, and fails for a screened potential.

items.name: The hydrogen spectrum
items.pic: Click transitions on an energy-level diagram: Lyman, Balmer and Paschen lines appear on a wavelength axis, matching the measured lines to the precision of the Rydberg constant.

items.name: Reduced mass and the isotope shift
items.pic: Swap the nucleus between hydrogen, deuterium and tritium: Balmer lines shift by parts in 10⁴ through the reduced mass, as in Urey’s discovery of deuterium.

items.name: Virial theorem in quantum mechanics
items.pic: For eigenstates of power-law potentials rⁿ, ⟨T⟩ and ⟨V⟩ are computed: they satisfy 2⟨T⟩ = n⟨V⟩, giving ⟨T⟩ = −E for hydrogen and equal shares for the oscillator.

items.name: Hydrogen-like ions
items.pic: Raise the nuclear charge Z: energies scale as Z², orbitals shrink as 1/Z, and the spectral lines of He⁺ interleave with those of hydrogen.

items.name: Rydberg atoms
items.pic: Excite hydrogen to n ~ 50 in a superposition of neighbouring levels: a localized wave packet orbits like a Kepler electron, spreads, and partially revives.

items.name: Rigid rotor and rotational spectra
items.pic: A diatomic rotor has levels ħ²l(l+1)/2I: the absorption spectrum shows equally spaced lines, and stretching the bond (larger I) squeezes them together.

items.name: A shallow 3D well need not bind
items.pic: Make a spherical well shallower: unlike in 1D, its bound state disappears at a threshold depth (V₀a² = π²ħ²/8m), the deuteron sitting just above it.

chapters.title: Magnetic order and correlated electrons
chapters.summary: Classical physics forbids magnetism in equilibrium, so magnetic order rests on quantum exchange. Building on the mean-field theory of ferromagnets, this chapter treats antiferromagnets and the Néel temperature, spin waves and the Bloch T^{3/2} law, giant magnetoresistance in layered devices, and what happens when interactions dominate: the Hubbard model’s Mott insulators and the Kondo resistance minimum of magnetic impurities.

refs: Kittel, Introduction to Solid State Physics

items.name: Antiferromagnetism and the Néel temperature
items.pic: Two interpenetrating sublattices with opposite spins: the staggered magnetization appears below T_N, and the susceptibility shows a cusp there instead of a divergence.

items.name: Spin waves (magnons)
items.pic: Precessing spins along a ferromagnetic chain with a phase advancing from site to site: the dispersion is quadratic in k, and counting thermal magnons gives the Bloch T^{3/2} fall of magnetization.

items.name: Giant magnetoresistance
items.pic: Two ferromagnetic layers separated by a spacer: in a two-current resistor model, parallel alignment gives one spin channel a short circuit and antiparallel does not, and the computed resistance drop is plotted against the field that flips one layer.

items.name: Hubbard model and Mott insulators
items.pic: Exactly diagonalise a few-site Hubbard ring at half filling: as U/t grows, charge fluctuations freeze, a gap opens where band theory predicts a metal, and the low-energy spectrum matches a Heisenberg antiferromagnet with J = 4t²/U.

items.name: Kondo effect: the resistance minimum
items.pic: Add dilute magnetic impurities to a metal: spin-flip scattering grows logarithmically as temperature falls, so the computed resistivity passes through a minimum instead of levelling off, as measured in gold with iron impurities.

chapters.title: Query algorithms and quantum search
chapters.summary: Hadamard layers query a function on all inputs at once, and interference extracts global properties: whether a function is constant or balanced (Deutsch–Jozsa), a hidden string (Bernstein–Vazirani) or a hidden period mod 2 (Simon). Grover’s algorithm finds a marked item among N in about √N queries by rotating the state toward the target — optimal by the BBBV bound — and amplitude amplification generalizes it. Interference tests and quantum walks round out the toolkit.

refs: Nielsen & Chuang, Quantum Computation and Quantum Information

items.name: Hadamard transform and quantum parallelism
items.pic: Apply H to each of n qubits: all 2ⁿ inputs appear with equal amplitude, an oracle writes f on all of them at once, and a second H layer shows which interference patterns survive.

items.name: Deutsch’s algorithm
items.pic: Pick one of the four one-bit functions: a single oracle query followed by H tells constant from balanced with certainty, while the amplitudes show the two paths interfering.

items.name: Deutsch–Jozsa algorithm
items.pic: Choose f constant or balanced on n bits: one query sends all amplitude to |0…0⟩ or entirely away from it, compared with the 2^{n−1} + 1 queries a deterministic classical algorithm needs.

items.name: Bernstein–Vazirani algorithm
items.pic: Hide a bit string s in f(x) = s·x mod 2: one quantum query reveals all of s at once, while a classical solver needs n queries, shown side by side.

items.name: Simon’s algorithm
items.pic: Each run returns a random y with y·s = 0; Gaussian elimination over GF(2) on the collected equations recovers the hidden period s after about n runs, versus about 2^{n/2} classical queries.

items.name: Grover’s search algorithm
items.pic: Grover as a rotation in the plane of |marked⟩ and |uniform⟩: each iteration turns the state by 2θ, and the success probability oscillates, peaking near (π/4)√N iterations.

items.name: Amplitude amplification
items.pic: Start from any algorithm with small success probability p: alternating reflections boost it to near 1 in about 1/√p rounds, with overshoot shown if you keep going.

items.name: Hadamard test and swap test
items.pic: A control qubit sandwiched by Hadamards estimates Re⟨ψ|U|ψ⟩; the swap-test version estimates |⟨ψ|φ⟩|² for two states you choose, converging with the number of shots.

items.name: Quantum walks
items.pic: A walker on a line with a coin qubit: the quantum walk spreads ballistically with peaks at the edges while the classical random walk spreads only as √t, plotted together.

chapters.title: Fields and matter in special relativity
chapters.summary: Electric and magnetic fields are two faces of one antisymmetric tensor, so a boost turns one into the other and magnetism appears as electrostatics seen from a moving frame. Maxwell’s equations and charge conservation take a compact covariant form. Matter is described by the stress–energy tensor, whose vanishing divergence packages the conservation of energy and momentum and gives the relativistic equations of a perfect fluid.

refs: Schutz, A First Course in General Relativity
Carroll, Lecture Notes on General Relativity

items.name: Electromagnetic field tensor
items.pic: The six field components are shown as an antisymmetric 4×4 matrix; boosting along x mixes E_y with B_z while the invariants E·B and E² − c²B² stay fixed in the readout.

items.name: Transformation of electric and magnetic fields
items.pic: A static line of charge viewed from a moving frame acquires a current and a circling magnetic field; field arrows are recomputed from the tensor law as the boost slider moves.

items.name: Magnetism as relativistic electrostatics
items.pic: A charge moves beside a neutral current-carrying wire; in the charge’s frame the contracted positive and negative line densities differ, and the resulting electric force equals the lab-frame magnetic force.

items.name: Maxwell’s equations in covariant form
items.pic: Choose a charge–current configuration and a boost: the four-current transforms as a vector, and the fields computed in either frame satisfy the same two tensor equations with residuals read out.

items.name: Charge conservation as a four-divergence
items.pic: Charge flows through a box drawn in spacetime: the four-current flux through its walls balances exactly, the divergence theorem applied in 1+1 dimensions.

items.name: Crossed fields and E×B drift
items.pic: A charge in crossed E and B fields drifts in cycloids; when E < cB a boost slider finds the frame where E vanishes and the motion becomes a pure circle.

items.name: Stress–energy tensor
items.pic: A box of particles: T⁰⁰ counts energy density, T⁰ⁱ energy flux and Tⁱʲ momentum flux, each tallied from the particles; give the box a velocity and watch the components mix.

items.name: Dust and the perfect fluid
items.pic: Random particle velocities in a box produce an isotropic pressure; the measured T is diag(ρc², p, p, p) in the rest frame and acquires off-diagonal terms when boosted.

items.name: Local conservation of energy and momentum
items.pic: For a perfect fluid, the time component of ∂_μT^{μν} = 0 gives the continuity equation and the space components a relativistic Euler equation; a pressure step drives a slab and the conserved totals are read out.

items.name: Electromagnetic stress–energy and radiation pressure
items.pic: For a plane wave the energy density, Poynting flux and radiation pressure are all equal (in units of c); a mirror recoils by the computed momentum when the wave reflects.

chapters.title: Radiative transfer and stellar atmospheres
chapters.summary: Light leaving a star is shaped by a competition between emission and absorption along each ray, described by the specific intensity and the transfer equation. Optical depth measures how far we see in — roughly to depth 2/3 — so photons random-walk for millennia before escaping. A grey atmosphere in the Eddington approximation explains limb darkening, opacity laws set how hard radiation is to push through matter, and line profiles and curves of growth turn spectra into temperatures, pressures and abundances.

refs: Carroll & Ostlie, An Introduction to Modern Astrophysics

items.name: Specific intensity
items.pic: A pencil of rays crosses a surface: intensity stays constant along a ray through empty space, while flux through a detector falls off — shown by moving a detector away from an extended source.

items.name: Opacity, optical depth and mean free path
items.pic: A beam passes through a slab of adjustable opacity and thickness: the transmitted fraction is e^{−τ}, photons’ free paths are sampled, and we see into a star down to about τ = 2/3.

items.name: Equation of radiative transfer
items.pic: Integrate the intensity along a ray through a slab with emission and absorption: it relaxes toward the source function as τ grows, and a temperature gradient decides whether lines appear in absorption or emission.

items.name: Photon random walk out of the Sun
items.pic: A photon random-walks with a mean free path you set: after N steps it has gone about √N steps, so escaping the Sun takes of order (R/ℓ)² steps — tens of thousands of years — compared with 2.3 s in a straight line.

items.name: Grey atmosphere in the Eddington approximation
items.pic: The temperature profile T⁴ = ¾T_e⁴(τ + 2/3) is drawn against optical depth, and the photosphere is found where T equals the effective temperature, at τ = 2/3.

items.name: Limb darkening
items.pic: Render the solar disk from the Eddington atmosphere: near the limb our line of sight reaches τ = 2/3 in cooler layers, so brightness falls to about 40% of the centre, matching observations.

items.name: Kramers opacity law
items.pic: Opacity against temperature and density on log axes: the bound–free and free–free Kramers slope κ ∝ ρT^{−3.5}, the electron-scattering floor and the H⁻ hump in cool stars are drawn as separate contributions.

items.name: Curve of growth
items.pic: Raise the column density of absorbers: the line deepens linearly, saturates, then grows damping wings; the equivalent width versus N on log axes traces the three regimes.

items.name: Spectral line broadening
items.pic: A Voigt profile is built from a thermal Gaussian core and a Lorentzian wing from natural and pressure broadening; temperature and pressure sliders separate giants from dwarfs of the same colour.

chapters.title: Aerofoils and lift
chapters.summary: A conformal map takes the flow round a circle to the flow round an aerofoil, and among all possible circulations nature picks the one that makes the flow leave the sharp trailing edge smoothly — the Kutta condition. That fixes the lift, gives the classic 2π slope of lift against angle of attack, and requires a starting vortex to be shed. Thin-aerofoil and lifting-line theories extend the picture to cambered sections and finite wings, where trailing vortices bring induced drag.

items.name: Joukowski transformation
items.pic: Drag the centre and radius of a circle in the ζ-plane: the map z = ζ + c²/ζ turns it live into a flat plate, a symmetric aerofoil or a cambered one with a cusped trailing edge.

items.name: Potential flow past a Joukowski aerofoil
items.pic: Potential flow past a Joukowski aerofoil via the conformal map: angle-of-attack and circulation sliders reshape the streamlines and the surface pressure distribution computed on both sides.

items.name: Kutta condition
items.pic: With zero circulation the flow whips round the sharp trailing edge at unbounded speed; raise the circulation until the rear stagnation point sits exactly on the edge and the singularity disappears.

items.name: Lift coefficient C_L = 2π sin α
items.pic: Sweep the angle of attack: the lift coefficient from the Kutta circulation follows 2π sin α (with a thickness correction), plotted against wind-tunnel data that agree until the wing stalls.

items.name: Starting vortex
items.pic: An aerofoil starts moving impulsively: a vortex rolls up at the trailing edge and is left behind, and the circulation round a loop enclosing both wing and wake stays at zero as Kelvin’s theorem demands.

items.name: The equal-transit-time fallacy
items.pic: Release paired particles just ahead of the aerofoil in the computed flow: the upper one reaches the trailing edge well before its partner, refuting the popular claim that they must meet again.

items.name: Thin-aerofoil theory
items.pic: Draw a camber line: the vortex-sheet strength along it is solved so the surface is a streamline, giving the lift and the pitching moment about the quarter chord as you reshape the line.

items.name: Lifting-line theory and induced drag
items.pic: A finite wing sheds a sheet of trailing vortices that roll up at the tips; the downwash they induce tilts the lift backward, and an aspect-ratio slider shows induced drag falling while elliptic loading minimises it.

chapters.title: Mixtures and solutions
chapters.summary: In a mixture each component carries its own chemical potential, and partial molar quantities and the Gibbs–Duhem equation keep the books. Raoult's law describes ideal solutions and Henry's law dilute solutes; activities measure the departure from both. Because a solute lowers the solvent's chemical potential, it changes boiling and freezing points and creates osmotic pressure — the colligative properties, which count particles regardless of their identity.

refs: McQuarrie & Simon, Physical Chemistry: A Molecular Approach

items.name: Partial molar quantities
items.pic: Add ethanol to water drop by drop and track the total volume: it falls short of the sum, and the tangent to the volume-versus-composition curve gives each partial molar volume, which changes with composition.

items.name: Chemical potential
items.pic: Two compartments share one component through a membrane: particles flow from high to low μ until the values equalize, shown as levels in connected vessels.

items.name: Gibbs–Duhem equation
items.pic: Drag the partial molar volume curve of one component in a binary mixture: the other component’s curve is recomputed by Gibbs–Duhem and moves in the opposite direction, weighted by the mole fractions.

items.name: Gibbs energy and entropy of mixing of perfect gases
items.pic: Remove the partition between two gases: ΔG_mix = nRT Σ xᵢ ln xᵢ is plotted against composition, always negative, with the enthalpy of mixing exactly zero — mixing is driven purely by entropy.

items.name: Raoult’s law and ideal solutions
items.pic: Plot partial and total vapour pressures over benzene–toluene against composition: straight lines from tabulated data, then switch to acetone–chloroform and watch the curves sag below them.

items.name: Henry’s law
items.pic: Raise the partial pressure of CO₂ over water: the dissolved concentration rises linearly with a temperature-dependent Henry constant, and opening a simulated soda bottle releases the excess as bubbles.

items.name: Ideal-dilute solutions
items.pic: For a real binary mixture, the solvent’s vapour pressure hugs Raoult’s line near pure solvent and the solute’s hugs a Henry line near infinite dilution; the shaded regions show where each limiting law is trustworthy.

items.name: Activity and activity coefficients
items.pic: Read activity coefficients off measured vapour-pressure curves with either the Raoult or Henry reference: the same data give coefficients that go to 1 at opposite ends, depending on the convention chosen.

items.name: Regular solutions
items.pic: Add an interaction parameter ξ to ideal mixing: ΔG_mix develops two minima when ξ > 2, and the activity coefficients follow ln γ = ξ(1 − x)² on the readout.

items.name: Colligative properties
items.pic: Dissolve particles in a solvent and show its chemical potential line dropping by RT ln x; the intersections with the solid and vapour lines move, the same for sugar, salt (counted as ions) or urea.

items.name: Boiling-point elevation
items.pic: Add solute molality with a slider: the boiling point rises by K_b·m, with water’s K_b computed from its enthalpy of vaporization, and salting pasta water is shown to change it by far less than a degree.

items.name: Freezing-point depression
items.pic: Salt an icy road: the freezing point of the brine falls with concentration until the eutectic at −21 °C, below which salt stops helping, and a cryoscopic molar-mass determination is run on a mystery solute.

items.name: Osmotic pressure (van ’t Hoff equation)
items.pic: A U-tube with a semipermeable membrane: solvent flows into the solution side until the column height balances Π = cRT, and the readout uses the height to find the molar mass of a protein.

items.name: Reverse osmosis desalination
items.pic: Push on the seawater side of a membrane: below the osmotic pressure fresh water flows the wrong way, above it the permeate flux grows linearly, and the minimum energy per cubic metre is read out.

items.name: Ideal solubility and the van ’t Hoff solubility equation
items.pic: Plot ln x_solute against 1/T for naphthalene in benzene: the slope is fixed by the enthalpy of fusion alone, independent of the solvent, until a strongly interacting solvent bends the line.

items.name: Nernst distribution law
items.pic: Shake iodine between water and an organic layer: the concentration ratio settles to a fixed partition coefficient, and repeated small extractions are shown to beat one big one.

items.name: Rolle des osmotischen Druckes: Lösungen und Gase
items.pic: Fill Pfeffer’s semipermeable cell with sugar solutions of rising strength and plot osmotic pressure against concentration and temperature: the points fall on πV = nRT with the gas constant itself, while salt solutions overshoot by a factor i the reader can tune.

chapters.title: Reactions in solution and at electrodes
chapters.summary: In a liquid, reactants meet slowly but stay together long: the solvent cage turns an encounter into many collisions. When chemistry is fast, the rate is limited by diffusion, as Smoluchowski calculated; for ions, charges and ionic strength modify it. Acid–base catalysis, the salt effect, Marcus theory of electron transfer and the Butler–Volmer description of electrode currents complete the solution-phase toolkit.

refs: Houston, Chemical Kinetics and Reaction Dynamics
Steinfeld, Francisco & Hase, Chemical Kinetics and Dynamics

items.name: Cage effect and encounter pairs
items.pic: Two solute particles meet in a crowded 2D liquid: they rattle against each other many times before escaping, and a histogram counts collisions per encounter compared with a gas.

items.name: Smoluchowski diffusion-limited rate constant
items.pic: Particles diffuse toward an absorbing sphere: the steady concentration profile is computed, the flux gives k = 4πRD, and the readout shows water’s typical 10⁹–10¹⁰ M⁻¹s⁻¹ limit.

items.name: Activation-controlled versus diffusion-controlled limits
items.pic: Lower the intrinsic barrier of a reaction in solution: the observed rate constant rises and then saturates at the diffusion limit, with viscosity becoming the only control knob.

items.name: Debye–Smoluchowski effect for ions
items.pic: Give the reactants charges of the same or opposite sign: the diffusion-limited rate is boosted or suppressed by the Coulomb factor, and adding salt screens the effect over the Debye length.

items.name: Primary kinetic salt effect (Brønsted–Bjerrum)
items.pic: Plot log k against √I for reactions with z_A z_B = +4, 0 and −2: three straight lines with slopes set by the charge product, valid only in dilute solutions where the Debye–Hückel law holds.

items.name: Brønsted catalysis law
items.pic: Catalyse a reaction with a series of acids: log k_cat against pKa falls on a line of slope α, and very strong acids drift off as proton transfer becomes diffusion-controlled.

items.name: Marcus theory of electron transfer
items.pic: Two parabolas represent reactant and product free energies: lowering the product parabola first lowers the crossing barrier, then raises it again, and the rate traces the inverted parabola in ln k against −ΔG°.

items.name: The Marcus inverted region
items.pic: Push −ΔG° beyond the reorganization energy: the computed rate decreases despite a stronger driving force, and measured data on linked donor–acceptor pairs are overlaid to confirm it.

items.name: Butler–Volmer equation
items.pic: Apply an overpotential to an electrode: anodic and cathodic currents grow exponentially in opposite directions, their sum is zero at equilibrium, and the transfer-coefficient slider skews the curve.

items.name: Tafel equation
items.pic: Replot the Butler–Volmer current on log axes: at large overpotential one branch becomes a straight Tafel line whose intercept gives the exchange current density, and mass-transport limits bend it at high current.

items.name: Oxidation–reduction reactions involving electron transfer
items.pic: Slide two parabolic free-energy curves past each other: the barrier (λ + ΔG°)²/4λ falls as the reaction grows more downhill, vanishes at −ΔG° = λ and rises again beyond it, and the reader fits measured self-exchange and cross rates with one reorganization energy.

chapters.title: The chemical bond in diatomic molecules
chapters.summary: The Born–Oppenheimer approximation separates electrons from nuclei and gives each molecule a potential energy curve. Building molecular orbitals as linear combinations of atomic orbitals explains why H₂⁺ binds, why bonding and antibonding are not symmetric, why He₂ does not exist and why O₂ is magnetic. Valence-bond theory offers the competing picture, and each fails where the other succeeds.

items.name: Potential energy curves
items.pic: Drag two atoms together and trace the energy curve point by point; mark the equilibrium length, the well depth and the curvature that sets the vibrational frequency.

items.name: H₂⁺ by LCAO
items.pic: Combine two 1s functions with + and − signs at an adjustable separation: the bonding orbital piles charge between the nuclei, the antibonding one has a node there, and both energy curves are computed live.

items.name: Overlap, Coulomb and resonance integrals
items.pic: Plot S, J and K against internuclear distance as two orbitals slide apart; the shaded overlap region shrinks to zero and the resonance integral that holds the bond together dies with it.

items.name: Antibonding is more antibonding than bonding is bonding
items.pic: With an overlap slider, the bonding level drops by (α+β)/(1+S) and the antibonding rises by more; at S = 0 the asymmetry disappears, which is exactly the Hückel simplification.

items.name: Valence-bond theory of H₂ (Heitler–London)
items.pic: Build the covalent spin-paired wavefunction and compare its energy curve with the triplet: only the singlet binds, and the readout gives the well depth against experiment.

items.name: MO theory’s failure at dissociation
items.pic: Pull H₂ apart: the simple MO curve dissociates to a mix of H + H and H⁺ + H⁻ and rises too high, while the valence-bond curve goes correctly to two atoms; a mixing slider shows how CI repairs it.

items.name: MO diagrams of second-row diatomics and bond order
items.pic: Pick a diatomic from Li₂ to Ne₂ and fill the MO diagram; bond order is counted live and plotted against measured bond lengths and energies, with He₂ and Ne₂ at zero.

items.name: Paramagnetism of O₂
items.pic: Fill O₂’s π* orbitals: two unpaired electrons follow Hund’s rule, and a simulated stream of liquid oxygen bends toward a magnet while liquid nitrogen falls straight.

items.name: s–p mixing and the N₂/O₂ level switch
