items.pic: Vary the 2s–2p gap across the row: when it is small, σ orbitals of the same symmetry repel and σ₂p rises above π₂p (as in N₂); when it is large the ordering flips back (as in O₂).

items.name: Heteronuclear diatomics and bond polarity
items.pic: Move one atomic level downward to mimic a more electronegative partner: the bonding orbital takes on its character, charge shifts, and the dipole moment readout grows toward the ionic limit.

items.name: Morse potential
items.pic: Overlay a Morse well and its harmonic approximation; the numerically computed levels crowd together toward the dissociation limit while the harmonic ladder marches on with equal steps forever.

items.name: The atom and the molecule
items.pic: Build molecules from Lewis’s cubical atoms: place valence electrons on the corners, let neighbouring cubes share an edge (one shared pair) or a face (a double bond), and see the octet rule predict the formulas of water, ammonia, methane, ethylene and common ions — then watch it strain at boron trifluoride.

items.name: Wechselwirkung neutraler Atome und homöopolare Bindung
items.pic: Bring two hydrogen atoms together and compute the energy with symmetric and antisymmetric combinations of atomic orbitals: the singlet curve dips into a bond near 0.87 Å with about 3.1 eV of binding, the triplet repels at every distance, and both are compared with the exact curve.

chapters.title: The reciprocal lattice
chapters.summary: Every lattice has a dual whose points correspond to families of lattice planes: the reciprocal lattice vector g_hkl is normal to (hkl) with length 1/d. It is also the set of wavevectors of plane waves with the lattice's periodicity, so a lattice-periodic density is a Fourier series over the reciprocal lattice — and the Fourier transform of a lattice of points is the reciprocal lattice. This is the language of diffraction.

refs: Hammond, The Basics of Crystallography and Diffraction
Giacovazzo et al., Fundamentals of Crystallography

items.name: Reciprocal lattice
items.pic: Drag the direct lattice vectors of a 2D lattice: the reciprocal vectors defined by aᵢ·bⱼ = δᵢⱼ are drawn beside them and swing perpendicular, lengthening as the direct vectors shorten.

items.name: g_hkl is normal to (hkl) with |g| = 1/d
items.pic: Click a reciprocal lattice point: the corresponding family of direct-lattice planes is drawn perpendicular to it, and the readout confirms the plane spacing is the reciprocal of the vector length.

items.name: Reciprocal of fcc is bcc
items.pic: Construct the reciprocal lattice of fcc in 3D: it is body-centred cubic and vice versa, and the first Brillouin zone of fcc appears as the truncated octahedron.

items.name: Brillouin zones
items.pic: Colour the reciprocal plane by how many Bragg planes separate each point from the origin: the first, second and third zones appear as interlocking shards, each with the same total area.

items.name: Periodic functions expand over the reciprocal lattice
items.pic: Build a 2D periodic density by adding plane waves with wavevectors on reciprocal-lattice points: any other wavevector breaks the periodicity, visible as a pattern that drifts from cell to cell.

items.name: The Fourier transform of a lattice is its reciprocal lattice
items.pic: Compute the FFT of a finite patch of lattice points: sharp peaks appear on the reciprocal lattice, narrowing as the patch grows, and distorting the lattice smears them into streaks.

chapters.title: Fracture, fatigue and creep
chapters.summary: Materials fail by cracks that grow, by repeated loading far below the yield stress, or by slow flow at high temperature. Griffith's energy balance and the stress-intensity factor explain why flaws control brittle strength and why that strength is statistical; S–N curves and the Paris law govern fatigue; and creep laws, Larson–Miller extrapolation and deformation-mechanism maps tell how long a hot component will last.

refs: Callister & Rethwisch, Materials Science and Engineering
Porter & Easterling, Phase Transformations in Metals and Alloys

items.name: Ductile versus brittle fracture
items.pic: Break a bar of copper and a bar of glass in simulation: cup-and-cone fracture with large strain versus a flat cleavage surface with almost none, drawn with the stress–strain curves side by side.

items.name: Stress concentration at holes and notches
items.pic: Pull a plate containing an elliptical hole: the computed stress at the tip rises as 1 + 2a/b, reaching 3 for a circle and diverging as the ellipse flattens into a crack.

items.name: Griffith criterion
items.pic: Grow a crack in a stressed plate: released elastic energy rises as a², the new-surface cost as a, and beyond the critical length the energy curve tips downhill and the crack runs.

items.name: Stress intensity and fracture toughness K_IC
items.pic: Choose a material and crack length: K = Yσ√(πa) is compared with K_IC, and a failure map shows which combinations of stress and flaw size are safe for steel, aluminium and glass.

items.name: Ductile-to-brittle transition
items.pic: Run simulated Charpy tests across temperature for bcc steel and fcc aluminium: the steel’s absorbed energy collapses below a transition temperature — the failure of the Liberty ships — while aluminium’s does not.

items.name: Weibull statistics of brittle strength
items.pic: Break hundreds of ceramic bars with random flaw populations: failure strengths follow a Weibull distribution, and larger specimens are weaker because they are likelier to contain a big flaw.

items.name: S–N curves and Basquin’s law
items.pic: Cycle a specimen at different stress amplitudes: cycles to failure fall on a straight line on log axes, and steel shows a flat fatigue limit while aluminium keeps declining.

items.name: Creep: primary, secondary and tertiary
items.pic: Hold a hot specimen at constant load: strain against time shows a decelerating, then steady, then accelerating stage, and raising the temperature or load shortens every stage.

items.name: Power-law creep and the Larson–Miller parameter
items.pic: Plot steady creep rate against stress on log axes for several temperatures: lines of slope n shifted by an Arrhenius factor, collapsed onto one master curve by the Larson–Miller parameter.

items.name: Deformation-mechanism maps
items.pic: Drag a point over a stress–homologous-temperature map for nickel: regions of dislocation glide, power-law creep and diffusional creep are coloured with contours of strain rate, and grain size moves the boundaries.

chapters.title: Gravity, isostasy and flexure
chapters.summary: Mountains float. Gravity surveys show that high topography is compensated by low-density roots (Airy) or lighter columns (Pratt), so the lithosphere stands in buoyant equilibrium on the mantle. On shorter scales the lithosphere bends like an elastic plate under loads, producing outer rises at trenches; when ice sheets melt, the land rebounds at a rate set by mantle viscosity.

refs: Stein & Wysession, An Introduction to Seismology, Earthquakes, and Earth Structure

items.name: Gravity anomalies: free-air and Bouguer
items.pic: Fly a gravimeter over a buried dense body and a mountain: free-air and Bouguer corrections are applied step by step, and the Bouguer anomaly over a compensated mountain is strongly negative.

items.name: Airy isostasy
items.pic: Raise a mountain of crust floating on mantle: a root about 6–7 times the height develops beneath it, as for an iceberg, and the pressure at a compensation depth is equal everywhere.

items.name: Pratt isostasy
items.pic: Compensate topography by varying column density instead of thickness: high regions are lighter, and the two models predict different gravity signatures you can compare.

items.name: Flexure of the lithosphere as an elastic plate
items.pic: Load an elastic plate floating on a fluid with a seamount: the plate bends into a moat with a peripheral bulge, and the flexural wavelength grows with the plate’s elastic thickness slider.

items.name: Outer rise at ocean trenches
items.pic: Bend a plate down at a trench: an outer rise a few hundred metres high forms seaward, and fitting its shape to real bathymetry yields the elastic thickness of the lithosphere.

items.name: Post-glacial rebound and mantle viscosity
items.pic: Remove an ice sheet and let the depressed lithosphere recover over a viscous half-space: uplift decays exponentially, and fitting Scandinavian rebound data gives a mantle viscosity near 10²¹ Pa·s (Haskell).

items.name: Geoid anomalies
items.pic: Compute the geoid height over compensated and uncompensated loads: compensated topography gives a small dipole-like signal while uncompensated loads give large bumps, so the geoid probes deep density.

chapters.title: Vorticity and potential vorticity
chapters.summary: Vorticity is the local spin of a fluid; on a rotating planet the planet's own spin adds to it. Kelvin's theorem makes circulation a conserved quantity, and its column form — potential vorticity — is the master variable of large-scale dynamics: squeezing a column slows its spin, moving it poleward changes its planetary vorticity. Sverdrup balance and western boundary currents follow directly.

refs: Vallis, Essentials of Atmospheric and Oceanic Dynamics

items.name: Relative, planetary and absolute vorticity
items.pic: Drop paddle-wheels into a weather map: each reads the relative vorticity of the wind, added to the planetary value f to give absolute vorticity, mapped in colour.

items.name: Kelvin’s circulation theorem in a rotating frame
items.pic: Move a material ring of air poleward: absolute circulation is conserved, so the ring spins up anticyclonically relative to the ground, and baroclinic density gradients are shown generating circulation.

items.name: Conservation of shallow-water potential vorticity
items.pic: Follow a fluid column through a shallow-water simulation: (ζ + f)/h stays constant along its path even as its depth, latitude and spin all change, with a running readout to check it.

items.name: Ertel potential vorticity
items.pic: Compute (ω + 2Ω)·∇θ/ρ on a 3D flow: it is conserved for adiabatic frictionless motion, and maps of it on an isentropic surface show stratospheric intrusions as tongues of high PV.

items.name: Flow over mountains and lee troughs
items.pic: Blow westerlies over a ridge: columns squash and turn anticyclonic over the crest, then stretch and turn cyclonic downstream, setting up a train of lee troughs as the β effect acts.

items.name: Sverdrup balance
items.pic: Apply a wind-stress curl over an ocean basin: the interior meridional transport βV equals the curl, so anticyclonic winds drive equatorward flow across the whole subtropical gyre interior.

items.name: Western intensification (Stommel)
items.pic: Solve Stommel’s gyre model with and without β: without it the gyre is symmetric, with it the return flow crowds into a narrow, fast western boundary current like the Gulf Stream.

items.name: Potential-vorticity inversion
items.pic: Paint a blob of high PV on a map: the balanced wind and temperature fields are computed by inverting an elliptic operator, giving a cyclone whose reach scales with the deformation radius.

items.name: The westward intensification of wind-driven ocean currents
items.pic: Drive Stommel’s rectangular ocean with the same wind and bottom friction three times — no rotation, uniform rotation, and a Coriolis parameter that grows northward — and watch the symmetric gyre crowd into a narrow, fast western boundary current only in the third case: the Gulf Stream in miniature.

chapters.title: Energy-balance models, bistability and tipping points
chapters.summary: Adding latitude and heat transport to the energy balance gives the Budyko–Sellers models, whose ice-albedo feedback creates multiple equilibria: a warm Earth with polar caps, an unstable small-cap state and a Snowball Earth, joined by saddle-node bifurcations and hysteresis. Similar bistability appears in the ocean overturning and in ice sheets, and critical slowing down offers a warning sign before a tipping point.

refs: Archer, Global Warming: Understanding the Forecast

items.name: Budyko–Sellers diffusive energy-balance model
items.pic: Solve the latitudinal energy balance with diffusive heat transport and temperature-dependent albedo: the equilibrium temperature profile and ice line are computed as the solar constant and diffusivity change.

items.name: Multiple equilibria of the ice line
items.pic: Plot equilibrium ice-line latitude against the solar constant: an S-shaped curve with stable warm and snowball branches and an unstable middle branch, joined at saddle-node points.

items.name: Snowball Earth hysteresis
items.pic: Lower the solar constant until the ice line runs to the equator, then raise it back: the planet stays frozen far above the original threshold, tracing a hysteresis loop on the bifurcation diagram.

items.name: Small ice-cap instability
items.pic: Shrink the polar cap in the diffusive model: below a critical size the cap cannot persist and vanishes abruptly, because diffusion smooths away a small cold region.

items.name: Escaping a Snowball by CO₂ build-up
items.pic: Freeze the planet, shut down weathering, and let volcanic CO₂ accumulate: after millions of years the forcing crosses the deglaciation threshold and the planet flips into a hot greenhouse state.

items.name: Daisyworld
items.pic: Grow black and white daisies with a temperature-dependent growth rate as the Sun brightens: the planet’s temperature stays nearly constant over a wide range of luminosity, then collapses at the edges.

items.name: Tipping points and critical slowing down
items.pic: Drive a noisy bistable system slowly toward a saddle-node: the recovery rate from perturbations falls, autocorrelation and variance rise in the time series, and the warning precedes the jump.

items.name: Stommel’s box model of thermohaline bistability
items.pic: Add freshwater to a two-box ocean: the temperature-driven overturning weakens and then collapses to a reversed salinity-driven state, with hysteresis as the freshwater flux is reduced again.

items.name: Ice-sheet hysteresis and the height–mass-balance feedback
items.pic: Grow an ice sheet whose surface cools as it thickens: under the same climate a high sheet survives while a low one cannot form, so melting it requires warming well beyond where it first grew.

items.name: The effect of solar radiation variations on the climate
items.pic: Run Budyko’s latitude-by-latitude energy balance with ice wherever the mean temperature falls below about −10 °C: lower the solar constant and the ice line creeps toward the equator until, after a cut of only a percent or two, it runs away and covers the planet; raise it again and the ice stays.

chapters.title: Scale, generalization and representation
chapters.summary: A map is a deliberate simplification. Its scale decides what can be shown, and coastlines reveal that measured length depends on the ruler. Generalization algorithms such as Douglas–Peucker thin lines, Töpfer's law says how many features to keep, and the way areas are aggregated or resized — choropleths, the modifiable areal unit problem, cartograms — can change the story a map tells. Four colours always suffice to tell neighbours apart.

refs: Snyder, Map Projections — A Working Manual (USGS, public domain)

items.name: Map scale and the representative fraction
items.pic: Zoom a map and watch the representative fraction change: on a world map the stated scale holds only along standard lines, and a scale bar is shown varying with latitude on Mercator.

items.name: The coastline paradox
items.pic: Measure a fractal coastline with rulers of decreasing length: the total keeps growing, and log length against log ruler size gives Richardson’s straight line whose slope reads the fractal dimension.

items.name: Douglas–Peucker line simplification
items.pic: Simplify a digitized coastline with a tolerance slider: the algorithm keeps the farthest point recursively, the vertex count falls fast, and the maximum deviation never exceeds the tolerance.

items.name: Töpfer’s radical law of selection
items.pic: Reduce the map scale and keep n_f = n_a √(M_a/M_f) features: towns are dropped in order of size, compared with keeping all of them, which clutters the small map illegibly.

items.name: Contours and the representation of relief
items.pic: Generate a terrain surface and slice it at regular heights: contour spacing reveals slope, the gradient arrows cross contours at right angles, and a hillshade toggle shows the same relief by illumination.

items.name: The modifiable areal unit problem
items.pic: Aggregate the same point data into different zone systems: the choropleth map and the computed correlation between two variables change dramatically with the zoning, even reversing sign.

items.name: Density-equalizing cartograms
items.pic: Let population diffuse until density is uniform, dragging the map with it (the Gastner–Newman method): countries swell or shrink to areas proportional to their populations while staying recognizable.

items.name: Four colour theorem for maps
items.pic: Colour a map of regions so neighbours differ: a greedy colouring may need five or six colours, but backtracking always succeeds with four, and the adjacency graph is shown to be planar.

chapters.title: Mutation, migration and load
chapters.summary: Selection rarely acts alone. Recurrent deleterious mutation keeps harmful alleles at low equilibrium frequencies and imposes a load on mean fitness that, remarkably, depends only on the mutation rate. Migration can swamp local adaptation or be held in check by it. Haldane’s dilemma about the cost of substitution and Eigen’s error threshold show how these balances limit the pace and fidelity of evolution.

refs: Gillespie, Population Genetics: A Concise Guide
Nielsen & Slatkin, An Introduction to Population Genetics

items.name: Mutation–selection balance
items.pic: Deleterious mutations flow in at rate μ and selection removes them; the equilibrium frequency settles at √(μ/s) for a recessive allele and μ/(hs) for a partially dominant one, both plotted against the simulation.

items.name: Genetic load
items.pic: Compare mean fitness with that of the best genotype in populations carrying mutational, segregational and drift load; each load is shown as the shortfall bar.

items.name: Haldane–Muller principle: load depends only on the mutation rate
items.pic: Vary the harmfulness s of the mutations over three orders of magnitude; the equilibrium load stays pinned at about μ (recessive) or 2μ (partially dominant), because milder alleles become commoner.

items.name: Haldane’s dilemma: the cost of substitution
items.pic: Count the selective deaths needed to substitute one allele by selection and compare with the reproductive excess available; at most about one substitution per few hundred generations seems affordable.

items.name: Error catastrophe in quasispecies (Eigen)
items.pic: A master sequence replicates with per-site error rate u; raise u past roughly ln(σ)/L and the master sequence is lost and the population delocalizes over sequence space.

items.name: Continent–island migration
items.pic: A fraction m of the island is replaced by continental migrants each generation; the island allele frequency approaches the continent’s geometrically at rate (1 − m).

items.name: Migration–selection balance
items.pic: Local selection favours an allele the migrants lack; when m exceeds s the local adaptation is swamped, and the equilibrium frequency is plotted against m/s.

items.name: Meiotic drive
items.pic: A driving allele is transmitted to more than half of a heterozygote’s gametes but harms homozygotes; the allele spreads to a polymorphic equilibrium despite lowering mean fitness.

chapters.title: Biochemical kinetics
chapters.summary: Molecules meet and react at rates set by mass action, and separating fast binding from slow catalysis produces the Michaelis–Menten law. This chapter treats that reduction honestly — when it is valid and how it can mislead in a linearized plot — and builds the toolkit of inhibition, cooperativity and allostery. Zero-order ultrasensitivity and autocatalysis show how simple chemistry produces switch-like and oscillatory behaviour that later chapters use.

items.name: Ligand binding and the Langmuir isotherm
items.pic: Add ligand to receptors and watch the fraction occupied rise hyperbolically; it is exactly one half at the dissociation constant K_d, marked on both linear and log axes.

items.name: Michaelis–Menten mechanism
items.pic: Integrate the full enzyme–substrate–complex–product system; the complex rises quickly to a plateau while substrate is consumed slowly, shown on two time scales.

items.name: Quasi-steady-state approximation
items.pic: Overlay the reduced Michaelis–Menten rate law on the full mass-action simulation; the product curves agree after a brief initial transient whose length is shown.

items.name: Validity of the QSSA (Segel–Slemrod condition)
items.pic: Raise total enzyme toward the substrate level; the error between reduced and full models grows exactly as the ratio E₀/(S₀ + K_m) stops being small.

items.name: Lineweaver–Burk plot and its distortions
items.pic: Generate noisy rate data and fit them by double-reciprocal regression and by direct nonlinear least squares; the reciprocal plot amplifies low-substrate noise and the fitted V_max wanders.

items.name: Competitive and uncompetitive inhibition
items.pic: Add inhibitor and watch the rate curve: competitive inhibition shifts the apparent K_m but not V_max, uncompetitive lowers both, and the Lineweaver–Burk lines rotate or shift accordingly.

items.name: Cooperative binding and the Hill equation
items.pic: Slide the Hill coefficient from 1 to 8 and the binding curve sharpens from hyperbolic to switch-like; the Hill plot’s slope reads the coefficient back.

items.name: Monod–Wyman–Changeux allosteric model
items.pic: Each four-site protein flips between tense and relaxed states while binding ligand; the population-averaged saturation curve is sigmoidal although no single site is cooperative.

items.name: Goldbeter–Koshland zero-order ultrasensitivity
items.pic: A protein is modified by a kinase and reverted by a phosphatase; as both enzymes approach saturation the steady-state modified fraction jumps from near 0 to near 1 over a tiny change in kinase activity.

items.name: Conservation laws and reduced reaction networks
items.pic: Draw a reaction network; the stoichiometric matrix is built and its left null space gives conserved totals, which stay flat in the simulation while individual species change.

items.name: Detailed balance and the Wegscheider condition
items.pic: In a three-state reaction cycle, edit the six rate constants; unless their cycle product ratio equals 1 a net circulating flux persists at steady state, which requires an energy source.

items.name: Autocatalysis and the Brusselator
items.pic: Raise the feed parameter of the Brusselator past its Hopf threshold; concentrations start to oscillate and the phase-plane trajectory settles onto a limit cycle.

items.name: Aggregation of Haemoglobin and its Dissociation Curves
items.pic: Hill’s curve fitting: oxygen saturation y = Kxⁿ/(1 + Kxⁿ) is fitted to a measured haemoglobin dissociation curve; slide n and K and see that n = 1, a single site, gives a hyperbola that cannot match the sigmoid, while a non-integer n well above 1 fits — Hill’s point that n need not count real binding sites — then read n off the Hill plot as a slope.

chapters.title: Predation, parasitism and mutualism
chapters.summary: Predators search, handle and choose prey in ways that optimal foraging theory predicts, and their functional and numerical responses decide whether predator–prey systems cycle or settle. Famous field and laboratory systems — hares and lynx, Huffaker’s mites — test the theory. Parasites and pathogens regulate host populations, shared enemies create apparent competition, and mutualistic networks have their own characteristic structure.

refs: Begon, Townsend & Harper, Ecology: From Individuals to Ecosystems
MacArthur & Wilson, The Theory of Island Biogeography
Brown et al., Toward a Metabolic Theory of Ecology

items.name: Holling’s disc equation
items.pic: A blindfolded searcher picks up sandpaper discs on a table; intake rate saturates with disc density as handling time eats into search time, matching aN/(1 + ahN).

items.name: Marginal value theorem (Charnov)
items.pic: Draw a diminishing gain curve within a patch and the travel time between patches; the optimal leaving time is where a line from the travel origin is tangent to the curve, and longer travel means staying longer.

items.name: Optimal diet model and the zero–one rule
items.pic: Rank prey types by energy per handling time; as the best prey becomes commoner, lower-ranked types drop out of the optimal diet abruptly, independent of their own abundance.

items.name: Snowshoe hare–lynx cycles
items.pic: Hudson’s Bay Company fur records show ten-year cycles; compare them with a fitted predator–prey model and with a version in which food limitation of hares also plays a part.

items.name: Ratio-dependent predation (Arditi–Ginzburg)
items.pic: Make the functional response depend on prey per predator; enrichment now raises both populations proportionally instead of destabilizing them, contrasted with the prey-dependent model.

items.name: Huffaker’s mites and spatial refuges
items.pic: Predatory and herbivorous mites on a grid of oranges: in a simple arena both crash quickly, but barriers that slow predator dispersal let the system persist through shifting local cycles.

items.name: Apparent competition
items.pic: Two prey that never compete share a predator; adding the second prey boosts predator numbers and drives the first prey down, as if they competed.

items.name: Non-consumptive effects: the landscape of fear
items.pic: Prey trade feeding for vigilance across a map of predation risk; reintroduce predators and grazing pressure shifts away from risky areas even before any prey are eaten.

items.name: Host–pathogen regulation of wildlife (Anderson–May)
items.pic: A pathogen that reduces host survival and fecundity is added to a growing host population; above a threshold virulence the host is regulated well below its disease-free density.

items.name: Biological control by aggregated parasitoids
items.pic: Release a parasitoid against a crop pest; with clumped attack the pest settles at a low stable density, while random attack gives the diverging Nicholson–Bailey oscillations.

items.name: Mutualistic networks and nestedness
items.pic: A plant–pollinator interaction matrix is sorted to reveal nestedness, specialists interacting with subsets of generalists’ partners; compare its nestedness score with randomized matrices.

items.name: Some Characteristics of Simple Types of Predation
items.pic: Holling’s disc experiment: a blindfolded “predator” taps for sandpaper discs on a table for a fixed time at different disc densities; because every capture costs handling time the catch saturates, and fitting y = aTx/(1 + aT_hx) to the counts recovers search rate and handling time — play predator yourself and fit the curve.

chapters.title: Synapses and integrate-and-fire neurons
chapters.summary: For network modelling, the spike can be replaced by a threshold and reset: the leaky integrate-and-fire neuron and its exponential and adaptive variants reproduce firing statistics with few parameters. Synapses add conductance changes with characteristic kinetics, NMDA receptors detect coincidences, transmitter release is quantal and probabilistic, and short-term depression and facilitation make synapses dynamic filters.

items.name: Leaky integrate-and-fire neuron
items.pic: Input charges the membrane until it hits threshold, a spike is recorded and the voltage resets; the voltage trace shows the sawtooth pattern for constant input.

items.name: LIF firing rate under constant current
items.pic: The simulated f–I curve of the LIF neuron is overlaid on the formula 1/(t_ref + τ ln(RI/(RI − θ))); it starts at rheobase with infinite slope and saturates at 1/t_ref.

items.name: Exponential integrate-and-fire neuron
items.pic: Add an exponential term that mimics sodium activation; the threshold becomes soft, and the measured I–V curve from a Hodgkin–Huxley-type model fits the exponential shape.

items.name: Adaptive exponential integrate-and-fire and spike-frequency adaptation
items.pic: An adaptation current builds with each spike; under a current step the interspike intervals lengthen, and the reset parameters select adapting, bursting or initial-burst patterns.

items.name: Spike response model
items.pic: Voltage is written as a sum of input filtered by κ and a spike-triggered kernel η; drawing the kernels and convolving shows the same trace as the equivalent integrate-and-fire neuron.

items.name: Synaptic conductances: AMPA, NMDA and GABA
items.pic: Trigger each receptor type and plot its conductance time course and the resulting postsynaptic potential; GABA_A near the resting potential produces little voltage change but large conductance.

items.name: NMDA receptors as coincidence detectors
items.pic: Magnesium blocks the NMDA channel at rest; current flows only when glutamate binding coincides with depolarization, shown by the voltage-dependent I–V curve.

items.name: Quantal transmitter release (del Castillo–Katz)
items.pic: Each of n release sites releases a vesicle with probability p; the amplitude histogram of simulated end-plate potentials shows binomial peaks at multiples of the quantal size.

items.name: Short-term depression and facilitation (Tsodyks–Markram)
items.pic: Drive a synapse with a spike train; depleting resources makes responses shrink while residual calcium makes them grow, and the steady-state response is plotted against input rate.

items.name: Shunting inhibition
items.pic: An inhibitory synapse with reversal near rest barely moves the voltage alone but divides an excitatory response when activated between it and the soma.

items.name: Quantal Components of the End-Plate Potential
items.pic: Del Castillo and Katz’s statistics: lower the calcium at a frog neuromuscular junction so each impulse releases only a few packets; the end-plate potentials then come in multiples of the spontaneous miniature, the amplitude histogram has peaks at 0, 1, 2, 3 quanta, and the Poisson law predicts both the failures (m = ln(trials/failures)) and the whole histogram — vary calcium and check that the two estimates of m agree.

chapters.title: Phylogenetic trees: distances and parsimony
chapters.summary: Evolutionary history is a tree, and the number of possible trees explodes super-exponentially. Distance methods build trees from pairwise distances — UPGMA assumes a clock, neighbour-joining does not and is exact for additive distances — once raw differences are corrected for multiple hits by substitution models. Parsimony instead counts the fewest changes on a tree, computed efficiently for a fixed tree by Fitch and Sankoff, but long-branch attraction can mislead it.

refs: Durbin, Eddy, Krogh & Mitchison, Biological Sequence Analysis

items.name: Trees and the number of topologies
items.pic: Add taxa one at a time to every branch of an unrooted tree; the count (2n − 5)!! is plotted on a log axis and passes the number of atoms in the universe near 50 taxa.

items.name: Additive tree metrics and the four-point condition
items.pic: Edit a distance matrix for four taxa; the three pairwise sums are compared, and the matrix fits a tree exactly when the two largest are equal.

items.name: UPGMA
items.pic: Repeatedly merge the closest pair of clusters and average distances; the growing ultrametric tree is drawn with node heights equal to half the merging distance.

items.name: Ultrametric trees and the molecular clock
items.pic: Simulate evolution with and without a clock; UPGMA recovers the true tree only when rates are equal, as rate variation is dialled up.

items.name: Neighbour-joining
items.pic: Compute the Q-matrix, join the minimizing pair and update distances step by step; the unrooted tree is built while the matrix shrinks.

items.name: Neighbour-joining recovers additive trees exactly
items.pic: Generate distances from a random tree and add noise of increasing size; NJ returns the true topology exactly at zero noise and degrades gracefully afterwards.

items.name: Jukes–Cantor model and distance correction
items.pic: Evolve a sequence under equal substitution rates; observed differences curve away from true substitutions, and the correction −¾ ln(1 − 4p/3) straightens them.

items.name: Kimura two-parameter model
items.pic: Separate transition and transversion rates; with a high transition bias the Jukes–Cantor correction underestimates distance and the Kimura correction fixes it.

items.name: Saturation: observed difference plateaus at 3/4
items.pic: Run substitutions for a long time; the fraction of differing sites levels off at 0.75 and corrected distances become wildly uncertain, shown by error bars blowing up.

items.name: Fitch’s small-parsimony algorithm
items.pic: Pass state sets up a fixed tree, taking intersections or unions at each node; the number of unions is the minimum number of changes, then states are assigned top-down.

items.name: Sankoff’s weighted parsimony
items.pic: With unequal substitution costs, a DP table of minimal costs per state is filled at every node; the root minimum gives the weighted parsimony score.

items.name: Large parsimony is NP-hard; heuristic tree search
items.pic: Nearest-neighbour interchanges move between trees on a landscape of parsimony scores; local search climbs to a local optimum that random restarts sometimes improve.

items.name: Long-branch attraction
items.pic: Simulate a four-taxon tree with two long non-sister branches; as sites accumulate, parsimony becomes ever more confident in the wrong tree that groups the long branches.

items.name: Phylogenetic Structure of the Prokaryotic Domain
items.pic: Cluster the paper’s table of ribosomal-RNA association coefficients S_AB between organisms: average-linkage clustering splits them into three groups — the eubacteria, the methanogens Woese and Fox called archaebacteria, and the eukaryotic “urkaryotes” — and dragging the cut height shows the methanogens are as far from ordinary bacteria as from eukaryotes.

chapters.title: Biological oscillators
chapters.summary: Negative feedback with enough delay oscillates, and the synthetic repressilator showed that three mutually repressing genes suffice. Delays from transcription and translation drive pulses of p53 and Hes1. Adding positive feedback produces relaxation oscillators whose amplitude is robust and whose frequency can be tuned, the design used by cell-cycle and many circadian clocks.

refs: Alon, An Introduction to Systems Biology

items.name: Repressilator (Elowitz–Leibler)
refs: Alon: How to Build a Biological Oscillator
items.pic: Three genes repress each other in a ring; their protein levels chase one another in a sustained oscillation, drawn both as time traces and as a closed loop in 3D.

items.name: Repressilator oscillation threshold
refs: Alon: How to Build a Biological Oscillator
items.pic: Scan cooperativity and the protein-to-mRNA lifetime ratio; the Hopf boundary computed from the linearization separates steady and oscillating regions, verified by clicking points to simulate.

items.name: Delayed negative autoregulation: Hes1 and p53 pulses
refs: Alon: How to Build a Biological Oscillator
items.pic: Add an explicit transcription–translation delay to negative autoregulation; once the delay exceeds a threshold the level pulses with period about four delays, like Hes1 in embryonic cells.

items.name: Robust tunable oscillator from positive plus negative feedback
refs: Alon: How to Build a Biological Oscillator
items.pic: Couple a fast positive loop to a slow negative loop; the frequency can be tuned over a wide range while the amplitude stays nearly fixed, unlike the pure negative-feedback design shown alongside.

items.name: KaiABC circadian clock and temperature compensation
refs: Alon: How to Build a Biological Oscillator
items.pic: Phosphorylation cycles of KaiC run in a test tube with a 24-hour period; raising temperature speeds each reaction yet the computed period barely changes when opposing rates compensate.

items.name: Cell-cycle oscillator (Cdk1–APC)
refs: Alon: How to Build a Biological Oscillator
items.pic: Cyclin synthesis, Cdk1 activation through bistable positive feedback and delayed APC-mediated destruction produce relaxation oscillations, with the hysteresis loop of Cdk1 against cyclin traced each cycle.

chapters.title: Respiration and gas exchange
chapters.summary: Breathing is driven by pressure differences created by the chest wall, resisted by lung elasticity and surface tension that surfactant tames. Gas laws set the partial pressures, the alveolar gas equation predicts alveolar oxygen, and Fick’s law governs transfer across the alveolar membrane. Matching ventilation to perfusion is the key to efficient exchange, and the chemical control of breathing is a feedback loop that can become unstable when delays grow.

refs: Guyton & Hall, Textbook of Medical Physiology

items.name: Boyle’s law and the mechanics of breathing
items.pic: Lower the diaphragm and the thoracic volume grows, alveolar pressure dips below atmospheric and air flows in; flow, volume and pressure traces are drawn through a breath.

items.name: Lung compliance and the pressure–volume curve
items.pic: Inflate a lung with air and with saline; the saline curve is far less stiff and shows no hysteresis, revealing how much of lung recoil comes from surface tension.

items.name: Laplace’s law for alveoli and the role of surfactant
items.pic: Connect two bubbles of different size: without surfactant the small one empties into the large one, but surfactant lowers tension as area shrinks and both stay stable.

items.name: Lung volumes and spirometry
items.pic: A spirometer trace shows tidal breathing, a maximal inspiration and a forced expiration; volumes and capacities are labelled, and an obstructive pattern slows the forced expiration.

items.name: Dead space and alveolar ventilation
items.pic: Compare deep slow and shallow fast breathing at the same minute ventilation; because each breath wastes the dead-space volume, alveolar ventilation is much lower for shallow breathing.

items.name: Henry’s law of gas solubility
items.pic: Equilibrate plasma with gas at different partial pressures; dissolved oxygen rises linearly and modestly while CO₂, twenty times more soluble, dissolves far more.

items.name: Alveolar gas equation
items.pic: Set inspired oxygen, arterial CO₂ and respiratory quotient; alveolar P_O₂ is computed, and hypoventilation that raises CO₂ visibly pushes alveolar oxygen down.

items.name: Fick’s law for alveolar gas transfer and diffusing capacity
items.pic: Thicken the alveolar–capillary barrier or shrink its area; the oxygen transfer rate falls in proportion and the diffusing-capacity readout drops, as in fibrosis or emphysema.

items.name: Perfusion-limited versus diffusion-limited transfer
items.pic: Follow capillary P_O₂ along the capillary transit: at rest it equilibrates in a third of the transit, but in exercise with a thickened barrier it falls short, while carbon monoxide never equilibrates.

items.name: Ventilation–perfusion ratio
items.pic: Slide V/Q from zero (shunt) to infinity (dead space); the alveolar P_O₂ and P_CO₂ point moves along the O₂–CO₂ curve, and mixing units with different ratios lowers arterial oxygen.

items.name: West’s zones of the lung
items.pic: In an upright lung, compare alveolar, arterial and venous pressures at each height; capillaries collapse at the apex, behave like waterfalls in the middle and flow freely at the base.

items.name: Chemical control of breathing: the CO₂ loop
items.pic: Raise inspired CO₂; chemoreceptors drive ventilation up along a nearly linear CO₂ response curve, and the closed loop settles where the metabolic and response curves intersect.

items.name: Cheyne–Stokes breathing as a delayed-feedback instability
items.pic: Lengthen the circulation delay between lungs and chemoreceptors, as in heart failure; the ventilation trace switches from steady to waxing–waning periodic breathing once loop gain times delay crosses the threshold.

chapters.title: Nonlinear kinetics, metabolism and interactions
chapters.summary: When metabolizing enzymes saturate, elimination follows Michaelis–Menten kinetics and small dose changes can produce large changes in steady-state concentration. Enzyme inhibition and induction underlie most drug–drug interactions, and genetic variation in enzymes splits populations into poor and ultra-rapid metabolizers. Metabolites, prodrugs and target binding add further nonlinear behaviour.

refs: Rowland & Tozer, Clinical Pharmacokinetics and Pharmacodynamics
Goodman & Gilman, The Pharmacological Basis of Therapeutics

items.name: Michaelis–Menten elimination
items.pic: Elimination rate saturates at V_max as concentration rises; the semilog decline after a large dose is concave, nearly linear at high concentrations and exponential at low ones.

items.name: Phenytoin: disproportionate rise at steady state
items.pic: Plot steady-state concentration against daily dose; as the dosing rate approaches V_max the curve shoots up, so a 20% dose increase can double the level.

items.name: Zero-order elimination of ethanol
items.pic: Blood alcohol after several drinks falls along a straight line at about one drink per hour, because alcohol dehydrogenase is saturated; the line bends only at low levels.

items.name: Enzyme inhibition and induction
items.pic: Add an inhibitor and intrinsic clearance falls; add an inducer and enzyme levels rise over days; the victim drug’s concentration curve shifts accordingly.

items.name: Predicting interaction size from the inhibitor’s Ki
items.pic: The AUC ratio 1/(f_m/(1 + I/K_i) + 1 − f_m) is plotted against inhibitor concentration; interactions become severe only when the inhibited pathway dominates elimination.

items.name: Pharmacogenetics: CYP2D6 metabolizer phenotypes
items.pic: Allele frequencies for null, reduced and duplicated CYP2D6 genes give Hardy–Weinberg genotype frequencies; each phenotype’s drug exposure is drawn as a separate concentration curve.

items.name: Autoinduction (carbamazepine)
items.pic: A drug induces its own metabolism over weeks; concentrations rise at first and then fall even at constant dosing, as clearance creeps up.

items.name: Parent–metabolite kinetics and prodrugs
items.pic: A prodrug is converted into its active metabolite; the metabolite curve lags the parent, and when its elimination is slower it outlasts the parent, as with codeine and morphine.

items.name: Saturable protein binding
items.pic: As total concentration rises, binding sites fill and the unbound fraction climbs; total and unbound steady-state levels then respond differently to dose increases.

items.name: Target-mediated drug disposition
items.pic: A biologic binds its target tightly and is cleared with it; low doses vanish quickly while high doses saturate the target and show slower linear elimination.

chapters.title: Study designs
chapters.summary: Cohort studies follow exposed and unexposed people forward; case-control studies sample on outcome and compare exposure, and with density sampling their odds ratio estimates the rate ratio exactly. Cross-sectional and ecological designs are cheap but limited — the ecological fallacy warns against reading individual effects from group data. Nested, matched and self-controlled designs refine the basic two, and genetic instruments offer a natural experiment.

items.name: Cohort studies
items.pic: Enrol exposed and unexposed groups and follow them; cases accumulate on timelines and the rate ratio with its confidence interval tightens as follow-up lengthens.

items.name: Case-control studies
items.pic: Sample all cases and a fraction of non-cases from a simulated population; the exposure odds ratio among them matches the population odds ratio at a fraction of the cost.

items.name: Density sampling: the case-control odds ratio estimates the rate ratio
items.pic: Pick controls from those at risk at each case’s event time; the odds ratio equals the rate ratio even for a common outcome, whereas controls picked at the end of follow-up give the cumulative OR.

items.name: Cross-sectional studies
items.pic: A survey measures exposure and disease at one time; prevalence ratios mix incidence with duration, so an exposure that prolongs survival looks like a cause.

items.name: Ecological fallacy
items.pic: Across regions, higher immigrant share correlates with higher literacy, yet within every region immigrants are less literate — the scatter shows group and individual slopes with opposite signs.

items.name: Nested case-control and case-cohort designs
items.pic: Within a large cohort, measure expensive biomarkers only on cases and sampled controls; the estimates agree with the full-cohort analysis while assays drop by 90%.

items.name: Matching in case-control studies
items.pic: Match controls to cases on age; the matched analysis using discordant pairs removes confounding by age, while an unmatched analysis of matched data is biased toward the null.

items.name: Case-crossover design
items.pic: Each case serves as its own control by comparing exposure just before the event with earlier windows; transient triggers such as heavy exertion stand out.

items.name: The Mortality of Doctors in Relation to Their Smoking Habits
items.pic: The British Doctors cohort’s first results: some 29 months after the questionnaire, the standardized lung-cancer death rate rose from nil in non-smokers through about 0.48 and 0.67 to 1.14 per 1000 a year in light, moderate and heavy smokers; plot the gradient, compare other causes of death, and see why a prospective design answered critics of the case-control evidence.

items.name: Factors of Risk in the Development of Coronary Heart Disease
items.pic: Framingham’s six-year follow-up: coronary heart disease incidence among some five thousand initially healthy adults climbs with serum cholesterol, blood pressure and ECG signs of left-ventricular hypertrophy, and multiplies when several are present; combine the “factors of risk” — the phrase this paper put into medicine — and read off the incidence.

chapters.title: Ultrasound
chapters.summary: Ultrasound images are built from echoes: pulses reflect at interfaces between tissues of different acoustic impedance, and the round-trip time gives depth. Attenuation forces a trade-off between frequency and penetration, resolution depends on pulse length and beam width, and arrays focus and steer electronically. The Doppler shift of echoes from moving blood measures velocity, with aliasing limits and clinical uses such as estimating pressure gradients.

refs: Prince & Links, Medical Imaging Signals and Systems
Kak & Slaney, Principles of Computerized Tomographic Imaging

items.name: Acoustic waves and the speed of sound in tissue
items.pic: A pressure pulse travels through layers of fat, muscle and bone; speeds computed from √(K/ρ) are shown, with soft tissue clustered near 1540 m/s.

items.name: Acoustic impedance and reflection at interfaces
items.pic: Choose two tissues; the reflection coefficient ((Z₂ − Z₁)/(Z₂ + Z₁))² is computed, small for soft-tissue boundaries and nearly total at tissue–air and tissue–bone interfaces.

items.name: Attenuation and the depth–frequency trade-off
items.pic: Attenuation of about 0.5 dB/cm/MHz is applied to the round trip; raise frequency and the maximum imaging depth shrinks while resolution improves.

items.name: Pulse-echo ranging
items.pic: Send a pulse into layered tissue and plot the received echoes against time; depths are computed as ct/2 to form an A-mode line, then many lines form a B-mode image.

items.name: Axial and lateral resolution
items.pic: Two reflectors are moved closer along and across the beam; they merge axially at half the pulse length and laterally at the beam width, which is narrowest at the focus.

items.name: Beamforming with phased arrays
items.pic: Apply time delays across array elements; the transmitted wavefronts converge at a chosen focus or steer at an angle, computed by superposition of element waves.

items.name: Time-gain compensation
items.pic: Echoes from deep tissue are weaker; drag the gain curve to amplify later echoes and flatten image brightness with depth.

items.name: Ultrasound speckle
items.pic: Many sub-resolution scatterers interfere to produce a granular texture with Rayleigh-distributed amplitude; averaging images from different angles reduces it.

items.name: Doppler equation for ultrasound
items.pic: Echoes from blood moving at speed v and angle θ are shifted by 2f₀v cos θ / c; drag the insonation angle and see the shift vanish at 90°.

items.name: Pulsed-wave Doppler and the Nyquist velocity limit
items.pic: Sample the Doppler signal at the pulse repetition frequency; velocities beyond the Nyquist limit wrap around in the spectral display, and lowering depth raises the limit.

items.name: Pressure gradients from Doppler velocities
items.pic: Measure the peak velocity jet through a narrowed valve; the simplified Bernoulli relation ΔP ≈ 4v² gives the pressure gradient used to grade stenosis.

items.name: Colour flow imaging by autocorrelation
items.pic: Estimate mean velocity at each pixel from the phase change between successive pulses; flow toward and away from the probe is coloured red and blue over the B-mode image.

chapters.title: The continuous-time Fourier transform
chapters.summary: Letting the period of a periodic signal grow without bound turns the line spectrum into a continuous one: the Fourier transform. Its properties — shifts become phase ramps, convolution becomes multiplication, energy is preserved — are the everyday tools of the subject. With distributions, impulses and sinusoids get transforms too, and the theory delivers deep limits: a signal cannot be concentrated in both time and frequency, and a band-limited signal cannot be time-limited.

items.name: Fourier transform as the limit of Fourier series
items.pic: Stretch the period of a pulse train: the harmonics crowd closer together while their envelope keeps its shape, converging to the continuous transform of a single pulse.

items.name: Fourier inversion
items.pic: Integrate the inverse transform over a band [−W, W] and increase W: the reconstruction converges to the original signal, with the error shown shrinking.

items.name: Linearity, time shift and frequency shift
items.pic: Drag a pulse in time: its magnitude spectrum is frozen while its phase tilts linearly; multiply it by a carrier and the whole spectrum slides along the frequency axis.

items.name: Time scaling: compress in time, spread in frequency
items.pic: Squeeze a pulse with a slider: the transform stretches and flattens by the reciprocal factor, the product of the two widths staying fixed.

items.name: Duality
items.pic: A rectangle transforms to a sinc and a sinc transforms back to a rectangle; a toggle swaps the time and frequency panels for a gallery of pairs.

items.name: Convolution theorem
items.pic: Convolve two signals by the sliding-kernel method and by multiplying their spectra and inverting: the two outputs agree, with timings for each method shown.

items.name: Multiplication (modulation) property
items.pic: Multiply a signal by a window or a cosine: the spectrum becomes the convolution of the two spectra, shown as the original spectrum smeared or copied to ±ω_c.

items.name: Differentiation and integration properties
items.pic: Differentiate a pulse and its spectrum gets multiplied by jω, boosting high frequencies; integrate it and low frequencies are boosted, with a delta appearing at DC when the area is nonzero.

items.name: Parseval–Plancherel: energy is preserved
items.pic: Shade |x(t)|² and |X(ω)|²/2π for a drawn signal: the two areas match to four digits however the signal is redrawn.

items.name: The Gaussian is its own Fourier transform
items.pic: Vary the width of a Gaussian: its transform is a Gaussian of reciprocal width, and at one special width the two plots are identical.

items.name: Rectangular pulse and sinc
items.pic: Widen a rectangular pulse: its sinc spectrum narrows, the zero crossings at multiples of 2π/T marked and moving inward.

items.name: Riemann–Lebesgue lemma
items.pic: For integrable signals with sharper and sharper corners, the spectra still decay to zero at high frequency — just more slowly — as log-scale envelopes show.

items.name: Transforms of impulses and sinusoids via distributions
items.pic: Lengthen a windowed cosine: its spectrum concentrates into two ever-narrower spikes of fixed area at ±ω₀, the transform of the eternal cosine.

items.name: Impulse train ↔ impulse train (Poisson summation)
items.pic: Change the spacing T of an impulse comb: its transform is a comb with spacing 2π/T, and summing a Gaussian’s samples checks the Poisson summation formula numerically.

items.name: Uncertainty principle for signals (Gabor limit)
items.pic: Draw any pulse: its RMS duration and RMS bandwidth are computed and their product is plotted against the lower bound ½, which only Gaussians reach.

items.name: Band-limited signals cannot be time-limited
items.pic: Truncate a band-limited signal to a finite window: its spectrum immediately grows tails outside the band, and no window can avoid them.

items.name: Magnitude, phase and group delay
items.pic: Scramble the phase of a signal’s spectrum while keeping the magnitude: speech becomes unintelligible, while keeping phase and flattening magnitude keeps it recognisable.

items.name: Energy spectral density and autocorrelation
items.pic: Compute the autocorrelation of a pulse by sliding it over itself; its transform matches |X(ω)|², the energy spectral density, overlaid.

chapters.title: PID control
chapters.summary: The proportional–integral–derivative controller acts on the present, past and predicted future of the error, and it runs most of the world's control loops. Each term has a clear role and a clear failure mode. This chapter covers how the terms work together, classic and modern tuning rules, and the practical details — windup, derivative filtering, setpoint weighting, cascades — that separate textbook PID from industrial PID.

refs: Franklin, Powell & Emami-Naeini, Feedback Control of Dynamic Systems

items.name: Proportional control and its offset
items.pic: Raise the proportional gain on a first-order plant: the steady-state error shrinks like 1/(1 + kP) but never vanishes, while the response speeds up.

items.name: Integral action removes the offset
items.pic: Switch on integral action: the integrator state keeps growing as long as any error remains, driving the error to exactly zero, and too much integral gain makes the response oscillate.

items.name: Derivative action adds damping
items.pic: Add derivative action to an oscillatory loop: the controller anticipates the error trend, the overshoot drops, and amplified sensor noise appears on the control signal.

items.name: The PID controller
items.pic: Three sliders for kP, kI and kD drive a live plant; the contributions of the three terms are plotted separately and summed into the control signal.

items.name: Ziegler–Nichols tuning
items.pic: Raise a pure proportional gain until the loop just oscillates; the ultimate gain and period are measured automatically and plugged into the Ziegler–Nichols table to give an aggressive PID.

items.name: Relay autotuning
items.pic: Replace the controller by a relay: the loop settles into a limit cycle whose amplitude and period reveal the ultimate gain, and the resulting PID tuning is applied with one click.

items.name: Integrator windup
items.pic: Command a large setpoint change through a saturating actuator: the integrator keeps charging while the actuator is pinned, causing a huge overshoot when the output finally arrives.

items.name: Anti-windup: clamping and back-calculation
items.pic: Toggle anti-windup on the saturating loop: the integrator is held back while the actuator saturates and the overshoot disappears, with the tracking-time constant adjustable.

items.name: Derivative filtering and setpoint weighting
items.pic: Step the setpoint with a raw derivative term and the control signal spikes; filter the derivative and weight the setpoint, and the kick disappears without changing disturbance rejection.

items.name: Lambda (IMC) tuning for dead-time processes
items.pic: Choose the desired closed-loop time constant λ for a first-order-plus-dead-time plant: the PI gains are computed and the response is as fast as requested, but no faster than the delay allows.

items.name: Two-degree-of-freedom control
items.pic: Shape the reference response with a prefilter while the feedback is tuned for disturbances: the two responses are adjusted independently with separate sliders.

items.name: Cascade control
items.pic: Add an inner flow loop under an outer temperature loop: a valve disturbance is corrected by the fast inner loop before the temperature even notices.

items.name: Optimum Settings for Automatic Controllers
items.pic: On a simulated process loop, raise a proportional gain until the output oscillates steadily, read off the ultimate gain and period, and apply the Ziegler–Nichols table for P, PI or PID; the step response shows the quarter-amplitude decay the rules aim for.

chapters.title: Capacitors, inductors and first-order transients
chapters.summary: Capacitors and inductors store energy in electric and magnetic fields, so circuits containing them have memory and evolve in time. A single storage element gives a first-order differential equation whose solution relaxes exponentially with time constant RC or L/R. These transients explain delays in digital logic, the CV² cost of switching, the voltage spike when an inductor is interrupted, and one of the classic paradoxes of circuit theory.

refs: Agarwal & Lang, Foundations of Analog and Digital Electronic Circuits
Horowitz & Hill, The Art of Electronics

items.name: Capacitor: i = C dv/dt
items.pic: Draw any voltage waveform across a capacitor with the mouse; the current is drawn as its scaled derivative, spiking at every steep edge.

items.name: Inductor: v = L di/dt
items.pic: Draw a current waveform through an inductor and see the voltage as its scaled derivative; a ramp in current gives a constant voltage.

items.name: Energy stored: ½CV² and ½LI²
items.pic: Charge a capacitor with a constant current: the power v·i integrated over time is shaded and equals ½CV² at every instant, with an analogous panel for an inductor.

items.name: Continuity of capacitor voltage and inductor current
items.pic: Close a switch in a circuit with storage elements: capacitor voltages and inductor currents evolve continuously while other variables jump, highlighted in different colours.

items.name: RC circuit: charging and discharging
items.pic: Flip a switch and watch the capacitor voltage approach the source exponentially; markers at τ, 2τ and 3τ show 63%, 86% and 95% of the final value as R and C are changed.

items.name: Time constant
items.pic: The tangent to an exponential at any point hits the final value exactly one time constant later — drag the tangent point along the curve to verify.

items.name: RL circuit transients
items.pic: Switch a source onto an inductor and resistor: the current builds up with time constant L/R while the inductor voltage decays, the two curves complementary.

items.name: First-order step response from initial, final value and τ
items.pic: For any first-order circuit drawn by the user, the solver finds the Thévenin resistance seen by the storage element, then sketches the response from three numbers and overlays the full simulation.

items.name: Inductive kick
items.pic: Open the switch feeding a relay coil: the inductor voltage spikes to hundreds of volts; add a flyback diode and the spike is clamped while the current decays gently.

items.name: RC integrator and differentiator
items.pic: Feed a square wave into an RC network and vary τ relative to the period: for long τ the output across C is a triangle (integral), for short τ the output across R is spikes (derivative).

items.name: Two-capacitor paradox
items.pic: Connect a charged capacitor to an identical empty one through a resistor: charge is conserved but exactly half the energy disappears as heat — whatever the resistance, the integrated I²R matches, and shrinking R only makes the pulse taller and shorter.

items.name: Gate delay and RC propagation in logic
items.pic: A chain of inverters drives capacitive loads; the threshold crossings march down the chain with a delay set by R_on·C, adjustable by sliders.

items.name: Switching power: P = fCV²
items.pic: Raise the clock frequency and supply voltage of a toy processor: dissipated power grows linearly with f and quadratically with V, explaining why chips lowered their supply voltage.

items.name: Switching power converter (buck)
items.pic: A switch chops a supply at high frequency into an inductor and diode: the inductor current ripples as a sawtooth, the output settles at the duty cycle times the input, and efficiency stays high unlike a resistive divider.

chapters.title: Wind, water, heat and biomass
chapters.summary: Moving air and water carry kinetic and potential energy that turbines can harvest. Wind power grows with the cube of wind speed, but no turbine can extract more than 16/27 of the energy flowing through its disk — the Betz limit. Hydropower, tides and waves follow from equally simple physics, geothermal energy draws on the Earth's heat flow, and biomass is limited by the inefficiency of photosynthesis.

refs: Tester et al., Sustainable Energy: Choosing Among Options
MacKay, Sustainable Energy — Without the Hot Air

items.name: Power in the wind: ½ρAv³
items.pic: Double the wind speed and the power through a rotor disk rises eightfold; a parcel of air passing through the disk carries its kinetic energy, drawn as a growing cube.

items.name: Betz limit: at most 16/27
items.pic: Slow the wind behind an actuator disk with a slider: extracted power rises then falls, peaking at 16/27 of the available power when the far wake is slowed to one third of the free-stream speed.

items.name: Tip-speed ratio and the power coefficient curve
items.pic: Spin a rotor at different speeds in a fixed wind: the power coefficient rises to a peak below the Betz line at an optimal tip-speed ratio, and stall or overspeed lose power on either side.

items.name: Wind-speed statistics and capacity factor
items.pic: A Weibull distribution of wind speeds is multiplied by a turbine power curve to give the energy yield; because of the cube law, the mean power is far above the power at the mean speed.

items.name: Wind shear: speed increases with height
items.pic: Raise a turbine hub: the logarithmic wind profile gives more speed and far more power at height, and the blade sweeps through a gradient of wind speeds.

items.name: Wake losses in wind farms
items.pic: Lay out turbines on a grid with adjustable spacing: each sits in the slowed wakes of those upwind, and the farm’s output per turbine falls, limiting power per unit area to a few W/m².

items.name: Hydropower: P = ρgQH
items.pic: Set a dam’s head and flow rate: the power and the turbine’s share of it are computed, and a rainfall-to-river catchment model shows how much a mountain region could supply.

items.name: Tidal power
items.pic: A tidal lagoon fills and empties with a 12.4-hour tide: the energy per cycle scales with the square of the tidal range, and two-way generation is compared with ebb-only operation.

items.name: Ocean wave power
items.pic: Choose wave height and period: power per metre of wave crest, carried at the group velocity, is computed and compared with the output of a line of wave machines along a coastline.

items.name: Geothermal energy and reservoir depletion
items.pic: Extract heat from hot rock faster than conduction resupplies it: the reservoir cools over decades, comparing sustainable heat flux (tens of mW/m²) with mining stored heat.

items.name: Biomass and the efficiency of photosynthesis
items.pic: Follow sunlight into a field of energy crops: losses at each step leave under 1% stored as biomass, so the land needed to fuel a country’s cars is drawn on a map.

items.name: Das Maximum der theoretisch möglichen Ausnützung des Windes
items.pic: Slow the wind through an actuator disk by an adjustable induction factor a and watch the stream tube widen; the power coefficient 4a(1 − a)² peaks at a = 1/3 with C_P = 16/27, and a real rotor’s curve sits below Betz’s ceiling.

chapters.title: Torsion
chapters.summary: Twisting a circular shaft shears it, with stress growing linearly from the centre. The resulting formulas for stress, angle of twist and power transmission are the basis of every drive shaft. Non-circular sections warp and need Prandtl's stress function and its soap-film analogy, thin closed tubes carry a constant shear flow, and open sections turn out to be remarkably weak in torsion.

items.name: Torsion formula: τ = Tr/J
items.pic: Twist a shaft with a draggable torque: a painted line on its surface becomes a helix, and the shear stress over a cross-section is drawn growing linearly from zero at the centre.

items.name: Angle of twist: φ = TL/GJ
items.pic: Compare shafts of different lengths, diameters and materials: the end rotation scales with length and inversely with the fourth power of diameter.

items.name: Power transmission: P = Tω
items.pic: Choose the power and rotation speed of a motor: the required shaft diameter for an allowable stress is computed, showing why fast-spinning shafts can be thin.

items.name: Hollow shafts carry torque efficiently
items.pic: Bore out the centre of a shaft: weight drops much faster than torque capacity, plotted against inner-to-outer radius ratio.

items.name: Pure shear and 45° failure in torsion
items.pic: Twist a stick of chalk and a steel bar: Mohr’s circle for pure shear shows tension at 45°, so the chalk breaks on a helix while the ductile bar shears flat across.

items.name: Thin-walled closed tubes: shear flow and Bredt’s formula
items.pic: Draw any closed thin-walled section: the shear flow around it is constant, the stress is highest where the wall is thinnest, and the stiffness depends on the enclosed area.

items.name: Torsion of non-circular sections: Prandtl stress function
items.pic: Twist a square or triangular bar: cross-sections warp out of plane, and the stress function solved on the section gives a shear-stress map that peaks at the middle of the longest sides, not at the corners.

items.name: Prandtl’s membrane (soap-film) analogy
items.pic: Inflate a membrane over a hole shaped like the section: the bubble’s slope maps the shear stress and its volume gives the torsional stiffness, computed live for a user-drawn section.

items.name: Open thin-walled sections are weak in torsion
items.pic: Cut a slit along a thin tube: its torsional stiffness drops by orders of magnitude, shown by twisting the closed and slit tubes with the same torque.

items.name: Stress concentrations in torsion
items.pic: Step a shaft from one diameter to another with an adjustable fillet radius: the peak shear stress at the shoulder rises sharply as the fillet becomes small.

chapters.title: Inverse kinematics
chapters.summary: Inverse kinematics asks for joint values that put the tool at a desired pose. Simple arms have closed-form solutions, usually several of them, while general robots need numerical iteration built on the Jacobian. Damped least squares, the pseudoinverse and heuristic methods trade accuracy, speed and robustness near singularities.

refs: Siciliano et al., Robotics: Modelling, Planning and Control

items.name: Analytic IK of the 2R arm: elbow up and elbow down
items.pic: Drag the target point: the two solutions (elbow up and down) are drawn as ghost arms, merge at the workspace boundary and disappear outside it.

items.name: Numerical IK by Newton–Raphson
items.pic: From an initial guess, Newton steps using the Jacobian move the arm toward the target; the error shrinks quadratically near the solution and the iteration count is displayed.

items.name: Pseudoinverse and resolved-rate control
items.pic: Command a tool velocity for a redundant arm: the pseudoinverse picks the joint velocity with the smallest norm, and adding a null-space term steers the elbow away from obstacles without moving the tool.

items.name: Jacobian transpose and damped least squares
items.pic: Track a target that passes near a singularity: plain Newton steps explode while damped least squares slows gracefully, with joint speeds plotted for both.

items.name: Multiple IK solutions: up to 16 for a 6R arm
items.pic: For a target pose of a six-axis arm, all distinct solutions (shoulder left/right, elbow up/down, wrist flip) are drawn simultaneously as translucent arms.

items.name: Cyclic coordinate descent and FABRIK
items.pic: A long animated chain reaches for the mouse: CCD rotates one joint at a time toward the target while FABRIK alternately drags the chain from tip and base, and their convergence speeds are compared.

chapters.title: Aircraft performance
chapters.summary: With the drag polar and the engine's thrust in hand, an aircraft's performance follows from Newton's laws in a few lines: the speeds for minimum drag and minimum power, the glide ratio, rate of climb, ceiling, range and endurance. Breguet's range equation sets the economics of air travel, and turning flight and the V–n diagram set the structural envelope.

refs: Curtis, Orbital Mechanics for Engineering Students

items.name: Steady level flight
items.pic: Balance four forces on an aircraft: at each speed the required lift coefficient is set by weight, and the thrust needed equals the drag computed from the polar, plotted as the thrust-required curve.

items.name: Minimum-drag and minimum-power speeds
items.pic: Thrust-required and power-required curves are drawn against speed; their minima — at different speeds — are marked, and changing weight or altitude shifts both.

items.name: Gliding flight: glide ratio equals L/D
items.pic: Fly a glider from a set height at different speeds: the distance covered is largest at the best-L/D speed, and the glide angle readout equals arctan(D/L).

items.name: Rate of climb from excess power
items.pic: The gap between power available and power required is shaded; dividing by weight gives the climb rate, which peaks at a particular speed and shrinks with altitude.

items.name: Absolute and service ceilings
items.pic: Climb through the standard atmosphere: maximum rate of climb falls with density, and the altitudes where it reaches 100 ft/min and zero are marked.

items.name: Breguet range equation
items.pic: Fly a jet across an ocean: as fuel burns the aircraft lightens, and the range grows with the logarithm of the initial-to-final weight ratio times speed × L/D over fuel consumption, with sliders for each factor.

items.name: Breguet endurance
items.pic: For a patrol mission, loiter time is maximised at a different speed from range; the two optimal speeds are marked on the polar for propeller and jet aircraft.

items.name: Turning flight, load factor and the V–n diagram
items.pic: Bank an aircraft in a level turn: the load factor 1/cos φ raises the stall speed, and the V–n envelope bounded by stall and structural limits is drawn with the current point on it.

items.name: Takeoff and landing distances
items.pic: Accelerate down a runway with thrust, drag and rolling friction integrated live: the ground roll to lift-off speed grows with weight squared and shrinks with air density.

items.name: The back side of the power curve
items.pic: Fly slower than the minimum-drag speed with fixed throttle: a small speed loss increases drag, which slows the aircraft further — a speed instability shown by perturbing the trim point on either side.

chapters.title: Factor markets and time
chapters.summary: Labour and capital are traded in markets of their own. Firms hire labour until its marginal value equals the wage, and households supply it by trading leisure for consumption, sometimes offering fewer hours at higher wages. A single dominant employer changes these conclusions, to the point that a minimum wage can raise employment. Discounting puts payments at different dates on a common scale and turns education into an investment decision.

items.name: Derived demand: the value of marginal product
items.pic: The value-of-marginal-product curve p·MP_L with a wage slider: the firm hires until the curve meets the wage, and raising the output price shifts the whole labour-demand curve outward.

items.name: Labour–leisure choice
items.pic: In the leisure–consumption plane a wage slider pivots the budget line around the time endowment plus non-labour income, and the optimal hours of work are read out.

items.name: Backward-bending labour supply
items.pic: Sweep the wage and plot hours worked: substitution and income arrows are drawn at each wage, and the supply curve bends back once the income effect on leisure wins.

items.name: Competitive labour market
items.pic: Market labour demand (the summed value of marginal product) meets labour supply; shift supply with an immigration slider or demand with a productivity slider and read off the changes in wage and employment.

items.name: Monopsony
items.pic: A sole employer facing upward-sloping labour supply sees a marginal-factor-cost curve above it; it hires where that curve meets labour’s marginal value and pays only the supply-curve wage, below the competitive level.

items.name: Minimum wages under monopsony
items.pic: Raise a minimum wage: under monopsony employment rises until the wage reaches the competitive level and only then falls, while a competitive-market toggle shows every binding minimum cutting jobs.

items.name: Compensating wage differentials
items.pic: Workers differ in how much they dislike a dangerous job (a slider sets the spread): its wage premium settles where the marginal worker is indifferent between the jobs, and workers who mind less earn a rent.

items.name: Intertemporal budget constraint
items.pic: Two-period consumption around an income endowment: an interest-rate slider pivots the budget line through the endowment with slope −(1 + r), and the chosen point labels the consumer a borrower or a lender.

items.name: Present value and discounting
items.pic: Two payment streams drawn as bars, with their discounted values shrinking geometrically; move the interest rate and watch the present values, and which stream is worth more, switch.

items.name: Human capital investment
items.pic: Choose years of schooling: forgone earnings early are traded for a higher earnings profile later, the present value of each plan is plotted against years of schooling, and its peak moves left as the interest rate rises.

items.name: Hotelling’s rule for exhaustible resources
items.pic: An owner of a fixed oil stock chooses when to extract: arbitrage between selling now and holding makes the price net of extraction cost rise at the interest rate, so the price path climbs exponentially until demand is choked off just as the stock runs out.

items.name: Fisher separation theorem
items.pic: In the two-period plane a curved investment frontier meets a market borrowing line: the firm invests until the frontier’s slope equals 1 + r, maximizing present value, and owners of very different patience then borrow or lend along the same line to their own optima.

items.name: Taste-based discrimination (Becker)
items.pic: Employers differ in a slider-set distaste for hiring one group: the wage gap is set by the marginal employer, and as the share of unprejudiced firms grows they hire the cheaper workers, out-earn their rivals and, with free entry, drive the gap toward zero.

chapters.title: Money and inflation
chapters.summary: Money is whatever serves as a medium of exchange, unit of account and store of value; banks create most of it by lending. In the long run the quantity theory links money growth to inflation, the Fisher equation links inflation to nominal interest rates, and money is neutral for real variables. Governments that finance spending by printing money collect an inflation tax that, pushed too far, ends in hyperinflation.

items.name: The functions of money
items.pic: A barter economy needs a double coincidence of wants; add a commonly accepted good and the number of trades needed to reach everyone’s desired goods collapses, counted in the simulation.

items.name: Fractional-reserve banking and the money multiplier
items.pic: A deposit is lent, redeposited and lent again; the geometric series of deposits sums to 1/reserve-ratio, with a toggle for the endogenous-money view in which loans create deposits.

items.name: The quantity theory of money
items.pic: Money growth against inflation across countries over decades: points cluster around the 45° line, while year-to-year data in low-inflation countries scatter widely.

items.name: The Fisher equation
items.pic: Nominal rate, inflation and real rate as three linked sliders: i = r + π (exactly (1 + i) = (1 + r)(1 + π)), with historical U.S. series and ex-ante versus ex-post real rates.

items.name: Monetary neutrality and the classical dichotomy
items.pic: Double the money supply in a flexible-price model: every price and wage doubles and every real quantity stays put, shown as two identical real panels.

items.name: Seigniorage and the inflation tax
items.pic: Revenue from money creation as a function of the inflation rate is a Laffer-type hump, because real money balances shrink as inflation rises.

items.name: The Cagan model of hyperinflation
items.pic: Money demand falling with expected inflation; finance a deficit beyond the seigniorage peak and the simulated price level explodes.

items.name: Hyperinflations: Germany 1923, Zimbabwe 2008
items.pic: Monthly price levels on a log axis for famous hyperinflations, with fiscal deficits and the stabilizations that ended them annotated.

items.name: The costs of inflation
items.pic: Separate the costs of expected inflation (shoe leather, menu costs, tax distortions) from unexpected inflation’s redistribution between lenders and borrowers, with sliders for each.

items.name: Money demand and liquidity preference
items.pic: Real money demand falls with the interest rate; shift money supply and the market interest rate moves along the demand curve.

chapters.title: Arbitrage, forwards and capital structure
chapters.summary: No-arbitrage reasoning — identical payoffs must have identical prices — is the most powerful tool in finance. It fixes forward prices from spot prices and interest rates, links currencies through covered interest parity, and, by separating hyperplanes, guarantees state prices whenever there is no free lunch. Applied to firms, it shows that capital structure cannot create value in a frictionless market.

refs: Hull, Options, Futures, and Other Derivatives

items.name: Pricing by replication
items.pic: Pick a target payoff across three states and solve for the holdings of available assets that reproduce it; the cost of the replicating portfolio is the only arbitrage-free price.

items.name: Forward prices by cost of carry
