items.pic: Buy the asset and borrow, or enter a forward: payoffs at expiry match only when F = S·e^{(r−q)T}; misprice the forward and a cash-and-carry arbitrage table appears.

items.name: Futures, margin and marking to market
items.pic: Daily settlement of a futures position over a volatile month: the margin account rises and falls, and a margin call is triggered when it hits the maintenance level.

items.name: Minimum-variance hedge ratio
items.pic: Hedge jet fuel with heating-oil futures: hedged-portfolio variance against hedge ratio is a parabola whose minimum is at ρσ_S/σ_F, computed from the scatter.

items.name: Covered interest parity
items.pic: Invest at home, or convert, invest abroad and sell the proceeds forward: the two routes give equal returns at the parity forward rate, and post-2008 deviations are plotted.

items.name: Interest-rate swaps as bond portfolios
items.pic: A fixed-for-floating swap drawn as arrows of cash flows; valuing it as a long fixed bond and short floating bond shows the swap rate that gives zero initial value.

items.name: Fundamental theorem of asset pricing
items.pic: Two assets and three states: the set of payoffs costing nothing is separated from the positive orthant by a hyperplane exactly when there is no arbitrage, and its normal vector gives positive state prices.

items.name: Modigliani–Miller proposition I
items.pic: Slice a firm’s cash flows into debt and equity in different proportions: the pie’s total value is unchanged, and an investor undoes any leverage by homemade borrowing.

items.name: Modigliani–Miller proposition II
items.pic: Raise the debt-to-equity ratio: the cost of equity rises linearly, the cost of debt stays fixed until default risk appears, and the weighted average stays flat.

items.name: Taxes, distress and the trade-off theory
items.pic: Add the debt tax shield and expected bankruptcy costs: firm value as a function of leverage becomes a hump, with its maximum marking the optimal capital structure.

items.name: The Cost of Capital, Corporation Finance and Investment
items.pic: Two firms with the same operating income, one of them levered: if the levered firm’s shares trade too high, an investor sells them and rebuilds the same income by borrowing personally and buying the unlevered firm (homemade leverage), so the values equalize; slide the debt–equity ratio and watch the cost of equity rise linearly while the overall cost of capital stays flat, then compare with their cross-sections of electric utilities and oil companies, where it does not fall with leverage either.

chapters.title: Repeated games and cooperation
chapters.summary: Repetition lets players reward and punish, so cooperation that is irrational in a one-shot Prisoner’s Dilemma can be sustained by trigger strategies when players value the future enough. Finite repetition unravels by backward induction unless a little doubt about rationality is allowed. The folk theorem describes everything that patient players can sustain, which explains tacit collusion; tournaments and spatial models show how reciprocal strategies fare among many.

refs: Osborne, An Introduction to Game Theory

items.name: Repeated games and discounted payoffs
items.pic: Play a stage game repeatedly against a chosen strategy; the stream of payoffs and its discounted average are tracked, with the discount factor δ on a slider.

items.name: The finitely repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma unravels
items.pic: Backward induction from the last round is animated: defection in round T makes round T − 1 a one-shot game, and so on to the first round.

items.name: Grim trigger and tit-for-tat
items.pic: Strategies are drawn as small automata; pairing any two (grim, tit-for-tat, always defect, pavlov) generates the resulting sequence of plays.

items.name: One-deviation principle
items.pic: Test a strategy profile by checking every single-period deviation at every history type; the app confirms that no longer deviation is profitable when no one-shot deviation is.

items.name: Cooperation in the infinitely repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma
items.pic: Slide δ and the stage payoffs; grim trigger is an equilibrium exactly when δ ≥ (T − R)/(T − P), shown as a threshold line that moves with the payoffs.

items.name: Folk theorem
items.pic: The feasible payoff set and the minmax point of a stage game are drawn; as δ → 1 every feasible strictly individually rational payoff is shaded as sustainable by a subgame perfect equilibrium.

items.name: Tacit collusion in repeated oligopoly
items.pic: Firms in a repeated Bertrand market sustain the monopoly price with trigger strategies; the critical discount factor 1 − 1/n is plotted against the number of firms.

items.name: Axelrod’s tournaments
items.pic: Enter strategies into a round-robin repeated Prisoner’s Dilemma with noise; scores are tabulated and an ecological simulation lets successful strategies multiply.

items.name: Spatial Prisoner’s Dilemma (Nowak–May)
items.pic: Players on a grid copy their most successful neighbour each round; clusters of cooperators survive and kaleidoscopic patterns form for intermediate temptation values.

items.name: Reputation in finitely repeated games (Kreps–Milgrom–Roberts–Wilson)
items.pic: Give one player a small prior probability of being a committed tit-for-tat type; equilibrium play cooperates for most of a long finite game, unravelling only near the end.

chapters.title: Social preferences and behavioral games
chapters.summary: In the lab people share money they could keep, reject offers they could accept, and pay to punish free riders. Models of inequity aversion and reciprocity capture these patterns, while level-k reasoning and noisy best responses explain why play in strategic games departs from Nash equilibrium. Incentives can even backfire when they crowd out intrinsic or social motives.

refs: Wilkinson & Klaes, An Introduction to Behavioral Economics

items.name: Ultimatum-game behaviour: low offers rejected
items.pic: Propose a split of $10 to simulated responders drawn from experimental data; offers below about 30% are often rejected, and your expected earnings by offer are plotted.

items.name: The dictator game
items.pic: Remove the right to reject: average giving drops but stays well above zero, and toggles for anonymity and “taking” options show how fragile the generosity is.

items.name: Public goods games with punishment (Fehr–Gächter)
items.pic: Ten rounds of contributions in a simulated group: without punishment contributions decay toward zero, with costly punishment they climb and stay high.

items.name: Inequity aversion (Fehr–Schmidt)
items.pic: Utility penalised by envy (α) and guilt (β); drag the parameters and see which ultimatum offers a responder rejects and what a proposer should offer.

items.name: The trust game and reciprocity
items.pic: Send money that triples in transit; simulated trustees return amounts drawn from experimental data, and the return per unit sent is plotted.

items.name: Level-k reasoning in the beauty contest
items.pic: Guess two-thirds of the average guess; a histogram of past responses shows spikes at 33 and 22 (level 1 and 2), far from the Nash answer of zero, and your guess is ranked.

items.name: Quantal response equilibrium
items.pic: Players choose by logit best responses with a precision slider; equilibrium choice probabilities move from uniform randomness at λ = 0 to Nash as λ grows, fitting lab data in between.

items.name: Motivation crowding out (the daycare fine)
items.pic: Late pickups per week at Israeli daycares before, during and after a fine: lateness rises once the fine is introduced and stays high after it is removed.

items.name: Ultimatum offers across fifteen societies
items.pic: Mean offers and rejection rates from the cross-cultural study plotted against market integration; the spread shows fairness norms vary widely between societies.

chapters.title: Colour vision
chapters.summary: A single cone class cannot tell wavelength from intensity, so colour needs comparisons: three cone types make colour three-dimensional, which is why lights with different spectra can match. The cone signals are then recoded into red–green and blue–yellow opponent channels, which explains hue cancellation, unique hues and afterimages. Constancy across illuminants is achieved, imperfectly, by adapting each channel — and when the illuminant is ambiguous, people can see the same image in different colours.

refs: Macmillan & Creelman, Detection Theory: A User’s Guide

items.name: The principle of univariance
items.pic: A single cone’s response to lights of different wavelength and intensity: find two lights it cannot tell apart, and add a second cone type to see the ambiguity resolved.

items.name: Metamers form the null space of the cone responses
items.pic: Edit a spectrum with control points; adding any spectrum from the null space of the 3-row cone matrix changes the curve but leaves the three cone readouts and the colour swatch unchanged.

items.name: Wavelength discrimination function
items.pic: Find the smallest wavelength step you can see at points along the spectrum; your Δλ curve dips where cone sensitivities cross and rises at the spectrum ends.

items.name: Hue cancellation (Hurvich–Jameson)
items.pic: Add green light to a yellowish-red until no red remains; repeating across wavelengths traces the red–green and blue–yellow opponent valence curves.

items.name: Unique hues
items.pic: Pick the yellow that is neither reddish nor greenish on a hue wheel; your unique yellow, blue and green are compared with a population distribution, which is surprisingly broad.

items.name: Zone model: cones feeding opponent channels
items.pic: A wiring diagram from L, M and S cones into L−M, S−(L+M) and L+M channels; drag a spectrum and watch all six signals, then knock out a cone to see which channel goes silent.

items.name: The McCollough effect
items.pic: Adapt to alternating red-horizontal and green-vertical gratings for a few minutes; black-and-white test gratings then look tinted by orientation, an aftereffect that can last for days.

items.name: Colour-vision tests: Ishihara plates and the anomaloscope
items.pic: Plates of coloured dots are rendered through simulated protan, deutan and tritan projections, so you see which numerals vanish for each deficiency; a Rayleigh-match slider mimics the anomaloscope.

items.name: #TheDress: disagreement about the illuminant
items.pic: One photograph, two interpretations: tell the page whether you assume warm or cool lighting and it discounts that illuminant, turning the same pixels white-gold or blue-black.

chapters.title: Diffusion, cascades and contagion
chapters.summary: Ideas, products and diseases spread through networks, but by different rules. Behaviours that need reinforcement from several neighbours spread as threshold cascades that tightly knit clusters can block, while diseases spread from single contacts and are helped by long-range ties and hubs. People also copy others because others’ choices carry information, which can lock a whole population into a wrong choice. Aggregate adoption often follows an S-curve that the Bass model describes.

refs: Easley & Kleinberg, Networks, Crowds, and Markets (free online)

items.name: Diffusion as a network coordination game
items.pic: Seed a few adopters of a new behaviour on a network; each node adopts when at least a fraction q of neighbours have, and the cascade either takes over or stalls as you vary q.

items.name: Dense clusters block cascades
items.pic: Paint a cluster where every node has more than 1 − q of its neighbours inside; the cascade stops at its edge, and the page proves the converse on graphs you draw.

items.name: Simple versus complex contagion (Centola)
items.pic: On a Watts–Strogatz network, a disease spreads faster as rewiring rises, while a two-neighbour-threshold behaviour spreads slower — two curves crossing over the rewiring axis.

items.name: Information cascades
items.pic: Agents in sequence get private signals and see predecessors’ choices; once two more choose one way than the other, everyone follows, and the page reports how often the cascade is wrong.

items.name: Herding in the urn experiment
items.pic: Guess which urn the balls come from after seeing your draw and others’ guesses; your choices are compared with the Bayesian posterior and the lab results of Anderson and Holt.

items.name: The Bass diffusion model
items.pic: Innovation (p) and imitation (q) sliders shape the adoption curve and the bell-shaped sales curve; fit p and q to historical TV or smartphone adoption.

items.name: S-curves and adopter categories (Rogers)
items.pic: Adoption times drawn as a normal curve split into innovators, early adopters, majorities and laggards, with the cumulative S-curve and the Bass fit overlaid.

items.name: Branching processes and the epidemic threshold
items.pic: Each case infects a random number of others with mean R; outbreak trees die out or explode, and the extinction probability is computed as R crosses one.

items.name: SIR epidemics on networks
items.pic: Run SIR on a lattice, a small world and a random network with equal transmission: final size and peak timing differ, compared with the well-mixed ODE curve.

items.name: Hubs, superspreaders and the vanishing threshold
items.pic: Effective R on a network is ⟨k²⟩/⟨k⟩ times transmissibility; growing a scale-free network shows the epidemic threshold sliding toward zero, and targeting hubs for vaccination restores it.

items.name: Random failure versus targeted attack
items.pic: Remove nodes at random or highest-degree first from a heavy-tailed network; the giant component barely shrinks under random removal and shatters under attack.

items.name: Influence maximization (independent cascades)
items.pic: Choose k seed nodes to maximize expected spread; the greedy algorithm’s picks and spread are compared with picking the highest-degree nodes, with its (1 − 1/e) guarantee drawn.

items.name: Network effects and tipping in markets
items.pic: Willingness to pay rises with the share of users; the demand curve crosses the price line twice, and a dynamic simulation shows the market dying below the tipping point and taking off above it.

items.name: The El Farol bar problem
items.pic: Agents with a toolbox of forecasting rules decide whether to go to a bar that is fun only if under 60% full; attendance fluctuates around 60 without anyone coordinating.

items.name: SIS epidemics and endemic infection
items.pic: Recovered individuals become susceptible again; above threshold the infected share settles at a nonzero endemic level, below it the infection dies out.

items.name: Concurrency and the timing of contacts
items.pic: The same set of partnerships run sequentially or overlapping in time; concurrency opens time-respecting paths and the outbreak size jumps, with the time-ordered paths highlighted.

items.name: Lock-in under increasing returns (Arthur)
items.pic: Adopters choose between two technologies whose payoff grows with installed base; repeated runs lock in to either one at random, as in a Pólya urn, regardless of which is better.

items.name: Genealogies coalesce: a recent common ancestor
items.pic: Trace maternal lines backwards in a fixed-size population; lineages merge until one remains, and the time to the common ancestor scales with population size as the coalescent predicts.

chapters.title: Electoral systems and party systems
chapters.summary: How votes become seats shapes how many parties there are. Single-member plurality districts reward the two largest parties and punish third parties, while proportional formulas translate vote shares into seat shares more faithfully. Political scientists measure the outcomes with the effective number of parties and disproportionality indices; Duverger’s law is a strong tendency with well-known exceptions rather than a law.

items.name: Single-member districts and proportional representation
items.pic: One national vote distribution counted two ways: district-by-district plurality and nationwide PR; the resulting parliaments are drawn as hemicycles side by side.

items.name: D’Hondt and Sainte-Laguë seat allocation
items.pic: A table of vote totals divided by 1, 2, 3… or 1, 3, 5…; seats go to the largest quotients in order, animated, with large parties favoured under D’Hondt.

items.name: Single transferable vote
items.pic: Multi-member STV with the Droop quota: surpluses of elected candidates and ballots of eliminated ones transfer fractionally until all seats fill.

items.name: Duverger’s law
items.pic: Simulated plurality elections with strategic voters: support for a third party drains away over repeated elections, while the same electorate under PR sustains several parties; real exceptions (India, Canada) are marked.

items.name: Cox’s M + 1 rule
items.pic: Vary district magnitude M: with strategic voters the number of viable candidates in equilibrium settles at M + 1, shown as vote shares collapsing onto that many.

items.name: Effective number of parties (Laakso–Taagepera)
items.pic: Drag vote shares and see 1/Σpᵢ² update: two equal parties give 2, a dominant party with many minnows gives less than 2.

items.name: The cube law of seats and votes
items.pic: Simulate plurality elections with normally distributed district swings; the seat-share curve S/(1−S) ≈ (V/(1−V))³ emerges, and its exponent changes with district heterogeneity.

items.name: Gallagher’s disproportionality index
items.pic: Bars of vote share and seat share per party for real elections; the index is the root-mean-square gap, ranked across electoral systems.

items.name: Mixed-member proportional systems
items.pic: District seats are topped up from party lists to match the PR total; overhang seats appear when a party wins more districts than its proportional share.

items.name: Les partis politiques
items.pic: Duverger’s mechanical and psychological effects taken apart: simulate plurality elections in single-member districts with three parties, first with sincere votes (the third party wins votes but almost no seats), then letting its voters desert to the nearer of the two leaders until two parties remain; switch to proportional representation and watch the third party survive.

chapters.title: Age structure and projection
chapters.summary: The age pyramid records a population’s history of births, deaths and migration, and it shapes the future: a young population keeps growing even after fertility falls to replacement. Cohort-component projection ages each cohort forward with survival rates and adds births; in matrix form it is the Leslie model, whose dominant eigenvalue and eigenvector govern long-run growth and structure. Projections today come with probability bands.

refs: Preston, Heuveline & Guillot, Demography: Measuring and Modeling Population Processes

items.name: The population pyramid
items.pic: Animated pyramids for Japan, Nigeria and France from 1950 to 2050; trace a cohort’s bar as it climbs the pyramid and see wars, booms and busts as notches.

items.name: Dependency ratios
items.pic: Shade the young, working-age and old parts of a pyramid; the dependency ratios update as you edit the pyramid or step through decades.

items.name: Cohort-component projection
items.pic: Step a population forward five years at a time: each bar shrinks by survival, shifts up, and new births fill the bottom bar; change the assumptions and see the pyramid in 2100.

items.name: The Leslie projection matrix for a human population
items.pic: The cohort-component step written as a matrix with fertility on the top row and survival on the subdiagonal; multiply it by the age vector and compare with the step-by-step projection.

items.name: Long-run growth is the dominant eigenvalue
items.pic: Project any starting pyramid with a fixed human Leslie matrix: the year-on-year growth factor converges to the dominant eigenvalue, with the second eigenvalue’s modulus setting the speed.

items.name: Strong ergodicity: populations forget their past
items.pic: Two wildly different pyramids under the same rates converge to the same proportional age structure; a distance-to-stable readout decays geometrically.

items.name: Population momentum
items.pic: Drop a young population’s fertility to replacement overnight: it keeps growing for decades as its large young cohorts pass through childbearing ages, ending perhaps 50% larger.

items.name: Keyfitz’s momentum formula
items.pic: Compare the simulated ultimate population after an instant fertility drop with Keyfitz’s closed-form estimate from b, e₀, R₀ and the mean age at childbearing, across many starting populations.

items.name: Baby booms and their echoes
items.pic: Insert a ten-year baby boom into a projection; its echo appears a generation later, damped and smeared by the spread of childbearing ages.

items.name: The demographic dividend
items.pic: As fertility falls the working-age share swells for a few decades before ageing sets in; the dividend window is shaded on the projected support ratio.

items.name: Probabilistic population projections
items.pic: Sample hundreds of fertility and mortality paths from a fitted model; the spaghetti of projected world populations becomes median and 80/95% bands, shown beside the old high/medium/low variants.

chapters.title: Harmony and the geometry of chords
chapters.summary: Chords are stacks of thirds with roots, functions and habitual successions, and voice leading is how their individual notes move from one chord to the next. Tymoczko’s geometry turns this into topology: the space of n-note chords is an orbifold, n-dimensional space folded by octave shifts and by permutations of the voices, where efficient voice leadings are short paths and nearly even chords sit near the centre. The neo-Riemannian operations, the Tonnetz and the circle of fifths reappear as lattices and loops inside these spaces. The chapter ends with the working vocabulary of tonal harmony: inversions and figured bass, cadences, the resolving dominant seventh, circle-of-fifths sequences, applied dominants, pivot-chord modulation and the jazz tritone substitution.

refs: Benson, Music: A Mathematical Offering (free online)
Rossing, Moore & Wheeler, The Science of Sound
Fletcher & Rossing, The Physics of Musical Instruments
Toussaint, The Geometry of Musical Rhythm

items.name: Triads and seventh chords
items.pic: Stack thirds on each scale degree to build major, minor, diminished and augmented triads and the common seventh chords, each drawn as a polygon on the pitch-class clock, labelled by quality and played.

items.name: Chord roots and the fundamental bass
items.pic: Play a triad in any inversion and voicing: a virtual-pitch model estimates its root from the pooled partials and draws Rameau’s fundamental bass beneath the progression, agreeing with the spelled root for major triads and wavering for minor ones.

items.name: Roman numerals and harmonic function (T, S, D)
items.pic: A transition graph of Roman-numeral chords with arrow widths taken from a chorale corpus; click to walk a progression and hear it, and watch the tonic → subdominant → dominant → tonic cycle emerge as the dominant flow.

items.name: Keys and key distance
items.pic: The twelve major keys around the circle of fifths with shared-note counts on each chord: neighbours share six of seven notes, so drag a modulation path and hear near keys slide while distant ones jolt.

items.name: Voice leading and its size
items.pic: Two chords on a staff and on the clock with an arrow per voice; drag voices to any assignment, read the size in taxicab, Euclidean or largest-move metrics, and let the diagram find and play the minimal voice leading.

items.name: Common-practice voice-leading rules
items.pic: A four-part chorale editable note by note: a checker flags parallel fifths and octaves, voice crossings and wide leaps as you drag, and the passage plays so you can hear what each rule protects.

items.name: Two-note chords live on a Möbius strip
items.pic: Fold the plane of (lower, upper) pitch pairs by octaves and by swapping voices and watch it become a Möbius strip with unisons along its edge; drag a dyad and follow voice leadings as paths, including ones that cross the twist.

items.name: Chord spaces are orbifolds
items.pic: Three-note chord space drawn as a triangular prism whose ends are glued with a twist: augmented triads run down the centre, major and minor triads circle them and clusters cling to the walls, and dragging a chord through it plays the chord.

items.name: Efficient voice leading needs nearly even chords
items.pic: For any chord the diagram finds the shortest voice leading to each of its transpositions: nearly even chords such as triads and seventh chords reach neighbours by tiny moves while clusters must leap, plotted against distance from the centre.

items.name: Neo-Riemannian P, L and R
items.pic: A triad on the clock with P, L and R buttons, each moving a single note by a semitone or whole tone to the parallel, leading-tone-exchange or relative triad; chain them and hear the smooth chromatic results.

items.name: The PLR group is dual to the T/I group
items.pic: The 24 major and minor triads as nodes of a dihedral Cayley graph with P, L and R edges; apply any transposition or inversion to the whole graph and verify live that it commutes with every P, L and R move.

items.name: The Tonnetz
items.pic: A triangular lattice of pitch classes with fifths along one axis and thirds along the others: triads are triangles, P, L and R are flips across their edges, a toggle wraps the lattice into a torus, and any path plays as a progression.

items.name: Hexatonic and octatonic cycles
items.pic: Alternate P and L to circle the six triads of a hexatonic cycle, or P and R through the eight of an octatonic one; each cycle is traced on the Tonnetz and the clock and played as a late-Romantic progression.

items.name: The circle of fifths as a voice-leading circle
items.pic: The twelve diatonic scales as points in scale space, each joined to two neighbours by moving one note a semitone; animate the moves and the circle of fifths reappears as the shortest voice-leading loop, the way triads circle the centre of the orbifold.

items.name: Chord inversion and figured bass
items.pic: Choose which chord tone sits in the bass and the figures 5/3, 6/3 or 6/4 (7, 6/5, 4/3 or 4/2 for a seventh chord) are computed from the intervals above it; type a figured bass line and hear it realized in four voices while the root stays the same.

items.name: Cadences
items.pic: End one phrase with V–I, IV–I, I–V or V–vi and hear authentic, plagal, half and deceptive cadences, with voice-leading arrows showing the leading tone rising to the tonic; move the final soprano note from degree 1 to degree 3 to turn a perfect authentic cadence into an imperfect one.

items.name: The dominant seventh and its resolution
items.pic: A V⁷ chord on the clock with its tritone highlighted: the third rises and the seventh falls by a semitone into the tonic triad, the minimal voice leading found by search, and inverting the chord shows the same tendency tones resolving in every position.

items.name: Circle-of-fifths progressions and sequences
items.pic: Roots falling by fifths through the diatonic triads I–IV–vii°–iii–vi–ii–V–I are traced on the circle of fifths and on the Tonnetz as the progression plays; transpose a two-chord model step by step to build a sequence and see the single diminished-fifth root move needed to stay in the key.

items.name: Applied dominants and tonicization
items.pic: Precede any diatonic triad with its own dominant (V/V, V/ii, V⁷/IV): the borrowed accidental lights on the keyboard, the target briefly sounds like a tonic, and the momentary key is marked on the circle of fifths.

items.name: Modulation by pivot chord
items.pic: The diatonic triads of two keys drawn as overlapping sets: the shared chords are the possible pivots, labelled with a Roman numeral in each key; pick one to write a modulation and hear it, and see that closely related keys offer several pivots while distant keys offer none.

items.name: Tritone substitution
items.pic: Two dominant seventh chords a tritone apart share the same tritone, which T₆ maps onto itself; swap one for the other in a ii–V–I and hear the bass slide down by semitones while the resolving third and seventh move exactly as before.

items.name: Traité de l’harmonie
items.pic: Rameau’s fundamental bass extracted live: the reader plays a progression with chords in any inversion, each chord is reduced to its root by stacking thirds, the roots form a second bass line under the music, and the cadences show the fundamental bass moving by fifths as Rameau claimed.

items.name: The Geometry of Musical Chords
items.pic: The paper’s chord spaces to walk in: two-note chords on a Möbius strip with unisons on its edge and tritones along its centre line, three-note chords in a twisted triangular prism with augmented triads on the axis; the reader drags a chord, sees voice leadings as paths whose length is their size, and finds that nearly even chords have the shortest moves to their transpositions.

chapters.title: Perceptual colour spaces and colour order
chapters.summary: Equal steps in XYZ are not equal steps to the eye. Colour-order systems such as Munsell’s organise colours by hue, value and chroma in perceptually even steps, and Hering’s opponent channels explain why no colour looks reddish-green. CIELAB combines both ideas into a space where distance approximates visible difference, which is what printers and paint mixers use every day.

refs: Conway, Burgiel & Goodman-Strauss, The Symmetries of Things

items.name: Hue, chroma and lightness
items.pic: Pick a colour and see it decomposed into hue angle, chroma and lightness; three sliders move it along each axis independently.

items.name: Lightness is a compressive function of luminance
items.pic: Arrange grey patches so the steps look equal: the luminances you chose follow roughly a cube root, plotted against the CIE L* curve.

items.name: The Munsell colour system
items.pic: Rotate Munsell’s colour tree: value up the trunk, hue around it, chroma outward, with its irregular outer surface showing that saturated yellows are light and blues dark.

items.name: MacAdam ellipses: chromaticity is not uniform
items.pic: Just-noticeable-difference ellipses drawn on the xy diagram, ten times enlarged: tiny in the blue corner, huge in the greens; switch to u′v′ and they become rounder.

items.name: CIELAB and CIELUV
items.pic: Convert XYZ to L*a*b* step by step (white normalisation, cube root, opponent differences) and see the ellipses redrawn far closer to circles.

items.name: Colour difference: from ΔE*ab to CIEDE2000
items.pic: Pick two patches and compare ΔE76 and ΔE2000 with your own judgement of how different they look, especially for saturated blues.

items.name: Opponent-process theory (Hering)
items.pic: Cone signals feed three channels (light–dark, red–green, yellow–blue): drag a colour and watch the channel bars, never both red and green at once.

items.name: Negative afterimages
items.pic: Stare at the centre of a coloured flag for 30 s, then at a white field: the afterimage appears in opponent colours, as predicted by adapting each channel.

items.name: Gamut mapping between screen and print
items.pic: Plot a photo’s colours in CIELAB against the sRGB and a CMYK gamut: out-of-gamut pixels are clipped or compressed, with three mapping strategies compared side by side.

chapters.title: Beams, columns and trusses
chapters.summary: A beam carries load by bending, with compression on one face and tension on the other, so material far from the middle does the most work. Columns fail by buckling long before crushing once they are slender. Trusses turn bending into axial forces in triangulated bars, and Maxwell’s counting rule and reciprocal diagrams make their analysis a matter of geometry.

items.name: The moment diagram is a funicular polygon
items.pic: Drag loads on a simply supported beam: its bending-moment diagram and the funicular polygon for the same loads are drawn together and coincide up to scale.

items.name: Structural depth and span-to-depth ratios
items.pic: Slide span and depth for a beam, a truss and an arch: required material and deflection are computed, explaining rules of thumb such as span/20 for beams and span/10 for trusses.

items.name: Form-active versus bending-active structures
items.pic: Span the same gap with a beam, a truss, an arch and a cable under the same load: the material each needs is computed, and the funicular forms win by an order of magnitude.

items.name: Galileo’s cantilever problem (1638)
items.pic: Galileo’s cantilever with a weight on the end: compare his assumption of a pivot at the bottom edge with the linear stress profile, which predicts one third of his breaking load.

items.name: Columns: from the classical orders to steel
items.pic: Line up Doric, Ionic, cast-iron and steel columns by slenderness: the buckling and crushing limits are drawn for each material, showing why stone columns are stocky and steel ones thin.

items.name: Maillart’s deck-stiffened arches
items.pic: A thin concrete arch braced by a stiff deck, as at Salginatobel: move a truck across and see the deck take the bending while the arch carries the thrust.

items.name: Triangulation and trusses
items.pic: Push on a square frame of pinned bars and it folds; add a diagonal and it locks; extend to a truss and see members coloured by tension and compression.

items.name: Funicular trusses: chords shaped to the moment
items.pic: Shape a truss’s bottom chord to the moment diagram of a uniform load: diagonal forces drop to zero, and a moving point load reintroduces them.

items.name: Maxwell–Cremona reciprocal diagrams
items.pic: A truss and its reciprocal force diagram side by side: every bar is parallel to its partner, whose length is the bar force; dragging a joint updates both.

items.name: Maxwell’s rule for rigid frameworks
items.pic: Add and remove bars in a planar framework: the count m = 2j − 3 is checked, and a flexing animation shows a mechanism whenever there are too few bars or they are badly placed.

items.name: Truss types: Pratt, Howe, Warren and bowstring
items.pic: Switch a bridge truss between types under the same load: which diagonals are in tension changes, and the total steel weight is compared.

items.name: Space frames and geodesic domes
items.pic: Subdivide an icosahedron and project to a sphere to make a geodesic dome; load one node and see forces spread through the triangulated net.

items.name: Cantilever bridges and the Forth Bridge model
items.pic: Recreate the 1887 human model of the Forth Bridge: two men as cantilevers, a suspended span between them, counterweights at the ends, with the load path traced.

items.name: Prestressed concrete
items.pic: Add a tensioned tendon low in a concrete beam: the stress diagram shifts so that tension under load is cancelled; raise the load until cracks appear.

items.name: On Reciprocal Figures and Diagrams of Forces
items.pic: A truss and its reciprocal figure: the reader drags the joints of a loaded roof truss and Maxwell’s reciprocal updates, each bar matched by a parallel line whose length is the bar’s force and each joint by a closed polygon, tension and compression coloured, and the external loads forming the load line.

chapters.title: Syntax: the structure of sentences
chapters.summary: Sentences are not strings but trees of constituents, as substitution and movement tests reveal. Phrase-structure rules generate these trees, recursion lets a finite grammar produce unboundedly many sentences, and limits of memory explain why some grammatical sentences are unusable. Natural languages sit just above the context-free level of the Chomsky hierarchy, and their constraints on movement and word order are among the deepest puzzles of the field.

refs: Fromkin, Rodman & Hyams, An Introduction to Language
Ladefoged & Johnson, A Course in Phonetics
Jurafsky & Martin, Speech and Language Processing (free draft)

items.name: Constituents and syntactic categories
items.pic: Bracket a sentence by dragging over words: proposed constituents are labelled NP, VP, PP, and crossing brackets are rejected.

items.name: Constituency tests
items.pic: Select a word string and apply substitution, clefting, movement and coordination: the sentence is rewritten for each test and you judge whether it remains grammatical.

items.name: Phrase-structure rules and syntax trees
items.pic: Edit a small grammar and type a sentence: the tree is drawn if the grammar derives it, and the derivation steps can be replayed.

items.name: Structural ambiguity
items.pic: “I saw the man with the telescope”: the parser returns both trees side by side, and a picture of each reading is shown.

items.name: Recursion and the infinitude of sentences
items.pic: Keep embedding: “the cat that the dog chased that the rat bit…” or “I think that you said that…”; the tree grows and the count of sentences up to length n explodes.

items.name: Centre embedding and the limits of memory
items.pic: Parse centre-embedded sentences with a pushdown stack shown live: right-branching versions need one stack cell, centre-embedded ones need more, and comprehension collapses at depth three.

items.name: Garden-path sentences
items.pic: “The horse raced past the barn fell”: a left-to-right parser commits to the main-verb reading, fails at “fell”, and backtracks; reading-time data are overlaid.

items.name: The Chomsky hierarchy and natural language
items.pic: Place language patterns — a*b*, aⁿbⁿ, nested and crossed dependencies — on the hierarchy, with the weakest machine that recognises each.

items.name: Swiss German is not context-free (Shieber)
items.pic: Swiss German verb clusters: link each noun to its verb and the links cross; intersecting with a regular language yields a non-context-free pattern.

items.name: X-bar theory: heads, complements, specifiers
items.pic: Build NP, VP, PP and AP with one shared template: head, complement and specifier slots light up, and switching head direction reorders the tree for Japanese.

items.name: Dependency grammar
items.pic: Convert a constituency tree into head–dependent arcs and back: arcs are labelled with relations, and non-projective crossings are highlighted.

items.name: Movement and wh-questions
items.pic: Form a question from a statement: the wh-word moves to the front, leaving a gap in the tree, and an arrow links filler and gap.

items.name: Island constraints (Ross)
items.pic: Try to question different positions in a sentence: extraction from complex noun phrases, coordinate structures and subjects is blocked, and the island boundary is drawn.

items.name: Word-order typology and Greenberg’s universals
items.pic: A world map of SOV, SVO, VSO and other orders, with a cross-tab showing implicational universals, e.g. verb-object languages tend to have prepositions.

items.name: CKY parsing
items.pic: Fill the CKY chart cell by cell for a sentence and a grammar in Chomsky normal form; ambiguous sentences end with several analyses in the top cell.

items.name: Syntactic Structures
items.pic: Chomsky’s three models side by side: a finite-state (Markov) generator, a phrase-structure grammar and a transformational rule; the reader sees why “Colorless green ideas sleep furiously” is grammatical yet improbable, why nested either–or and if–then dependencies defeat any finite-state machine, and applies the passive and question transformations to a phrase-structure tree.

chapters.title: Decision theory and its puzzles
chapters.summary: A decision problem pairs acts with states of the world and outcomes. Under ignorance there are several reasonable rules — maximin, minimax regret, insufficient reason — and they disagree. Under risk, expected-utility theory is the standard, and its puzzles are among the liveliest in philosophy: infinite expectations, preferences that violate its axioms, and Newcomb’s problem, which splits evidential from causal decision theory.

refs: Resnik, Choices: An Introduction to Decision Theory

items.name: Decision matrices: acts, states and outcomes
items.pic: Edit a table of payoffs for acts against states: the tool flags dominated acts and computes what each decision rule recommends.

items.name: Dominance
items.pic: Strike out acts that are no better in any state and worse in some; then make the states depend on the act and watch dominance reasoning go wrong.

items.name: Maximin, maximax and the Hurwicz index
items.pic: Slide an optimism index α from 0 (maximin) to 1 (maximax): the recommended act changes at computed thresholds.

items.name: Minimax regret (Savage)
items.pic: Convert the payoff table to a regret table and choose the act with the smallest maximum regret; adding an irrelevant act can change the choice.

items.name: Principle of insufficient reason
items.pic: Assign equal probabilities to the states and maximise the average; repartitioning the same states changes the probabilities and the answer.

items.name: Expected-utility maximisation
items.pic: Assign probabilities and utilities: each act’s expected utility is a weighted bar, and a sensitivity plot shows where the best act switches.

items.name: Risk aversion from concave utility (Bernoulli)
items.pic: Switch utility from linear to logarithmic: the St Petersburg game’s expected utility becomes finite, and a certainty-equivalent readout shows what a player would pay.

items.name: The sure-thing principle and the Allais choices
items.pic: Restate the Allais lotteries as tickets in a 100-ticket draw: the tickets on which both options agree are greyed out, and the sure-thing principle says they should not affect your choice.

items.name: Ambiguity and imprecise credences (Ellsberg)
items.pic: Represent belief about the unknown urn by a set of probabilities rather than one: maximin expected utility over the set reproduces the Ellsberg choices that no single prior fits.

items.name: Pascal’s wager
items.pic: A 2×2 matrix of belief and existence with an infinite payoff: any positive probability makes wagering win, until rival gods or mixed strategies are added.

items.name: Pascal’s mugging
items.pic: A mugger promises a payoff that grows faster than your credence shrinks: expected value favours paying, unless utilities are bounded, shown by a toggle.

items.name: Newcomb’s problem
items.pic: Simulate a predictor of adjustable accuracy against one-boxers and two-boxers: one-boxers walk away richer on average, while two-boxing dominates in every fixed state.

items.name: Evidential versus causal decision theory
items.pic: Compute both theories’ recommendations in Newcomb, the smoking lesion and a medical case; a causal diagram shows which correlations each theory conditions on.

items.name: Kavka’s toxin puzzle
items.pic: A timeline: you are paid at midnight for intending to drink a mild toxin tomorrow; the decision tree shows why intending is rational but drinking is not.

items.name: Buridan’s ass
items.pic: An ass between two haybales: as its position varies continuously, the intermediate value theorem forces some starting point where it cannot decide in bounded time.

items.name: Newcomb’s Problem and Two Principles of Choice
items.pic: Nozick’s two principles in conflict: the reader sets the predictor’s accuracy and the contents of the boxes, the dominance argument (taking both boxes always adds $1,000) and the expected-utility argument (one box wins once accuracy exceeds 50.05%) are computed side by side, and a simulated population of one-boxers and two-boxers shows who walks away richer.

chapters.title: Lenses, printing and gunpowder
chapters.summary: Ground glass lenses gave old eyes their sight back and, combined in tubes, revealed moons of Jupiter and microbes. Movable type, oil-based ink, paper and the screw press combined into Gutenberg’s printing system, which made books cheap enough to change how knowledge spread. Gunpowder reshaped warfare, and the barometer and air pump revealed the atmospheric pressure the steam engine would exploit.

refs: Cardwell, Wheels, Clocks, and Rockets: A History of Technology
Usher, A History of Mechanical Inventions

items.name: Spectacles
items.pic: Model a presbyopic eye focusing on a page: the near point recedes with age, and a convex lens of the right power brings the image back onto the retina.

items.name: Woodblock printing
items.pic: Carve a mirror-image block and print: compare carving time per page with copying by hand as the print run grows.

items.name: Movable type in East Asia
items.pic: Typeset a page from a case of reusable characters: the number of distinct sorts needed for Chinese versus an alphabet is shown as a growth curve.

items.name: Gutenberg’s printing press
items.pic: Step through the system: cast type in a hand mould, compose, ink with oil-based ink, and press with a screw; pages per hour and cost per book are tracked.

items.name: The printing revolution
items.pic: Book output in Europe on a log scale before and after 1450 with book prices falling: drag the start date to see the curve bend at Gutenberg.

items.name: The telescope
items.pic: Combine a weak convex objective and a strong eyepiece: magnification is the ratio of focal lengths, and the moons of Jupiter appear as you raise it.

items.name: The microscope
items.pic: Compare a compound microscope of the 1600s with van Leeuwenhoek’s tiny single lens: magnification and aberrations are computed, and his lens wins on resolution.

items.name: The reflecting telescope and the achromat
items.pic: White starlight through a single lens splits into coloured foci; switch to a mirror (Newton) or a crown–flint doublet (Dollond) and the foci merge.

items.name: Gunpowder
items.pic: Vary the proportions of saltpetre, charcoal and sulphur: burn rate and gas volume peak near the classic 75:15:10 mix.

items.name: Cannon and firearms
items.pic: Fire a ball from barrels of different length: gas pressure acting along the bore sets muzzle velocity, and the trajectory is integrated with drag.

items.name: The barometer and the air pump
items.pic: Invert a mercury tube: the column stops at about 76 cm whatever its length; pump air from Magdeburg hemispheres and the force needed to separate them grows with area.

items.name: The Printing Press as an Agent of Change
items.pic: Eisenstein’s effects of print made measurable: the reader follows a text through generations of hand copying, where errors accumulate and copies drift apart, and through printed editions, where identical copies spread, errata are corrected in later editions and scattered sources can be collated side by side, with the count of surviving editions per decade after 1450 climbing alongside.

chapters.title: Farming and the first states
chapters.summary: After the last ice age, farming was invented independently in several regions and spread outward. Its spread across Europe advanced at about a kilometre a year, close to what a reaction–diffusion model of growing, wandering farmers predicts, and ancient DNA shows that farmers themselves moved, not just ideas. Farming fed more people at the cost of health, and dense populations gave rise to cities, writing and states.

items.name: The Holocene and the Younger Dryas
items.pic: Greenland temperature over the last 20,000 years: an abrupt cold snap about 12,900 years ago, then the unusually stable Holocene in which farming began.

items.name: Independent centres of domestication
items.pic: A world map of domestication centres with dates and crops — Fertile Crescent, China, New Guinea, Mesoamerica, the Andes, Africa — and the spread from each.

items.name: Farming spreads as a wave of advance
items.pic: Fisher–KPP on a map of Europe with sliders for growth rate and dispersal: the front’s speed approaches 2√(rD) and is compared with the observed advance.

items.name: Neolithic radiocarbon dates trace the front
items.pic: Earliest farming dates at European sites against distance from the Near East: a regression slope of roughly one kilometre per year (Ammerman and Cavalli-Sforza).

items.name: Demic versus cultural diffusion
items.pic: Mix migrating farmers and converting foragers in the wave model: the genetic gradient left behind differs, and ancient-DNA ancestry proportions decide between them.

items.name: Continental axes and the spread of crops (contested)
items.pic: Compare spread rates of crops along east–west and north–south routes, with latitude bands shaded: the data partly support and partly complicate Diamond’s claim.

items.name: The Neolithic demographic transition
items.pic: The fraction of juveniles in cemeteries rises after farming arrives, signalling higher fertility, while skeletal stature and dental health decline.

items.name: Indo-European expansion: farmers or herders?
items.pic: Overlay Anatolian-farmer and steppe-herder expansion fronts with language-tree root ages and ancient-DNA ancestry maps to see which fits each region.

items.name: Cities, writing and the first states
items.pic: Uruk’s growth on a timeline beside the first administrative tablets, monumental buildings and population estimates for the largest cities over 5,000 years.

items.name: Settlement scaling with population
items.pic: Settlement area against population for ancient and modern towns on log–log axes: the slope below 1 shows denser living in bigger places, with fitted exponents for each dataset.

items.name: The sizes of empires over time
items.pic: Area of the largest empires since 3000 BCE on a log axis (after Taagepera): growth curves for each empire and the rising envelope across them.

items.name: Measuring the Rate of Spread of Early Farming in Europe
items.pic: The paper’s regression made live: radiocarbon dates of the earliest farming sites across Europe are plotted against distance from a Near Eastern origin, the fitted slope gives about one kilometre per year, and the reader moves the origin or drops sites to see how the rate changes, then compares it with the speed of a wave of advance driven by population growth and local migration.
